title: On the Distribution of the Number of Local Minima of a Random Function on a Graph

abstract: We analyze the "query by committee" algorithm, a method for fil(cid:173) tering informative queries from a random stream of inputs. We show that if the two-member committee algorithm achieves infor(cid:173) mation gain with positive lower bound, then the prediction error decreases exponentially with the number of queries. We show that, in particular, this exponential decrease holds for query learning of thresholded smooth functions.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes query by committee, a learning method that selects informative queries from a randomly arriving stream of inputs. Its focus is the relationship between the information obtained from those selected queries and the resulting prediction error. This asks how much learning progress can be attributed to the queries the algorithm chooses.

For a committee with two members, the authors establish a conditional guarantee. If its information gain has a positive lower bound, prediction error decreases exponentially as the number of queries grows. The lower-bound condition means that the relevant information gain remains bounded away from zero, providing the continuing informativeness required by the result.

The authors also show that this exponential decrease applies when learning thresholded smooth functions through queries. This supplies a particular setting where the general information-based guarantee holds. The result concerns error relative to the number of queries, making it a statement about the effectiveness of selective querying and the conditions that support rapid improvement.
summary.tldr: Two-member query by committee achieves exponentially decreasing prediction error when its information gain stays positively bounded.

title: Information, Prediction, and Query by Committee

abstract: This paper describes a technique for learning both the number of states and the topology of Hidden Markov Models from examples. The induction process starts with the most specific model consistent with the training data and generalizes by successively merging states. Both the choice of states to merge and the stopping criterion are guided by the Bayesian posterior probability. paragraphs: This paper learns the structure of a hidden Markov model from example sequences. An HMM uses probabilistic transitions between hidden states and probabilistic generation of outputs. Instead of selecting the number of states and their connections by hand, the proposed method learns both of these structural choices alongside the model.

The procedure starts with the most specific model consistent with the training data. It then generalizes by repeatedly merging states. Bayesian posterior probability guides which states to combine and when to stop, providing one criterion for both the individual changes and the final model. Learning therefore proceeds by simplifying an initially highly specific account of the observations.

The authors compare this approach with Baum-Welch estimation for fixed-size models. They report cases where model merging produces minimal HMMs while fixed-model estimation fails to converge or needs redundant parameters to converge. The result highlights the value of learning structural choices directly: changing which states exist can matter as much as estimating probabilities within a predetermined structure.
summary.tldr: Bayesian state merging learns HMM size and connectivity, finding minimal models in cases that challenge fixed-size Baum-Welch estimation.

title: Hidden Markov Model Induction by Bayesian Model Merging

abstract: We consider the problem of how the CNS learns to control dynam(cid:173) ics of a mechanical system. By using a paradigm where a subject's hand interacts with a virtual mechanical environment, we show that learning control is via composition of a model of the imposed dynamics. Some properties of the computational elements with which the CNS composes this model are inferred through the gen(cid:173) eralization capabilities of the subject outside the training data.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of how the CNS learns to control dynam(cid:173) ics of a mechanical system. By using a paradigm where a subject's hand interacts with a virtual mechanical environment, we show that learning control is via composition of a model of the imposed dynamics. Some properties of the computational elements with which the CNS composes this model are inferred through the gen(cid:173) eralization capabilities of the subject outside the training data.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how the central nervous system learns to control a mechanical system. Its experimental setting lets a person's hand interact with a virtual mechanical environment. This provides a way to study adaptation to imposed dynamics: the relationship between movement and the mechanical effects the person experiences while interacting with the environment.

The authors report that learning proceeds by composing a model of those dynamics. In this account, adaptation involves computational elements that together represent the mechanical behavior being controlled. The question therefore extends beyond whether a person improves with practice to how the nervous system builds the representation supporting that improvement.

To investigate those elements, the authors examine performance outside the training data. How learning generalizes provides evidence about the components used to construct the model. Transfer to untrained situations becomes a way to probe the organization of the learned controller. The stated result links behavioral adaptation to model composition and uses generalization to infer properties of the underlying computation.
summary.tldr: Human adaptation to a virtual mechanical environment suggests that the nervous system composes a dynamics model whose elements can be probed through generalization.

title: Computational Elements of the Adaptive Controller of the Human Arm

abstract: A stability criterion for dynamic parameter adaptation is given. In the case of the learning rate of backpropagation, a class of stable algorithms is presented and studied, including a convergence proof.
originalAbstract: A stability criterion for dynamic parameter adaptation is given. In the case of the learning rate of backpropagation, a class of stable algorithms is presented and studied, including a convergence proof.
title: Stable Dynamic Parameter Adaption

abstract: We introduce a constructive, incremental learning system for regression problems that models data by means of locally linear experts. In contrast to other approaches, the experts are trained independently and do not compete for data during learning. Only when a prediction for a query is required do the experts cooperate by blending their individual predic(cid:173) tions. Each expert is trained by minimizing a penalized local cross vali(cid:173) dation error using second order methods. In this way, an expert is able to find a local distance metric by adjusting the size and shape of the recep(cid:173) tive field in which its predictions are valid, and also to detect relevant in(cid:173) put features by adjusting its bias on the importance of individual input dimensions. We derive asymptotic results for our method. In a variety of simulations the properties of the algorithm are demonstrated with respect to interference, learning speed, prediction accuracy, feature detection, and task oriented incremental learning.

paragraphs: This paper introduces an incremental regression system made of locally linear experts. Each expert learns independently, without competing with the others for training data. Cooperation happens when a prediction is requested: the system blends the experts' individual outputs. This separates the process of learning local models from the process of combining their answers.

Each expert minimizes a penalized local cross-validation error using second-order optimization. It adjusts the size and shape of the region where its predictions apply, effectively learning its own local distance measure. It also adjusts the importance assigned to individual input dimensions, allowing it to detect features relevant to its prediction task.

The authors derive asymptotic results and use simulations to examine interference, learning speed, accuracy, feature detection, and task-oriented incremental learning. The approach matters because each local predictor can adapt both its fitted relationship and its definition of locality. Blending then brings these separately developed views together when the system needs to answer a specific query.
summary.tldr: Independent local experts learn their own relevant features and regions, then cooperate by blending predictions.

title: From Isolation to Cooperation: An Alternative View of a System of Experts

abstract: Many algorithms for approximate reinforcement learning are not known to converge. In fact, there are counterexamples showing that the adjustable weights in some algorithms may oscillate within a region rather than converging to a point. This paper shows that, for two popular algorithms, such oscillation is the worst that can happen: the weights cannot diverge, but instead must converge to a bounded region. The algorithms are SARSA(O) and V(O); the latter algorithm was used in the well-known TD-Gammon program.
originalAbstract: Many algorithms for approximate reinforcement learning are not known to converge. In fact, there are counterexamples showing that the adjustable weights in some algorithms may oscillate within a region rather than converging to a point. This paper shows that, for two popular algorithms, such oscillation is the worst that can happen: the weights cannot diverge, but instead must converge to a bounded region. The algorithms are SARSA(O) and V(O); the latter algorithm was used in the well-known TD-Gammon program.

paragraphs: Approximate reinforcement learning uses adjustable weights to represent quantities needed for learning. Whether those weights settle into stable behavior is an important theoretical question. The paper starts from the observation that convergence is unknown for many algorithms, and that counterexamples already show some weights can keep oscillating instead of approaching a single point.

The authors establish a weaker but meaningful form of convergence for SARSA(0) and V(0). For these two algorithms, the weights cannot diverge without bound; they must approach a bounded region. Persistent oscillation within a region is therefore the worst behavior covered by the stated result, even when convergence to one weight vector does not occur.

This separates two different concerns: failure to settle at a point and uncontrolled growth of the weights. The theorem rules out the latter for the algorithms addressed while allowing the former. The abstract identifies V(0) as an algorithm used in TD-Gammon, connecting the theoretical question to an established application. The contribution is a boundedness guarantee, rather than a claim of convergence to a single solution.
summary.tldr: For SARSA(0) and V(0), approximate-learning weights approach a bounded region even if they continue oscillating.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Function Approximation Converges to a Region

abstract: In [1] we introduced a linear statistical model of joint color changes in images due to variation in lighting and certain non-geometric camera pa- rameters. We did this by measuring the mappings of colors in one image of a scene to colors in another image of the same scene under different lighting conditions. Here we increase the ﬂexibility of this color ﬂow model by allowing ﬂow coefﬁcients to vary according to a low order polynomial over the image. This allows us to better ﬁt smoothly vary- ing lighting conditions as well as curved surfaces without endowing our model with too much capacity. We show results on image matching and shadow removal and detection.
originalAbstract: In [1] we introduced a linear statistical model of joint color changes in images due to variation in lighting and certain non-geometric camera pa- rameters. We did this by measuring the mappings of colors in one image of a scene to colors in another image of the same scene under different lighting conditions. Here we increase the ﬂexibility of this color ﬂow model by allowing ﬂow coefﬁcients to vary according to a low order polynomial over the image. This allows us to better ﬁt smoothly vary- ing lighting conditions as well as curved surfaces without endowing our model with too much capacity. We show results on image matching and shadow removal and detection.

paragraphs: Images of the same scene can have different colors because lighting and certain camera settings change. The authors previously modeled these joint color changes statistically by measuring mappings between colors in paired images of a scene. This paper extends that color-flow model to handle changes that vary across different positions in an image.

The extension allows the color-flow coefficients to follow a low-order polynomial over image position. Instead of requiring the same coefficients everywhere, the model can express smooth spatial variation. This gives it greater flexibility for smoothly changing illumination and curved surfaces, while the low-order form keeps the additional capacity controlled.

The authors show results for image matching, shadow removal, and shadow detection. These applications use the model's treatment of appearance changes caused by lighting. The main contribution is a structured increase in spatial flexibility: color transformations can vary across an image without making that variation unrestricted, allowing the model to better fit the stated lighting and surface conditions.
summary.tldr: Spatially varying color-flow coefficients improve modeling of smooth lighting changes, with demonstrations in image matching and shadow processing.

title: Unsupervised Color Constancy

abstract: A population of neurons typically exhibits a broad diversity of responses to sensory inputs. The intuitive notion of functional classiﬁcation is that cells can be clustered so that most of the diversity is captured by the iden- tity of the clusters rather than by individuals within clusters. We show how this intuition can be made precise using information theory, with- out any need to introduce a metric on the space of stimuli or responses. Applied to the retinal ganglion cells of the salamander, this approach re- covers classical results, but also provides clear evidence for subclasses beyond those identiﬁed previously. Further, we ﬁnd that each of the gan- glion cells is functionally unique, and that even within the same subclass only a few spikes are needed to reliably distinguish between cells.

The intuitive notion of functional classiﬁcation is that cells can be clustered so that most of the diversity is captured by the iden- tity of the clusters rather than by individuals within clusters. We show how this intuition can be made precise using information theory, with- out any need to introduce a metric on the space of stimuli or responses. paragraphs: Neurons can respond very differently to the same sensory input, raising the question of how to group them by function. The paper formalizes a useful intuition: a good classification should explain much of this response diversity through the group a neuron belongs to, while leaving less diversity among neurons within each group.

The authors express this objective using information theory. Their approach does not require a predefined distance measure between stimuli or between responses. This matters because deciding what counts as a similar response can otherwise become a separate modeling choice that shapes the resulting groups before classification even begins.

Applied to salamander retinal ganglion cells, the method recovers established classifications and supplies clear evidence for additional subclasses. Yet group membership does not erase individual differences: the authors find that every recorded ganglion cell is functionally distinctive, with only a few spikes needed to distinguish cells reliably even within a subclass. The results support both useful categories and meaningful individuality.
summary.tldr: Information-theoretic clustering identifies established and additional retinal neuron subclasses while revealing distinctive responses within each subclass.

title: An Information Theoretic Approach to the Functional Classification of Neurons

abstract: Greedy importance sampling is an unbiased estimation technique that re- duces the variance of standard importance sampling by explicitly search- ing for modes in the estimation objective. Previous work has demon- strated the feasibility of implementing this method and proved that the technique is unbiased in both discrete and continuous domains. In this paper we present a reformulation of greedy importance sampling that eliminates the free parameters from the original estimator, and introduces a new regularization strategy that further reduces variance without com- promising unbiasedness. The resulting estimator is shown to be effective for difﬁcult estimation problems arising in Markov random ﬁeld infer- ence. In particular, improvements are achieved over standard MCMC estimators when the distribution has multiple peaked modes.

Previous work has demon- strated the feasibility of implementing this method and proved that the technique is unbiased in both discrete and continuous domains. In this paper we present a reformulation of greedy importance sampling that eliminates the free parameters from the original estimator, and introduces a new regularization strategy that further reduces variance without com- promising unbiasedness. The resulting estimator is shown to be effective for difﬁcult estimation problems arising in Markov random ﬁeld infer- ence. In particular, improvements are achieved over standard MCMC estimators when the distribution has multiple peaked modes.

paragraphs: Greedy importance sampling is an estimation method that searches explicitly for modes in the estimation objective. This search reduces variance relative to standard importance sampling while preserving unbiasedness. The paper builds on earlier work that established feasibility and unbiasedness in both discrete and continuous domains.

The authors reformulate the estimator to remove the free parameters in its original version. They also introduce regularization that further reduces variance without sacrificing unbiasedness. These are distinct benefits: eliminating free parameters simplifies the estimator's specification, while variance reduction makes its estimates less variable without changing their expected target.

The resulting method is shown to work effectively on difficult estimation problems in Markov random field inference. In particular, the authors report improvements over standard Markov chain Monte Carlo estimators when distributions contain multiple sharply peaked modes. That setting is central to the stated finding because the method explicitly searches for modes. The contribution combines a simpler formulation with a regularization strategy that retains the estimator's unbiased character.
summary.tldr: A reformulated greedy importance sampler removes free parameters and reduces variance through regularization while preserving unbiasedness.

title: Regularized Greedy Importance Sampling

abstract: We investigate the problem of learning a classiﬂcation task for datasets which are described by matrices. Rows and columns of these matrices correspond to objects, where row and column ob- jects may belong to diﬁerent sets, and the entries in the matrix express the relationships between them. We interpret the matrix el- ements as being produced by an unknown kernel which operates on object pairs and we show that - under mild assumptions - these ker- nels correspond to dot products in some (unknown) feature space. Minimizing a bound for the generalization error of a linear classi- ﬂer which has been obtained using covering numbers we derive an objective function for model selection according to the principle of structural risk minimization. The new objective function has the advantage that it allows the analysis of matrices which are not pos- itive deﬂnite, and not even symmetric or square. We then consider the case that row objects are interpreted as features. We suggest an additional constraint, which imposes sparseness on the row objects and show, that the method can then be used for feature selection. Finally, we apply this method to data obtained from DNA microar- rays, where \column" objects correspond to samples, \row" objects correspond to genes and matrix elements correspond to expression levels. Benchmarks are conducted using standard one-gene classiﬂ- cation and support vector machines and K-nearest neighbors after standard feature selection. Our new method extracts a sparse set of genes and provides superior classiﬂcation results.

paragraphs: The paper studies classification when data arrive as a matrix of relationships between row objects and column objects. These objects may come from different sets. The authors interpret each entry as the output of an unknown kernel and show that, under mild assumptions, these kernels correspond to dot products in an unknown feature space.

They derive a model-selection objective by minimizing a generalization-error bound based on covering numbers. This follows structural risk minimization and permits matrices that are not positive definite, symmetric, or even square. When rows represent features, an additional sparsity constraint turns the same framework into a feature-selection method.

The authors apply the method to DNA microarray data, with genes as rows, samples as columns, and expression levels as entries. Their method selects a sparse set of genes and achieves superior classification results in the reported benchmarks. Those comparisons include single-gene classification and support vector machines and nearest neighbors following standard feature selection. The findings connect the general matrix framework to compact feature sets in this application.
summary.tldr: A generalization-bound objective supports classification on general relationship matrices and sparse gene selection with strong reported benchmark results.

title: Feature Selection and Classification on Matrix Data: From Large Margins to Small Covering Numbers

abstract: We exploit some useful properties of Gaussian process (GP) regression models for reinforcement learning in continuous state spaces and dis- crete time. We demonstrate how the GP model allows evaluation of the value function in closed form. The resulting policy iteration algorithm is demonstrated on a simple problem with a two dimensional state space. Further, we speculate that the intrinsic ability of GP models to charac- terise distributions of functions would allow the method to capture entire distributions over future values instead of merely their expectation, which has traditionally been the focus of much of reinforcement learning.
originalAbstract: We exploit some useful properties of Gaussian process (GP) regression models for reinforcement learning in continuous state spaces and dis- crete time. We demonstrate how the GP model allows evaluation of the value function in closed form. The resulting policy iteration algorithm is demonstrated on a simple problem with a two dimensional state space. Further, we speculate that the intrinsic ability of GP models to charac- terise distributions of functions would allow the method to capture entire distributions over future values instead of merely their expectation, which has traditionally been the focus of much of reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: The paper applies Gaussian process regression to reinforcement learning with continuous states and discrete time steps. Its focus is the value function, which describes expected future value and supports policy improvement. The authors investigate how properties of the Gaussian process model can make this part of the learning procedure analytically manageable.

They show that the model permits value-function evaluation in closed form and use this result in a policy-iteration algorithm. The algorithm is demonstrated on a simple problem with a two-dimensional state space. This establishes a concrete example of the proposed connection between probabilistic regression and repeated policy evaluation and improvement.

The authors also suggest a broader possibility: Gaussian processes describe distributions over functions, which might allow a method to represent entire distributions of future values instead of only expectations. They explicitly present this as speculation. The demonstrated contribution is the closed-form evaluation and policy-iteration example; representing full future-value distributions is a proposed direction motivated by the model’s probabilistic structure.
summary.tldr: Gaussian process regression enables closed-form value-function evaluation in a policy-iteration method demonstrated on a simple continuous-state problem.

title: Gaussian Processes in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We present a competitive analysis of some non-parametric Bayesian al- gorithms in a worst-case online learning setting, where no probabilistic assumptions about the generation of the data are made. We consider models which use a Gaussian process prior (over the space of all func- tions) and provide bounds on the regret (under the log loss) for com- monly used non-parametric Bayesian algorithms — including Gaussian regression and logistic regression — which show how these algorithms can perform favorably under rather general conditions. These bounds ex- plicitly handle the inﬁnite dimensionality of these non-parametric classes in a natural way. We also make formal connections to the minimax and minimum description length (MDL) framework. Here, we show precisely how Bayesian Gaussian regression is a minimax strategy.
originalAbstract: We present a competitive analysis of some non-parametric Bayesian al- gorithms in a worst-case online learning setting, where no probabilistic assumptions about the generation of the data are made. We consider models which use a Gaussian process prior (over the space of all func- tions) and provide bounds on the regret (under the log loss) for com- monly used non-parametric Bayesian algorithms — including Gaussian regression and logistic regression — which show how these algorithms can perform favorably under rather general conditions. These bounds ex- plicitly handle the inﬁnite dimensionality of these non-parametric classes in a natural way. We also make formal connections to the minimax and minimum description length (MDL) framework. Here, we show precisely how Bayesian Gaussian regression is a minimax strategy.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes Bayesian learning algorithms in an online setting without making probabilistic assumptions about how the data are generated. Although the algorithms themselves use Gaussian process priors over functions, the evaluation asks how they perform on worst-case data sequences. This separates the learner's probabilistic model from assumptions imposed on incoming observations.

The authors provide regret bounds under logarithmic loss for methods including Gaussian regression and logistic regression. Regret measures the extra loss incurred relative to a comparison strategy. The bounds show how these methods can perform favorably under broad conditions, while explicitly accounting for the infinite-dimensional function classes involved in nonparametric modeling.

The work also establishes formal connections with minimax analysis and minimum description length. In particular, it specifies the sense in which Bayesian Gaussian regression is a minimax strategy. These results give a worst-case justification for selected Bayesian methods beyond a data-generation story based on their priors. Their strength comes from the stated bounds and conditions, rather than an unconditional promise of superior prediction.
summary.tldr: Worst-case regret bounds justify selected Gaussian process Bayesian methods without probabilistic assumptions on data generation.

title: Worst-Case Bounds for Gaussian Process Models

abstract: We present a probabilistic generative model of visual attributes, together with an efﬁcient learning algorithm. Attributes are visual qualities of objects, such as ‘red’, ‘striped’, or ‘spotted’. The model sees attributes as patterns of image segments, repeatedly sharing some characteristic properties. These can be any combination of appearance, shape, or the layout of segments within the pattern. Moreover, attributes with general appearance are taken into account, such as the pattern of alternation of any two colors which is characteristic for stripes. To enable learning from unsegmented training images, the model is learnt discriminatively, by optimizing a likelihood ratio. As demonstrated in the experimental evaluation, our model can learn in a weakly supervised setting and encompasses a broad range of attributes. We show that attributes can be learnt starting from a text query to Google image search, and can then be used to recognize the attribute and determine its spatial extent in novel real-world images.

paragraphs: Visual attributes describe qualities such as color, stripes, or spots. This paper develops a probabilistic generative model that represents an attribute through recurring patterns of image segments. The shared properties can involve appearance, shape, spatial arrangement, or combinations of these features, allowing the model to express several kinds of visual regularity.

The representation also handles attributes defined by a general relationship among appearances. Stripes, for example, can involve alternating colors without requiring one particular pair of colors. Although the model is generative, its learning procedure is discriminative: it optimizes a likelihood ratio so that training can use images without supplied segmentations.

Experiments demonstrate learning across a broad range of attributes in a weakly supervised setting. The authors show a workflow beginning with a text query to Google image search and ending with a model that recognizes an attribute and identifies its spatial extent in new real-world images. The contribution connects flexible attribute representations with a learning procedure that does not require segmented training examples.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic model learns visual attributes from weakly supervised, unsegmented images and can locate those attributes in new images.

title: Learning Visual Attributes

abstract: This paper investigates a new machine learning strategy called translated learning. Unlike many previous learning tasks, we focus on how to use labeled data from one feature space to enhance the classification of other entirely different learning spaces. For example, we might wish to use labeled text data to help learn a model for classifying image data, when the labeled images are difficult to obtain. An important aspect of translated learning is to build a "bridge" to link one feature space (known as the "source space") to another space (known as the "target space") through a translator in order to migrate the knowledge from source to target. The translated learning solution uses a language model to link the class labels to the features in the source spaces, which in turn is translated to the features in the target spaces. Finally, this chain of linkages is completed by tracing back to the instances in the target spaces. We show that this path of linkage can be modeled using a Markov chain and risk minimization. Through experiments on the text-aided image classification and cross-language classification tasks, we demonstrate that our translated learning framework can greatly outperform many state-of-the-art baseline methods.

paragraphs: Transfer learning becomes especially challenging when source and target data use entirely different features. This paper proposes translated learning to move useful label information across that divide. Its motivating example is using labeled text to help classify images when labeled images are difficult to obtain.

The method builds a sequence of connections between the two spaces. A language model first relates class labels to source features. A translator connects those source features to target features, and the chain then reaches the target instances. The authors express this linked pathway using a Markov chain and risk minimization, turning cross-space transfer into a statistical learning framework.

Experiments cover text-assisted image classification and classification across languages. In these tasks, the authors report that translated learning can substantially outperform many leading baseline methods. The important idea is that knowledge transfer can proceed through explicit intermediate links even when the source and target do not share a feature representation. The empirical claim concerns the tested tasks rather than every possible pair of learning spaces.
summary.tldr: Translated learning transfers label information across different feature spaces through a probabilistic chain linking labels, features, and target instances.

title: Translated Learning: Transfer Learning across Different Feature Spaces

abstract: One crucial assumption made by both principal component analysis (PCA) and probabilistic PCA (PPCA) is that the instances are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.). However, this common i.i.d. assumption is unreasonable for relational data. In this paper, by explicitly modeling covariance between instances as derived from the relational information, we propose a novel probabilistic dimensionality reduction method, called probabilistic relational PCA (PRPCA), for relational data analysis. Although the i.i.d. assumption is no longer adopted in PRPCA, the learning algorithms for PRPCA can still be devised easily like those for PPCA which makes explicit use of the i.i.d. assumption. Experiments on real-world data sets show that PRPCA can effectively utilize the relational information to dramatically outperform PCA and achieve state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: The paper addresses dimensionality reduction for data whose instances are related to one another. It identifies the independent-and-identically-distributed assumption in PCA and probabilistic PCA as a poor fit for relational data. Treating instances as independent can leave their relationships outside the model used to construct a lower-dimensional representation.

Probabilistic relational PCA explicitly models covariance between instances using relational information. This changes the probabilistic account of the data so that relationships contribute to the representation. The authors also show that learning algorithms remain easy to devise in a manner similar to probabilistic PCA, despite dropping its independence assumption.

Experiments on real-world datasets report that the method uses relational information effectively, substantially outperforms PCA, and achieves state-of-the-art performance. These are empirical findings for the studied data. The broader methodological contribution is to incorporate dependence between examples directly into probabilistic dimensionality reduction while preserving an accessible learning formulation. It demonstrates that accounting for relationships need not require giving up the practical modeling approach associated with probabilistic PCA.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic relational PCA models dependence between instances and reports substantial empirical gains over PCA on relational data.

title: Probabilistic Relational PCA

abstract: An algorithm is presented for online learning of rotations. The proposed algorithm involves matrix exponentiated gradient updates and is motivated by the Von Neumann divergence. The additive updates are skew-symmetric matrices with trace zero which comprise the Lie algebra of the rotation group. The orthogonality and unit determinant of the matrix parameter are preserved using matrix logarithms and exponentials and the algorithm lends itself to interesting interpretations in terms of the computational topology of the compact Lie groups. The stability and the computational complexity of the algorithm are discussed.

paragraphs: The paper presents an online algorithm for learning rotations. A rotation matrix must satisfy specific structural constraints: it is orthogonal and has determinant one. Learning therefore requires more than adjusting matrix entries to improve predictions; the update process must also keep the parameter within the set of valid rotations.

The proposed method uses matrix exponentiated-gradient updates motivated by the Von Neumann divergence. Its additive updates are skew-symmetric matrices with zero trace, belonging to the Lie algebra associated with the rotation group. Matrix logarithms and exponentials connect these updates to the rotation parameter while preserving orthogonality and unit determinant.

The significance of this construction is that the update rule incorporates the geometry of the parameter space. The authors also discuss interpretations involving the computational topology of compact Lie groups, together with stability and computational complexity. The contribution is an online learning procedure designed around rotation constraints, with analysis of how that structure affects its mathematical interpretation and computation.
summary.tldr: An online matrix-update algorithm learns rotations while preserving orthogonality and determinant one through logarithms and exponentials.

title: On Learning Rotations

abstract: The problem of selecting the right state-representation in a reinforcement learning problem is considered. Several models (functions mapping past observations to a finite set) of the observations are given, and it is known that for at least one of these models the resulting state dynamics are indeed Markovian. Without knowing neither which of the models is the correct one, nor what are the probabilistic characteristics of the resulting MDP, it is required to obtain as much reward as the optimal policy for the correct model (or for the best of the correct models, if there are several). We propose an algorithm that achieves that, with a regret of order T^{2/3} where T is the horizon time.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning when the agent is given several possible ways to summarize its observation history into a finite state. At least one candidate is assumed to produce genuinely Markovian dynamics, meaning that its current state supplies the relevant history for the resulting decision process. The agent does not know which candidate has this property.

The agent also lacks the probabilistic characteristics of the Markov decision process induced by a correct representation. It must therefore learn how to act while resolving uncertainty about how its observations should be represented. The performance target is the optimal policy for a correct model, or the best correct model when several candidates qualify.

The authors propose an algorithm with regret of order T^(2/3), where T is the time horizon. Because this grows more slowly than T, the average reward shortfall relative to the target decreases with the horizon at the stated order. The result supplies a learning guarantee despite representation uncertainty, conditional on the candidate collection containing at least one Markovian representation.
summary.tldr: An algorithm learns among candidate state representations with order T^(2/3) regret, assuming at least one candidate yields Markovian dynamics.

title: Selecting the State-Representation in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Rational models of causal induction have been successful in accounting for people's judgments about the existence of causal relationships. However, these models have focused on explaining inferences from discrete data of the kind that can be summarized in a 2 ✕ 2 contingency table. This severely limits the scope of these models, since the world often provides non-binary data. We develop a new rational model of causal induction using continuous dimensions, which aims to diminish the gap between empirical and theoretical approaches and real-world causal induction. This model successfully predicts human judgments from previous studies better than models of discrete causal inference, and outperforms several other plausible models of causal induction with continuous causes in accounting for people's inferences in a new experiment.

paragraphs: The paper asks how people judge causal relationships when causes vary continuously. Earlier rational models had explained judgments mainly using binary observations, such as whether a cause and an outcome were present or absent. That setup leaves out information whenever observations differ by degree rather than falling into two categories.

The authors develop a rational model that works with continuous dimensions. Its purpose is to bring formal accounts of causal reasoning closer to the kinds of evidence people encounter outside simplified binary tasks. The central change is therefore in the information the model can accommodate, while retaining the goal of explaining human causal judgments.

The model predicts judgments from previous studies better than models designed for discrete causal inference. In a new experiment, it also explains participants’ inferences better than several plausible alternatives that accommodate continuous causes. These comparisons support the proposed account in the studies examined and show why explicitly representing continuous variation can matter when modeling human causal reasoning.
summary.tldr: A rational model using continuous causes explains human causal judgments better than the compared discrete and continuous alternatives in the reported studies.

title: A rational model of causal inference with continuous causes

abstract: We propose two classes of second-order optimization methods for solving the sparse inverse covariance estimation problem. The first approach, which we call the Newton-LASSO method, minimizes a piecewise quadratic model of the objective function at every iteration to generate a step. We employ the fast iterative shrinkage thresholding method (FISTA) to solve this subproblem. The second approach, which we call the Orthant-Based Newton method, is a two-phase algorithm that first identifies an orthant face and then minimizes a smooth quadratic approximation of the objective function using the conjugate gradient method. These methods exploit the structure of the Hessian to efficiently compute the search direction and to avoid explicitly storing the Hessian. We show that quasi-Newton methods are also effective in this context, and describe a limited memory BFGS variant of the orthant-based Newton method. We present numerical results that suggest that all the techniques described in this paper have attractive properties and constitute useful tools for solving the sparse inverse covariance estimation problem. Comparisons with the method implemented in the QUIC software package are presented.

paragraphs: This paper develops optimization methods for estimating a sparse inverse covariance matrix. The methods use second-order information about the objective to choose updates. A central computational concern is how to benefit from this curvature information without explicitly storing the full Hessian matrix.

The first approach, Newton-LASSO, constructs a piecewise quadratic approximation at each iteration and solves the resulting subproblem with FISTA. The second, Orthant-Based Newton, first selects a face corresponding to a pattern of signs and zeros, then uses conjugate gradients to minimize a smooth quadratic approximation there. Both exploit Hessian structure when computing search directions.

The authors also show that quasi-Newton approaches are effective and describe a limited-memory BFGS version of the orthant-based method. Numerical results suggest that the proposed techniques have useful practical properties, and the paper compares them with the method in QUIC. The evidence supports them as additional tools for this estimation problem without claiming that one approach uniformly dominates the others.
summary.tldr: Newton and quasi-Newton methods exploit curvature efficiently to solve sparse inverse covariance estimation without storing the full Hessian.

title: Newton-Like Methods for Sparse Inverse Covariance Estimation

abstract: Finding maximum aposteriori (MAP) assignments in graphical models is an important task in many applications. Since the problem is generally hard, linear programming (LP) relaxations are often used. Solving these relaxations efficiently is thus an important practical problem. In recent years, several authors have proposed message passing updates corresponding to coordinate descent in the dual LP. However,these are generally not guaranteed to converge to a global optimum. One approach to remedy this is to smooth the LP, and perform coordinate descent on the smoothed dual. However, little is known about the convergence rate of this procedure. Here we perform a thorough rate analysis of such schemes and derive primal and dual convergence rates. We also provide a simple dual to primal mapping that yields feasible primal solutions with a guaranteed rate of convergence. Empirical evaluation supports our theoretical claims and shows that the method is highly competitive with state of the art approaches that yield global optima.

paragraphs: Finding the most probable assignment in a graphical model is generally difficult, so practitioners often solve a linear programming relaxation. Message-passing algorithms can update coordinates of the relaxation’s dual problem, but these updates do not generally guarantee convergence to a global optimum. Smoothing the relaxation offers a way to address this difficulty.

The paper analyzes how quickly coordinate minimization converges on the smoothed dual. It derives convergence rates for both the dual formulation used by the updates and the primal formulation of the optimization problem. This matters because progress in the internal optimization representation must ultimately translate into useful solutions to the problem being solved.

The authors also provide a simple conversion from dual iterates to feasible primal solutions, with a guaranteed convergence rate. Experiments support the theoretical claims and show competitive performance against approaches that obtain global optima. These conclusions concern solving the relaxation framework; they do not establish that every resulting solution exactly solves the original discrete assignment problem.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes convergence rates and feasible-solution recovery for coordinate methods applied to smoothed MAP linear-programming relaxations.

title: Convergence Rate Analysis of MAP Coordinate Minimization Algorithms

abstract: We introduce a new prior for use in Nonparametric Bayesian Hierarchical Clustering. The prior is constructed by marginalizing out the time information of Kingman’s coalescent, providing a prior over tree structures which we call the Time-Marginalized Coalescent (TMC). This allows for models which factorize the tree structure and times, providing two benefits: more flexible priors may be constructed and more efficient Gibbs type inference can be used. We demonstrate this on an example model for density estimation and show the TMC achieves competitive experimental results.
originalAbstract: We introduce a new prior for use in Nonparametric Bayesian Hierarchical Clustering. The prior is constructed by marginalizing out the time information of Kingman’s coalescent, providing a prior over tree structures which we call the Time-Marginalized Coalescent (TMC). This allows for models which factorize the tree structure and times, providing two benefits: more flexible priors may be constructed and more efficient Gibbs type inference can be used. We demonstrate this on an example model for density estimation and show the TMC achieves competitive experimental results.

paragraphs: Bayesian hierarchical clustering uses a probability model over possible clustering trees. This paper introduces a prior called the Time-Marginalized Coalescent, constructed from Kingman's coalescent by integrating out its time information. The resulting prior describes tree structures without carrying the original timing variables along with them.

This construction allows models to factorize tree structure and times. The separation provides two stated benefits: greater flexibility in constructing priors and access to more efficient Gibbs-type inference. It changes how the hierarchy can be modeled and explored computationally, because the tree's branching structure and its timing information need no longer be tied together in the original way.

The authors demonstrate the approach in an example density-estimation model and report competitive experimental results. This shows that the new prior can support a practical statistical task alongside its structural and computational motivations. The contribution is a reusable choice of prior for nonparametric Bayesian hierarchical clustering, with the density-estimation experiment illustrating its usefulness rather than establishing universal superiority.
summary.tldr: Integrating time out of Kingman's coalescent yields a flexible tree prior that supports more efficient Gibbs-type hierarchical-clustering inference.

title: The Time-Marginalized Coalescent Prior for Hierarchical Clustering

abstract: One of the main challenges in data clustering is to define an appropriate similarity measure between two objects. Crowdclustering addresses this challenge by defining the pairwise similarity based on the manual annotations obtained through crowdsourcing. Despite its encouraging results, a key limitation of crowdclustering is that it can only cluster objects when their manual annotations are available. To address this limitation, we propose a new approach for clustering, called \textit{semi-crowdsourced clustering} that effectively combines the low-level features of objects with the manual annotations of a subset of the objects obtained via crowdsourcing. The key idea is to learn an appropriate similarity measure, based on the low-level features of objects, from the manual annotations of only a small portion of the data to be clustered. One difficulty in learning the pairwise similarity measure is that there is a significant amount of noise and inter-worker variations in the manual annotations obtained via crowdsourcing. We address this difficulty by developing a metric learning algorithm based on the matrix completion method. Our empirical study with two real-world image data sets shows that the proposed algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art distance metric learning algorithms in both clustering accuracy and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Clustering depends on deciding which objects are similar. Crowdclustering uses human annotations to define those similarities, but its reliance on annotations limits it to objects that have been labeled. This paper proposes semi-crowdsourced clustering, which combines object features with crowd annotations for only a subset of the data.

The key step is learning a similarity measure over low-level features from the annotated portion. Once learned, that measure can be applied to objects without their own manual annotations. The authors address noise and differences between crowd workers through a metric-learning algorithm based on matrix completion, making inconsistent human judgments part of the learning problem.

An empirical study on two real image datasets finds that the proposed algorithm outperforms leading distance-metric learning methods in both clustering accuracy and computational efficiency. The contribution is a way to extend the usefulness of a limited annotation effort across a larger collection. The reported results support learning a feature-based similarity from imperfect crowd feedback instead of requiring annotations for every object.
summary.tldr: Semi-crowdsourced clustering learns a robust feature-based similarity from partial crowd annotations so that unannotated objects can also be clustered.

title: Semi-Crowdsourced Clustering: Generalizing Crowd Labeling by Robust Distance Metric Learning

abstract: Randomized decision trees and forests have a rich history in machine learning and have seen considerable success in application, perhaps particularly so for computer vision. However, they face a fundamental limitation: given enough data, the number of nodes in decision trees will grow exponentially with depth. For certain applications, for example on mobile or embedded processors, memory is a limited resource, and so the exponential growth of trees limits their depth, and thus their potential accuracy. This paper proposes decision jungles, revisiting the idea of ensembles of rooted decision directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), and shows these to be compact and powerful discriminative models for classification. Unlike conventional decision trees that only allow one path to every node, a DAG in a decision jungle allows multiple paths from the root to each leaf. We present and compare two new node merging algorithms that jointly optimize both the features and the structure of the DAGs efficiently. During training, node splitting and node merging are driven by the minimization of exactly the same objective function, here the weighted sum of entropies at the leaves. Results on varied datasets show that, compared to decision forests and several other baselines, decision jungles require dramatically less memory while considerably improving generalization.

paragraphs: Decision trees can grow exponentially in node count as their depth increases, making memory a barrier to richer classifiers. This is particularly relevant for mobile and embedded processors. The paper proposes decision jungles: ensembles of rooted directed acyclic graphs that allow multiple paths to reach the same leaf, sharing nodes within the classifier.

Training must determine both which features to use and how the graph should connect. The authors introduce and compare two node-merging algorithms that optimize these choices jointly. Node splitting and merging use the same training objective, the weighted sum of leaf entropies, so expansion and compression are guided by a common measure of classification quality.

Across the evaluated datasets, decision jungles use dramatically less memory and considerably improve generalization compared with decision forests and several other baselines. The findings show that shared graph structure can support both compact storage and strong classification performance. The contribution therefore addresses the memory cost of deeper decision models while also improving predictive behavior in the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: Decision jungles share nodes within decision graphs, reducing memory use and improving generalization in the reported classification experiments.

title: Decision Jungles: Compact and Rich Models for Classification

abstract: We propose a family of maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) kernel two-sample tests that have low sample complexity and are consistent. The test has a hyperparameter that allows one to control the tradeoff between sample complexity and computational time. Our family of tests, which we denote as B-tests, is both computationally and statistically efficient, combining favorable properties of previously proposed MMD two-sample tests. It does so by better leveraging samples to produce low variance estimates in the finite sample case, while avoiding a quadratic number of kernel evaluations and complex null-hypothesis approximation as would be required by tests relying on one sample U-statistics. The B-test uses a smaller than quadratic number of kernel evaluations and avoids completely the computational burden of complex null-hypothesis approximation while maintaining consistency and probabilistically conservative thresholds on Type I error. Finally, recent results of combining multiple kernels transfer seamlessly to our hypothesis test, allowing a further increase in discriminative power and decrease in sample complexity.

paragraphs: A two-sample test asks whether two collections of observations come from the same distribution. This paper introduces B-tests, a family of kernel tests based on maximum mean discrepancy. Their purpose is to combine efficient use of data with manageable computation, rather than requiring a quadratic number of kernel evaluations to obtain useful statistical estimates.

A tunable parameter controls the tradeoff between computational time and sample requirements. The tests use the available observations to obtain low-variance estimates in finite samples, while avoiding the complicated null-hypothesis approximation required by the comparison approach based on one-sample U-statistics. This connects the statistical design directly to the cost of carrying out the test.

The authors establish consistency and probabilistically conservative thresholds for Type I error, the error of rejecting a true same-distribution hypothesis. Existing methods for combining multiple kernels also carry over to B-tests, potentially improving discrimination and reducing sample requirements further. The contribution is therefore both a testing family and a flexible computation-versus-data tradeoff.
summary.tldr: B-tests offer consistent kernel two-sample testing with tunable computational cost, low-variance estimates, and conservative Type I error thresholds.

title: B-test: A Non-parametric, Low Variance Kernel Two-sample Test

abstract: A central challenge to many fields of science and engineering involves minimizing non-convex error functions over continuous, high dimensional spaces. Gradient descent or quasi-Newton methods are almost ubiquitously used to perform such minimizations, and it is often thought that a main source of difficulty for these local methods to find the global minimum is the proliferation of local minima with much higher error than the global minimum. Here we argue, based on results from statistical physics, random matrix theory, neural network theory, and empirical evidence, that a deeper and more profound difficulty originates from the proliferation of saddle points, not local minima, especially in high dimensional problems of practical interest. Such saddle points are surrounded by high error plateaus that can dramatically slow down learning, and give the illusory impression of the existence of a local minimum. Motivated by these arguments, we propose a new approach to second-order optimization, the saddle-free Newton method, that can rapidly escape high dimensional saddle points, unlike gradient descent and quasi-Newton methods. We apply this algorithm to deep or recurrent neural network training, and provide numerical evidence for its superior optimization performance.

paragraphs: Training complex models often requires minimizing a non-convex error function in a high-dimensional space. A common explanation for slow or unsuccessful optimization is that the algorithm becomes trapped in poor local minima. This paper argues that saddle points can present a deeper difficulty, especially in practical high-dimensional problems.

The argument draws on statistical physics, random matrix theory, neural network theory, and empirical evidence. Saddle points are surrounded by high-error plateaus that can slow learning dramatically and create the appearance of a local minimum. This perspective shifts attention toward places where progress stalls even though the surrounding landscape offers directions of improvement.

Motivated by this analysis, the authors propose saddle-free Newton, a second-order optimization method designed to escape high-dimensional saddle points rapidly. They apply it to deep and recurrent neural network training and provide numerical evidence of superior optimization performance. The paper combines a proposed explanation of optimization difficulty with an algorithm responding to that explanation; its empirical results support the method on the studied training problems.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that saddle-point plateaus are a major high-dimensional optimization obstacle and introduces saddle-free Newton to escape them.

title: Identifying and attacking the saddle point problem in high-dimensional non-convex optimization

abstract: The key challenge of face recognition is to develop effective feature representations for reducing intra-personal variations while enlarging inter-personal differences. In this paper, we show that it can be well solved with deep learning and using both face identification and verification signals as supervision. The Deep IDentification-verification features (DeepID2) are learned with carefully designed deep convolutional networks. The face identification task increases the inter-personal variations by drawing DeepID2 features extracted from different identities apart, while the face verification task reduces the intra-personal variations by pulling DeepID2 features extracted from the same identity together, both of which are essential to face recognition. The learned DeepID2 features can be well generalized to new identities unseen in the training data. On the challenging LFW dataset, 99.15% face verification accuracy is achieved. Compared with the best previous deep learning result on LFW, the error rate has been significantly reduced by 67%.

paragraphs: Face recognition needs representations that distinguish different people while remaining consistent across images of the same person. The paper learns such representations by combining two forms of supervision in deep convolutional networks. Its features, called DeepID2, are trained using both identity classification and verification of whether faces belong to the same person.

The two objectives shape the features in complementary ways. Identification separates representations associated with different identities, increasing differences between people. Verification draws representations of the same identity together, reducing variation within a person. Joint training directly addresses both requirements, and the authors report that the resulting features generalize well to identities absent from the training data.

On the LFW dataset, the method achieves 99.15% face-verification accuracy. The authors report a 67% reduction in error relative to the best previous deep-learning result on that dataset. This is a relative reduction in mistakes, distinct from a percentage-point gain in accuracy. The findings support combining identification and verification signals when learning transferable face features.
summary.tldr: DeepID2 combines identification and verification supervision to learn transferable face features, achieving 99.15% verification accuracy on LFW.

title: Deep Learning Face Representation by Joint Identification-Verification

abstract: Basic decisions, such as judging a person as a friend or foe, involve categorizing novel stimuli. Recent work finds that people’s category judgments are guided by a small set of examples that are retrieved from memory at decision time. This limited and stochastic retrieval places limits on human performance for probabilistic classification decisions. In light of this capacity limitation, recent work finds that idealizing training items, such that the saliency of ambiguous cases is reduced, improves human performance on novel test items. One shortcoming of previous work in idealization is that category distributions were idealized in an ad hoc or heuristic fashion. In this contribution, we take a first principles approach to constructing idealized training sets. We apply a machine teaching procedure to a cognitive model that is either limited capacity (as humans are) or unlimited capacity (as most machine learning systems are). As predicted, we find that the machine teacher recommends idealized training sets. We also find that human learners perform best when training recommendations from the machine teacher are based on a limited-capacity model. As predicted, to the extent that the learning model used by the machine teacher conforms to the true nature of human learners, the recommendations of the machine teacher prove effective. Our results provide a normative basis (given capacity constraints) for idealization procedures and offer a novel selection procedure for models of human learning.

paragraphs: People's category decisions can depend on a small, randomly retrieved set of remembered examples. This limited retrieval helps explain why training examples that reduce the prominence of ambiguous cases can improve later judgments. The paper seeks a principled way to construct these idealized training sets, replacing the heuristic choices used in previous work.

It recommends idealized training sets, connecting the structure of the examples to the learner's capacity constraints rather than treating idealization as an arbitrary adjustment.

title: Optimal Teaching for Limited-Capacity Human Learners

abstract: We show the existence of a Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH) family for the angular distance that yields an approximate Near Neighbor Search algorithm with the asymptotically optimal running time exponent. Unlike earlier algorithms with this property (e.g., Spherical LSH (Andoni-Indyk-Nguyen-Razenshteyn 2014) (Andoni-Razenshteyn 2015)), our algorithm is also practical, improving upon the well-studied hyperplane LSH (Charikar 2002) in practice. We also introduce a multiprobe version of this algorithm and conduct an experimental evaluation on real and synthetic data sets.We complement the above positive results with a fine-grained lower bound for the quality of any LSH family for angular distance. Our lower bound implies that the above LSH family exhibits a trade-off between evaluation time and quality that is close to optimal for a natural class of LSH functions.

paragraphs: The paper develops locality-sensitive hashing for approximate near-neighbor search using angular distance. This type of hashing organizes points so that similar ones can be found efficiently. The authors establish an LSH family whose resulting search algorithm achieves the asymptotically optimal running-time exponent, addressing a central theoretical measure of search efficiency.

The method also improves on hyperplane LSH in practice, connecting the theoretical exponent with an implementable algorithm. The authors introduce a multiprobe version and evaluate the approach on both real and synthetic datasets. These experiments complement the asymptotic result by examining practical performance, which the abstract distinguishes from earlier algorithms with the same optimal-exponent property.

A further contribution is a fine-grained lower bound on the quality of angular-distance LSH families. It shows that the proposed family's tradeoff between evaluation time and quality is close to optimal within a natural class of hashing functions. This qualifies the optimality claim: the exponent is asymptotically optimal, while the evaluation-cost tradeoff is near-optimal for the specified class.
summary.tldr: An angular-distance hashing method combines an asymptotically optimal search exponent with practical improvements over hyperplane LSH.

title: Practical and Optimal LSH for Angular Distance

abstract: We consider the problem of finding M best diverse solutions of energy minimization problems for graphical models. Contrary to the sequential method of Batra et al., which greedily finds one solution after another, we infer all $M$ solutions jointly. It was shown recently that such jointly inferred labelings not only have smaller total energy but also qualitatively outperform the sequentially obtained ones. The only obstacle for using this new technique is the complexity of the corresponding inference problem, since it is considerably slower algorithm than the method of Batra et al. In this work we show that the joint inference of $M$ best diverse solutions can be formulated as a submodular energy minimization if the original MAP-inference problem is submodular, hence fast inference techniques can be used. In addition to the theoretical results we provide practical algorithms that outperform the current state-of-the art and can be used in both submodular and non-submodular case.

Joint inference chooses all M solutions together. Earlier work had shown that joint solutions could have lower total energy and better qualitative results, but their computational cost hindered use.

The authors show that the joint problem can be expressed as submodular energy minimization when the original maximum a posteriori inference problem is submodular. This preserves a useful optimization structure while asking for several diverse answers. Consequently, fast methods for submodular minimization can be applied to the joint inference task.

The paper also presents practical algorithms that outperform the current state of the art and apply to both submodular and non-submodular cases. The theoretical reformulation remains conditional on submodularity of the original problem. The broader practical algorithms extend the paper’s reach beyond that condition, addressing the computational obstacle that made joint selection difficult to use.
summary.tldr: Jointly finding diverse labelings becomes submodular optimization when the original inference problem is submodular, enabling faster inference.

title: M-Best-Diverse Labelings for Submodular Energies and Beyond

abstract: A key problem in structured output prediction is enabling direct optimization of the task reward function that matters for test evaluation. This paper presents a simple and computationally efficient method that incorporates task reward into maximum likelihood training. We establish a connection between maximum likelihood and regularized expected reward, showing that they are approximately equivalent in the vicinity of the optimal solution. Then we show how maximum likelihood can be generalized by optimizing the conditional probability of auxiliary outputs that are sampled proportional to their exponentiated scaled rewards. We apply this framework to optimize edit distance in the output space, by sampling from edited targets. Experiments on speech recognition and machine translation for neural sequence to sequence models show notable improvements over maximum likelihood baseline by simply sampling from target output augmentations.

paragraphs: Structured prediction models are often trained by maximum likelihood but evaluated using a task-specific reward. This paper introduces a simple, computationally efficient way to bring that reward into likelihood training. The aim is to make the training signal reflect the quality of complete structured outputs.

The authors establish an approximate connection between maximum likelihood and regularized expected reward near an optimal solution. They then generalize likelihood training using auxiliary outputs sampled in proportion to exponentiated, scaled rewards. Reward therefore influences which alternative outputs receive training emphasis, connecting output augmentation with the evaluation objective.

The framework is applied to edit distance by sampling edited versions of target outputs. In experiments with neural sequence-to-sequence models for speech recognition and machine translation, this produces notable improvements over a maximum-likelihood baseline. The findings show that sampling target augmentations can provide a practical route for incorporating task reward. The theoretical equivalence remains local and approximate, while the reported gains come from the tested training procedure.
summary.tldr: Reward-weighted sampling of alternative targets incorporates task reward into maximum-likelihood training and improves tested sequence prediction tasks.

title: Reward Augmented Maximum Likelihood for Neural Structured Prediction

abstract: We study a general adversarial online learning problem, in which we are given a decision set X' in a reflexive Banach space X and a sequence of reward vectors in the dual space of X. At each iteration, we choose an action from X', based on the observed sequence of previous rewards. Our goal is to minimize regret, defined as the gap between the realized reward and the reward of the best fixed action in hindsight. Using results from infinite dimensional convex analysis, we generalize the method of Dual Averaging (or Follow the Regularized Leader) to our setting and obtain upper bounds on the worst-case regret that generalize many previous results. Under the assumption of uniformly continuous rewards, we obtain explicit regret bounds in a setting where the decision set is the set of probability distributions on a compact metric space S. Importantly, we make no convexity assumptions on either the set S or the reward functions. We also prove a general lower bound on the worst-case regret for any online algorithm. We then apply these results to the problem of learning in repeated two-player zero-sum games on compact metric spaces. In doing so, we first prove that if both players play a Hannan-consistent strategy, then with probability 1 the empirical distributions of play weakly converge to the set of Nash equilibria of the game. We then show that, under mild assumptions, Dual Averaging on the (infinite-dimensional) space of probability distributions indeed achieves Hannan-consistency.

paragraphs: The paper extends adversarial online learning to decision sets in reflexive Banach spaces, which can accommodate infinite-dimensional choices. At each step, an action is selected using previously observed rewards. Performance is measured by regret: the shortfall relative to the best single action that could have been chosen after seeing the entire reward sequence.

Using infinite-dimensional convex analysis, the authors generalize Dual Averaging, also called Follow the Regularized Leader, and derive worst-case regret bounds. For decisions that are probability distributions over a compact metric space, uniformly continuous rewards yield explicit bounds. The convergence statement concerns accumulated distributions of play, rather than requiring each successive action to settle at an equilibrium.
summary.tldr: The paper extends regret minimization to infinite-dimensional decisions and connects consistent learning to equilibrium distributions in continuous zero-sum games.

title: Minimizing Regret on Reflexive Banach Spaces and Nash Equilibria in Continuous Zero-Sum Games

abstract: We consider the assortment optimization problem when customer preferences follow a mixture of Mallows distributions. The assortment optimization problem focuses on determining the revenue/profit maximizing subset of products from a large universe of products; it is an important decision that is commonly faced by retailers in determining what to offer their customers. There are two key challenges: (a) the Mallows distribution lacks a closed-form expression (and requires summing an exponential number of terms) to compute the choice probability and, hence, the expected revenue/profit per customer; and (b) finding the best subset may require an exhaustive search. Our key contributions are an efficiently computable closed-form expression for the choice probability under the Mallows model and a compact mixed integer linear program (MIP) formulation for the assortment problem.

paragraphs: A retailer choosing which products to offer must consider how customers will choose among the available options. This paper studies that assortment decision when customer preferences follow a mixture of Mallows distributions. The objective is to select the subset of products that maximizes expected revenue or profit from a larger product universe.

Two computational obstacles arise. First, evaluating an assortment requires choice probabilities, whose direct computation can involve summing exponentially many terms. Second, even if one assortment can be evaluated, searching through all possible subsets can require exhaustive enumeration. These are distinct difficulties: calculating the value of a candidate and finding the best candidate.

The paper addresses them with an efficiently computable closed-form choice probability expression under the Mallows model and a compact mixed integer linear program for assortment selection. The expression makes customer choice calculations more accessible, while the optimization formulation organizes the subset decision into a standard mathematical form. A compact formulation does not itself mean every instance is easy, but it supplies a concrete alternative to explicitly listing all assortments.
summary.tldr: A closed-form choice calculation and compact mixed integer formulation address assortment optimization under Mallows preference models.

title: Assortment Optimization Under the Mallows model

abstract: We propose the coupled generative adversarial nets (CoGAN) framework for generating pairs of corresponding images in two different domains. The framework consists of a pair of generative adversarial nets, each responsible for generating images in one domain. We show that by enforcing a simple weight-sharing constraint, the CoGAN learns to generate pairs of corresponding images without existence of any pairs of corresponding images in the two domains in the training set. In other words, the CoGAN learns a joint distribution of images in the two domains from images drawn separately from the marginal distributions of the individual domains. This is in contrast to the existing multi-modal generative models, which require corresponding images for training. We apply the CoGAN to several pair image generation tasks. For each task, the CoGAN learns to generate convincing pairs of corresponding images. We further demonstrate the applications of the CoGAN framework for the domain adaptation and cross-domain image generation tasks.
