In other words, the CoGAN learns a joint distribution of images in the two domains from images drawn separately from the marginal distributions of the individual domains. This is in contrast to the existing multi-modal generative models, which require corresponding images for training. We apply the CoGAN to several pair image generation tasks. For each task, the CoGAN learns to generate convincing pairs of corresponding images. We further demonstrate the applications of the CoGAN framework for the domain adaptation and cross-domain image generation tasks.

paragraphs: Generating corresponding images in two domains usually suggests training on examples that are already paired. This paper introduces Coupled Generative Adversarial Networks, or CoGAN, to learn from separate collections of images instead. Its objective is to produce related image pairs even though the training data contain no corresponding pairs across the two domains.

CoGAN contains two generative adversarial networks, with one responsible for each domain. A weight-sharing constraint couples the networks. Through that shared structure, the framework learns a joint image distribution from samples drawn separately from the two individual distributions. The coupling is therefore the key modeling ingredient that connects otherwise unpaired training collections.

The authors apply CoGAN to several paired-image generation tasks and report convincing corresponding images in each task. They also demonstrate domain adaptation and cross-domain image generation applications. These results show how shared network weights can support learning cross-domain relationships without paired examples, broadening the training settings available for the demonstrated generative tasks.
summary.tldr: CoGAN uses weight sharing between two adversarial networks to generate corresponding images from training collections that contain no paired examples.

title: Coupled Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: Tensor networks are approximations of high-order tensors which are efficient to work with and have been very successful for physics and mathematics applications. We demonstrate how algorithms for optimizing tensor networks can be adapted to supervised learning tasks by using matrix product states (tensor trains) to parameterize non-linear kernel learning models. For the MNIST data set we obtain less than 1% test set classification error. We discuss an interpretation of the additional structure imparted by the tensor network to the learned model.

paragraphs: Tensor networks provide efficient approximations of high-order tensors and have been useful in physics and mathematics. This paper brings that representation machinery into supervised learning. It investigates how existing algorithms for optimizing tensor networks can be adapted to train predictive models from labeled data.

The authors use matrix product states, also called tensor trains, to parameterize nonlinear kernel learning models. The tensor network supplies an organized representation of the model’s parameters, drawing on the efficiency of working with these tensor approximations. The contribution connects a particular model representation with optimization methods developed for that representation, giving tensor networks a concrete role in supervised prediction.

On MNIST, the resulting approach achieves a test-set classification error below one percent. This provides an empirical demonstration that the adapted methods can support accurate classification on the dataset studied. The paper also discusses how to interpret the additional structure that the tensor network imposes on the learned model, addressing the character of the representation as well as its predictive performance.
summary.tldr: Tensor-network optimization is adapted to nonlinear kernel learning, achieving below one percent test classification error on MNIST.

title: Supervised Learning with Tensor Networks

abstract: One-shot learning is usually tackled by using generative models or discriminative embeddings. Discriminative methods based on deep learning, which are very effective in other learning scenarios, are ill-suited for one-shot learning as they need large amounts of training data. In this paper, we propose a method to learn the parameters of a deep model in one shot. We construct the learner as a second deep network, called a learnet, which predicts the parameters of a pupil network from a single exemplar. In this manner we obtain an efficient feed-forward one-shot learner, trained end-to-end by minimizing a one-shot classification objective in a learning to learn formulation. In order to make the construction feasible, we propose a number of factorizations of the parameters of the pupil network. We demonstrate encouraging results by learning characters from single exemplars in Omniglot, and by tracking visual objects from a single initial exemplar in the Visual Object Tracking benchmark.

paragraphs: One-shot learning asks a model to adapt from a single example, which poses a difficulty for deep discriminative methods that usually require substantial training data. This paper addresses the problem by training a network to produce the parameters of another network. The example becomes an input to a learned parameter-generation process.

The parameter-producing network is called a learnet, and the network it configures is the pupil. A single exemplar passes through the learnet to determine the pupil's parameters, creating an efficient feed-forward adaptation mechanism. The overall system is trained end to end using a one-shot classification objective, so the training process explicitly teaches the system how to learn from one example.

To make parameter generation feasible, the authors introduce factorizations of the pupil's parameters. They report encouraging results for recognizing Omniglot characters from individual exemplars and tracking objects from a single initial exemplar in the Visual Object Tracking benchmark. These applications demonstrate the proposed learning-to-learn mechanism in both recognition and tracking settings.
summary.tldr: A trained learnet generates another network's parameters from one exemplar, enabling feed-forward one-shot recognition and tracking.

title: Learning feed-forward one-shot learners

abstract: A differentiable estimation of the distance between two distributions based on samples is important for many deep learning tasks. One such estimation is maximum mean discrepancy (MMD). However, MMD suffers from its sensitive kernel bandwidth hyper-parameter, weak gradients, and large mini-batch size when used as a training objective. In this paper, we propose population matching discrepancy (PMD) for estimating the distribution distance based on samples, as well as an algorithm to learn the parameters of the distributions using PMD as an objective. PMD is defined as the minimum weight matching of sample populations from each distribution, and we prove that PMD is a strongly consistent estimator of the first Wasserstein metric. We apply PMD to two deep learning tasks, domain adaptation and generative modeling. Empirical results demonstrate that PMD overcomes the aforementioned drawbacks of MMD, and outperforms MMD on both tasks in terms of the performance as well as the convergence speed.

paragraphs: Many deep-learning tasks need a training objective that measures how different two distributions are using only samples. Maximum mean discrepancy is one option, but the paper identifies sensitivity to kernel bandwidth, weak gradients, and large minibatch requirements as difficulties when using it for training. Population matching discrepancy offers an alternative based on matching sampled populations.

PMD is defined through the minimum-weight matching between samples from the two distributions. The authors prove that it is a strongly consistent estimator of the first Wasserstein metric. This connects a finite sample-matching calculation to a population-level distribution distance. They also provide an algorithm for learning distribution parameters with PMD as the objective.

The method is applied to domain adaptation and generative modeling. In the reported experiments, PMD addresses the identified MMD drawbacks and outperforms MMD in both task performance and convergence speed. The statistical result explains what distance the estimator approaches, while the experiments support its usefulness as a training signal in the two evaluated applications.
summary.tldr: Population matching discrepancy estimates Wasserstein distance through sample matching and improves on MMD in the reported learning experiments.

title: Population Matching Discrepancy and Applications in Deep Learning

abstract: Aiming to augment generative models with external memory, we interpret the output of a memory module with stochastic addressing as a conditional mixture distribution, where a read operation corresponds to sampling a discrete memory address and retrieving the corresponding content from memory. This perspective allows us to apply variational inference to memory addressing, which enables effective training of the memory module by using the target information to guide memory lookups. Stochastic addressing is particularly well-suited for generative models as it naturally encourages multimodality which is a prominent aspect of most high-dimensional datasets. Treating the chosen address as a latent variable also allows us to quantify the amount of information gained with a memory lookup and measure the contribution of the memory module to the generative process. To illustrate the advantages of this approach we incorporate it into a variational autoencoder and apply the resulting model to the task of generative few-shot learning. The intuition behind this architecture is that the memory module can pick a relevant template from memory and the continuous part of the model can concentrate on modeling remaining variations. We demonstrate empirically that our model is able to identify and access the relevant memory contents even with hundreds of unseen Omniglot characters in memory.

paragraphs: The paper augments generative models with external memory by treating a memory read as a probabilistic operation. A read samples a discrete address and retrieves its contents, making the memory output a conditional mixture distribution. This interpretation gives memory addressing a place inside the model's probabilistic description.

Treating the address as a latent variable allows variational inference to train the memory module, using target information to guide lookups. Stochastic addressing also encourages multiple modes, matching an important feature of high-dimensional data. The formulation lets the authors quantify information gained through a lookup and measure how much the memory contributes to generation.

The architectural intuition is that memory supplies a relevant template while the continuous part of the model represents remaining variations. This supports the proposed division between selecting stored content and modeling variation around it.
summary.tldr: Modeling memory addresses as latent variables enables variational training of generative memory lookups and successful retrieval among unseen Omniglot characters.

title: Variational Memory Addressing in Generative Models

abstract: Markov random fields are a popular model for high-dimensional probability distributions. Over the years, many mathematical, statistical and algorithmic problems on them have been studied. Until recently, the only known algorithms for provably learning them relied on exhaustive search, correlation decay or various incoherence assumptions. Bresler gave an algorithm for learning general Ising models on bounded degree graphs. His approach was based on a structural result about mutual information in Ising models. Here we take a more conceptual approach to proving lower bounds on the mutual information. Our proof generalizes well beyond Ising models, to arbitrary Markov random fields with higher order interactions. As an application, we obtain algorithms for learning Markov random fields on bounded degree graphs on $n$ nodes with $r$-order interactions in $n^r$ time and $\log n$ sample complexity. Our algorithms also extend to various partial observation models.

Here we take a more conceptual approach to proving lower bounds on the mutual information. paragraphs: Markov random fields describe high-dimensional probability distributions through interactions among variables. Learning these models with guarantees has often required exhaustive search or structural assumptions such as correlation decay. Earlier work on bounded-degree Ising models showed that a structural property of mutual information could instead support a provable learning algorithm.

This paper develops a more conceptual proof of lower bounds on mutual information. Its reach extends beyond Ising models to arbitrary Markov random fields with higher-order interactions, where an interaction can involve more than two variables. The information-theoretic result therefore supplies a foundation for learning a broader family of models.

As an application, the authors obtain algorithms for bounded-degree graphs with n nodes and interactions of order r. They report running time scaling as n to the r and sample complexity scaling as log n. The algorithms also extend to several partial-observation models. The contribution links a structural statement about information to concrete learning guarantees, with bounded degree and interaction order defining the stated algorithmic setting.
summary.tldr: Mutual-information bounds support provable learning algorithms for bounded-degree Markov random fields with higher-order interactions.

title: Information Theoretic Properties of Markov Random Fields, and their Algorithmic Applications

abstract: We explore the top-K rank aggregation problem in which one aims to recover a consistent ordering that focuses on top-K ranked items based on partially revealed preference information. We examine an M-wise comparison model that builds on the Plackett-Luce (PL) model where for each sample, M items are ranked according to their perceived utilities modeled as noisy observations of their underlying true utilities. As our result, we characterize the minimax optimality on the sample size for top-K ranking. The optimal sample size turns out to be inversely proportional to M. We devise an algorithm that effectively converts M-wise samples into pairwise ones and employs a spectral method using the refined data. In demonstrating its optimality, we develop a novel technique for deriving tight $\ell_\infty$ estimation error bounds, which is key to accurately analyzing the performance of top-K ranking algorithms, but has been challenging. Recent work relied on an additional maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE) stage merged with a spectral method to attain good estimates in $\ell_\infty$ error to achieve the limit for the pairwise model. In contrast, although it is valid in slightly restricted regimes, our result demonstrates a spectral method alone to be sufficient for the general M-wise model. We run numerical experiments using synthetic data and confirm that the optimal sample size decreases at the rate of 1/M. Moreover, running our algorithm on real-world data, we find that its applicability extends to settings that may not fit the PL model.

title: Optimal Sample Complexity of M-wise Data for Top-K Ranking

abstract: We consider the problem of recovering a signal x in R^n, from magnitude-only measurements, y i = |a i^T x| for i={1,2...m}. Also known as the phase retrieval problem, it is a fundamental challenge in nano-, bio- and astronomical imaging systems, astronomical imaging, and speech processing. The problem is ill-posed, and therefore additional assumptions on the signal and/or the measurements are necessary. In this paper, we first study the case where the underlying signal x is s-sparse. We develop a novel recovery algorithm that we call Compressive Phase Retrieval with Alternating Minimization, or CoPRAM. Our algorithm is simple and can be obtained via a natural combination of the classical alternating minimization approach for phase retrieval, with the CoSaMP algorithm for sparse recovery. Despite its simplicity, we prove that our algorithm achieves a sample complexity of O(s^2 log n) with Gaussian samples, which matches the best known existing results. It also demonstrates linear convergence in theory and practice and requires no extra tuning parameters other than the signal sparsity level s. We then consider the case where the underlying signal x arises from to structured sparsity models. We specifically examine the case of block-sparse signals with uniform block size of b and block sparsity k=s/b. For this problem, we design a recovery algorithm that we call Block CoPRAM that further reduces the sample complexity to O(ks log n). For sufficiently large block lengths of b=Theta(s), this bound equates to O(s log n). To our knowledge, this constitutes the first end-to-end linearly convergent family of algorithms for phase retrieval where the Gaussian sample complexity has a sub-quadratic dependence on the sparsity level of the signal.

summary.tldr: CoPRAM combines sparse recovery and alternating minimization, with block structure enabling lower Gaussian measurement requirements.

title: Fast, Sample-Efficient Algorithms for Structured Phase Retrieval

abstract: Humans routinely retrace a path in a novel environment both forwards and backwards despite uncertainty in their motion. In this paper, we present an approach for doing so. Given a demonstration of a path, a first network generates an abstraction of the path. Equipped with this abstraction, a second network then observes the world and decides how to act in order to retrace the path under noisy actuation and a changing environment. The two networks are optimized end-to-end at training time. We evaluate the method in two realistic simulators, performing path following both forwards and backwards. Our experiments show that our approach outperforms both a classical approach to solving this task as well as a number of other baselines.

paragraphs: Retracing a demonstrated path becomes difficult when actions are noisy or the environment changes. The paper studies how a learned system can follow a route both forwards and backwards under those conditions. Its approach uses a visual abstraction of the demonstration to support decisions during the later traversal.

Two networks divide the task. The first converts the demonstrated path into an abstract representation. The second combines that representation with its observations of the world to decide how to act. Both networks are optimized together end to end, so the path representation is learned in connection with the needs of the network that must use it.

The authors evaluate forward and backward path following in two realistic simulators. Their approach outperforms a classical method and several other baselines in these experiments. The results support the usefulness of jointly learning a path memory and an action policy for retracing routes under uncertainty. The reported evidence comes from simulated environments, where noisy actuation and environmental changes are part of the task being addressed.
summary.tldr: Two jointly trained networks learn a visual path memory and use it to retrace routes forwards and backwards under uncertainty.

title: Visual Memory for Robust Path Following

abstract: Generating long and coherent reports to describe medical images poses challenges to bridging visual patterns with informative human linguistic descriptions. We propose a novel Hybrid Retrieval-Generation Reinforced Agent (HRGR-Agent) which reconciles traditional retrieval-based approaches populated with human prior knowledge, with modern learning-based approaches to achieve structured, robust, and diverse report generation. HRGR-Agent employs a hierarchical decision-making procedure. For each sentence, a high-level retrieval policy module chooses to either retrieve a template sentence from an off-the-shelf template database, or invoke a low-level generation module to generate a new sentence. HRGR-Agent is updated via reinforcement learning, guided by sentence-level and word-level rewards. Experiments show that our approach achieves the state-of-the-art results on two medical report datasets, generating well-balanced structured sentences with robust coverage of heterogeneous medical report contents. In addition, our model achieves the highest detection precision of medical abnormality terminologies, and improved human evaluation performance.

This gives the system access to established report language while retaining the ability to produce new wording for the content it needs to describe.

Reinforcement learning updates the agent using rewards at both sentence and word levels. The architecture therefore coordinates the choice of reporting strategy with the production of the individual words.

On two medical report datasets, the authors report state-of-the-art results, structured sentence output, and robust coverage of varied report content. They also report the highest detection precision for medical abnormality terminology and improved human evaluation performance. These results support combining retrieval and generation for the evaluated reporting tasks, with the two components contributing to structure and diversity within the same report.
summary.tldr: HRGR-Agent learns when to retrieve template sentences and when to generate new ones, improving medical image reports on two evaluated datasets.

title: Hybrid Retrieval-Generation Reinforced Agent for Medical Image Report Generation

abstract: In the adaptive setting, many multi-armed bandit applications allow the learner to adaptively draw samples and adjust sampling strategy in rounds. In many real applications, not only the query complexity but also the round complexity need to be optimized. In this paper, we study both PAC and exact top-$k$ arm identification problems and design efficient algorithms considering both round complexity and query complexity. For PAC problem, we achieve optimal query complexity and use only $O(\log_{\frac{k}{\delta}}^*(n))$ rounds, which matches the lower bound of round complexity, while most of existing works need $\Theta(\log \frac{n}{k})$ rounds. For exact top-$k$ arm identification, we improve the round complexity factor from $\log n$ to $\log_{\frac{1}{\delta}}^*(n)$, and achieve near optimal query complexity. In experiments, our algorithms conduct far fewer rounds, and outperform state of the art by orders of magnitude with respect to query cost.

paragraphs: In a multi-armed bandit identification problem, a learner samples alternatives to determine which are best. When sampling is organized into rounds, two costs matter: the total number of queries and the number of opportunities to revise the sampling strategy. This paper develops algorithms that account for both costs when identifying the top k alternatives.

The authors study a probably approximately correct version of the problem and an exact identification version. For the approximate problem, they achieve optimal query complexity together with a round complexity matching the lower bound. The round count involves an iterated logarithm, a much slower-growing expression than the ordinary logarithmic round counts required by most of the compared work.

For exact top-k identification, the paper similarly improves a logarithmic round-complexity factor to an iterated-logarithmic one while retaining near-optimal query complexity. Experiments report substantially fewer rounds and query-cost improvements of orders of magnitude over the compared state of the art. The contribution shows that reducing repeated adaptation need not require giving up strong guarantees on the overall amount of sampling.
summary.tldr: New top-k bandit identification algorithms sharply reduce adaptive rounds while preserving optimal or near-optimal query complexity.

title: Efficient Pure Exploration in Adaptive Round model

abstract: Lipschitz constraints under L2 norm on deep neural networks are useful for provable adversarial robustness bounds, stable training, and Wasserstein distance estimation. While heuristic approaches such as the gradient penalty have seen much practical success, it is challenging to achieve similar practical performance while provably enforcing a Lipschitz constraint. In principle, one can design Lipschitz constrained architectures using the composition property of Lipschitz functions, but Anil et al. recently identified a key obstacle to this approach: gradient norm attenuation. They showed how to circumvent this problem in the case of fully connected networks by designing each layer to be gradient norm preserving. We extend their approach to train scalable, expressive, provably Lipschitz convolutional networks. In particular, we present the Block Convolution Orthogonal Parameterization (BCOP), an expressive parameterization of orthogonal convolution operations. We show that even though the space of orthogonal convolutions is disconnected, the largest connected component of BCOP with 2n channels can represent arbitrary BCOP convolutions over n channels. Our BCOP parameterization allows us to train large convolutional networks with provable Lipschitz bounds. Empirically, we find that it is competitive with existing approaches to provable adversarial robustness and Wasserstein distance estimation.

paragraphs: Lipschitz constraints bound how much a network’s output can change as its input changes. Such bounds are useful for provable adversarial robustness, stable training, and Wasserstein distance estimation. Building networks from individually constrained layers can enforce these bounds, but gradients may progressively shrink, creating an obstacle to effective learning.

This paper extends a gradient-norm-preserving approach from fully connected networks to convolutional networks. Its main construction is Block Convolution Orthogonal Parameterization, or BCOP, an expressive way to parameterize orthogonal convolution operations. The aim is to retain useful learning behavior while enforcing a provable constraint on the network.

The authors also address the disconnected structure of the space of orthogonal convolutions. They show that the largest connected component of BCOP with twice as many channels can represent arbitrary BCOP convolutions at the original channel count. The parameterization enables large convolutional networks with provable Lipschitz bounds, and experiments find competitive performance for certified adversarial robustness and Wasserstein distance estimation.
summary.tldr: BCOP enables scalable, provably Lipschitz convolutional networks by extending gradient-preserving orthogonal constructions to convolutions.

title: Preventing Gradient Attenuation in Lipschitz Constrained Convolutional Networks

abstract: Even though neural networks enjoy widespread use, they still struggle to learn the basic laws of physics. How might we endow them with better inductive biases? In this paper, we draw inspiration from Hamiltonian mechanics to train models that learn and respect exact conservation laws in an unsupervised manner. We evaluate our models on problems where conservation of energy is important, including the two-body problem and pixel observations of a pendulum. Our model trains faster and generalizes better than a regular neural network. An interesting side effect is that our model is perfectly reversible in time.

paragraphs: A neural network can fit observations of motion without respecting the physical laws behind them. This paper explores how a model's built-in assumptions can better match physical dynamics. It draws on Hamiltonian mechanics to train models that learn and obey exact conservation laws in an unsupervised manner.

The central idea is to make conservation part of how the model represents dynamics, giving learning a physically meaningful structure. The authors evaluate the approach on problems where conserving energy matters, including the two-body problem and a pendulum observed through pixels. These settings examine the proposal both in interacting-body motion and with visual observations.

The reported models train faster and generalize better than a regular neural network on the evaluated problems. The authors also identify exact time reversibility as a consequence of their model: its dynamics can be reversed in time. Together, these findings show the value of incorporating relevant physical structure into learning. The empirical improvements concern the studied problems, while conservation and reversibility describe the properties emphasized in the model's construction.
summary.tldr: Hamiltonian structure lets neural networks learn conservation-respecting, time-reversible dynamics while improving training speed and generalization on the studied physics problems.

title: Hamiltonian Neural Networks

abstract: We developed a Nonlinear Level-set Learning (NLL) method for dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional function approximation with small data. This work is motivated by a variety of design tasks in real-world engineering applications, where practitioners would replace their computationally intensive physical models (e.g., high-resolution fluid simulators) with fast-to-evaluate predictive machine learning models, so as to accelerate the engineering design processes. There are two major challenges in constructing such predictive models: (a) high-dimensional inputs (e.g., many independent design parameters) and (b) small training data, generated by running extremely time-consuming simulations. Thus, reducing the input dimension is critical to alleviate the over-fitting issue caused by data insufficiency. Existing methods, including sliced inverse regression and active subspace approaches, reduce the input dimension by learning a linear coordinate transformation; our main contribution is to extend the transformation approach to a nonlinear regime. Specifically, we exploit reversible networks (RevNets) to learn nonlinear level sets of a high-dimensional function and parameterize its level sets in low-dimensional spaces. A new loss function was designed to utilize samples of the target functions' gradient to encourage the transformed function to be sensitive to only a few transformed coordinates. The NLL approach is demonstrated by applying it to three 2D functions and two 20D functions for showing the improved approximation accuracy with the use of nonlinear transformation, as well as to an 8D composite material design problem for optimizing the buckling-resistance performance of composite shells of rocket inter-stages.

Two obstacles arise together: there may be many design variables but only a small number of simulation results. This paper develops Nonlinear Level-set Learning, or NLL, to reduce the effective input dimension and help address overfitting under limited data.

Existing approaches such as active subspaces learn linear changes of coordinates. NLL extends this idea to nonlinear transformations using reversible networks. The authors demonstrate improved approximation accuracy using nonlinear transformations on three two-dimensional and two twenty-dimensional functions. They also apply NLL to an eight-dimensional composite-material design problem involving the buckling resistance of rocket inter-stage shells. The approach thus connects gradient-informed coordinate learning with both function approximation and an engineering optimization application.
summary.tldr: NLL uses reversible networks and target-function gradients to learn nonlinear coordinates that improve low-dimensional function approximation.

title: Learning nonlinear level sets for dimensionality reduction in function approximation

abstract: We investigate the sample complexity of networks with bounds on the magnitude of its weights. In particular, we consider the class \[ \cn = \left\{W_t\circ\rho\circ W_{t-1}\circ\rho\ldots\circ \rho\circ W_{1} : W_1,\ldots,W_{t-1}\in M_{d\times d}, W_t\in M_{1,d} \right\} \] where the spectral norm of each $W_i$ is bounded by $O(1)$, the Frobenius norm is bounded by $R$, and $\rho$ is the sigmoid function $\frac{e^x}{1 + e^x}$ or the smoothened ReLU function $ \ln\left(1 + e^x\right)$. We show that for any depth $t$, if the inputs are in $[-1,1]^d$, the sample complexity of $\cn$ is $\tilde O\left(\frac{dR^2}{\epsilon^2}\right)$. This bound is optimal up to log-factors, and substantially improves over the previous state of the art of $\tilde O\left(\frac{d^2R^2}{\epsilon^2}\right)$, that was established in a recent line of work. We furthermore show that this bound remains valid if instead of considering the magnitude of the $W_i$'s, we consider the magnitude of $W_i - W_i^0$, where $W_i^0$ are some reference matrices, with spectral norm of $O(1)$. By taking the $W_i^0$ to be the matrices in the onset of the training process, we get sample complexity bounds that are sub-linear in the number of parameters, in many {\em typical} regimes of parameters. To establish our results we develop a new technique to analyze the sample complexity of families $\ch$ of predictors. We start by defining a new notion of a randomized approximate description of functions $f:\cx\to\reals^d$. We then show that if there is a way to approximately describe functions in a class $\ch$ using $d$ bits, then $\frac{d}{\epsilon^2}$ examples suffices to guarantee uniform convergence. Namely, that the empirical loss of all the functions in the class is $\epsilon$-close to the true loss. Finally, we develop a set of tools for calculating the approximate description length of classes of functions that can be presented as a composition of linear function classes and non-linear functions.

paragraphs: This paper asks how many examples suffice for neural networks with controlled weights to generalize. It considers networks of width d with sigmoid or smoothened ReLU activations, inputs in [-1,1]^d, constant-order spectral norm bounds, and Frobenius norm bounded by R. These assumptions define the network class covered by the result.

For any depth, the authors establish a sample complexity bound of order dR²/ε², up to logarithmic factors, where ε specifies the accuracy tolerance. This improves the previous d²R²/ε² dependence and is optimal up to logarithmic factors. A related bound controls deviations from reference weight matrices, allowing initialization-based guarantees that are sublinear in parameter count in many typical parameter regimes.

The proof introduces randomized approximate descriptions of functions. Roughly, if a function class admits descriptions using a given number of bits, that description budget controls the examples needed for uniform convergence: empirical and true losses remain close across the class. Tools for composing linear and nonlinear function classes make this principle applicable to the networks studied.
summary.tldr: Randomized approximate description length yields nearly optimal sample complexity bounds for specified neural networks with controlled weight norms.

title: Generalization Bounds for Neural Networks via Approximate Description Length

abstract: Tensor-network techniques have recently proven useful in machine learning, both as a tool for the formulation of new learning algorithms and for enhancing the mathematical understanding of existing methods. Inspired by these developments, and the natural correspondence between tensor networks and probabilistic graphical models, we provide a rigorous analysis of the expressive power of various tensor-network factorizations of discrete multivariate probability distributions. These factorizations include non-negative tensor-trains/MPS, which are in correspondence with hidden Markov models, and Born machines, which are naturally related to the probabilistic interpretation of quantum circuits. When used to model probability distributions, they exhibit tractable likelihoods and admit efficient learning algorithms. Interestingly, we prove that there exist probability distributions for which there are unbounded separations between the resource requirements of some of these tensor-network factorizations. Of particular interest, using complex instead of real tensors can lead to an arbitrarily large reduction in the number of parameters of the network. Additionally, we introduce locally purified states (LPS), a new factorization inspired by techniques for the simulation of quantum systems, with provably better expressive power than all other representations considered. The ramifications of this result are explored through numerical experiments.

Additionally, we introduce locally purified states (LPS), a new factorization inspired by techniques for the simulation of quantum systems, with provably better expressive power than all other representations considered. paragraphs: This paper asks how efficiently different tensor-network representations can express discrete probability distributions over many variables. The representations connect to familiar probabilistic constructions: nonnegative tensor trains correspond to hidden Markov models, while Born machines relate to the probabilistic interpretation of quantum circuits. These models offer tractable likelihood evaluation and admit efficient learning algorithms.

The authors rigorously compare the resources that different factorizations need to represent distributions. They prove that some distributions produce unbounded separations between certain representations. One striking result is that allowing complex-valued tensors instead of real-valued tensors can reduce the required number of parameters by an arbitrarily large amount. This is an existence result about representational efficiency, rather than a claim about every distribution.

The paper also introduces locally purified states, a factorization inspired by quantum-system simulation. It proves that this representation has greater expressive power than every other representation considered and explores the consequences numerically. The findings show that the choice of factorization can fundamentally affect model compactness, even when the models all provide tractable likelihoods.
summary.tldr: Tensor-network factorizations can differ arbitrarily in parameter efficiency, and locally purified states have provably greater expressive power than the alternatives studied.

title: Expressive power of tensor-network factorizations for probabilistic modeling

abstract: Graphical models are powerful tools for modeling high-dimensional data, but learning graphical models in the presence of latent variables is well-known to be difficult. In this work we give new results for learning Restricted Boltzmann Machines, probably the most well-studied class of latent variable models. Our results are based on new connections to learning two-layer neural networks under $\ell_{\infty}$ bounded input; for both problems, we give nearly optimal results under the conjectured hardness of sparse parity with noise. Using the connection between RBMs and feedforward networks, we also initiate the theoretical study of {\em supervised RBMs} \citep{hinton2012practical}, a version of neural-network learning that couples distributional assumptions induced from the underlying graphical model with the architecture of the unknown function class. We then give an algorithm for learning a natural class of supervised RBMs with better runtime than what is possible for its related class of networks without distributional assumptions.

paragraphs: Learning a graphical model becomes difficult when some of its variables are hidden. This paper studies Restricted Boltzmann Machines, a prominent family of such latent-variable models, by connecting their learnability to that of two-layer neural networks. The connection lets the authors address two learning problems through a common theoretical framework.

For the neural-network side, inputs are bounded in the infinity norm, meaning that their individual coordinates are bounded. The authors obtain nearly optimal results for both problems under a conjecture about the computational difficulty of sparse parity with noise. That qualification matters: the claimed near-optimality is tied to the stated hardness conjecture, rather than being an unconditional characterization.

The paper also begins a theoretical study of supervised Restricted Boltzmann Machines. Here, the underlying graphical model supplies distributional assumptions linked to the architecture of the function being learned. For a natural class of these models, the authors give an algorithm with better runtime than is possible for the related network class without those assumptions. This shows how distributional structure can change computational learnability.
summary.tldr: Connections between Restricted Boltzmann Machines and two-layer networks yield learning guarantees and show how distributional assumptions can improve runtime.

title: From Boltzmann Machines to Neural Networks and Back Again

abstract: We present a federated, asynchronous, and $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differentially private algorithm for $\PCA$ in the memory-limited setting. % Our algorithm incrementally computes local model updates using a streaming procedure and adaptively estimates its $r$ leading principal components when only $\mathcal{O}(dr)$ memory is available with $d$ being the dimensionality of the data. % We guarantee differential privacy via an input-perturbation scheme in which the covariance matrix of a dataset $\B{X} \in \R^{d \times n}$ is perturbed with a non-symmetric random Gaussian matrix with variance in $\mathcal{O}\left(\left(\frac{d}{n}\right)^2 \log d \right)$, thus improving upon the state-of-the-art. % Furthermore, contrary to previous federated or distributed algorithms for $\PCA$, our algorithm is also invariant to permutations in the incoming data, which provides robustness against straggler or failed nodes. % Numerical simulations show that, while using limited-memory, our algorithm exhibits performance that closely matches or outperforms traditional non-federated algorithms, and in the absence of communication latency, it exhibits attractive horizontal scalability.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis identifies leading directions of variation in data. This paper develops a federated version that operates asynchronously, uses limited memory, and provides differential privacy. Local updates are computed incrementally through a streaming procedure, allowing the method to estimate r leading components with memory proportional to d times r, where d is data dimensionality.

Privacy is obtained by perturbing the covariance matrix with a nonsymmetric Gaussian random matrix. The authors give a noise-variance order proportional to the square of d divided by sample count, multiplied by log d, and describe this as an improvement over prior work. The algorithm is also invariant to permutations of incoming data, supporting robustness to delayed or failed nodes.

Numerical simulations show performance close to or better than traditional nonfederated algorithms despite the limited-memory setting. They also indicate attractive scaling as more computing resources are added when communication latency is absent. That condition matters: the reported scalability statement explicitly excludes communication delays.
summary.tldr: A streaming federated PCA algorithm combines limited memory, asynchronous updates, differential privacy, and robustness to incoming-data order.

title: Federated Principal Component Analysis

abstract: Stochastic linear bandits with high-dimensional sparse features are a practical model for a variety of domains, such as personalized medicine and online advertising. We derive a novel O(n^{2/3}) dimension-free minimax regret lower bound for sparse linear bandits in the data-poor regime where the horizon is larger than the ambient dimension and where the feature vectors admit a well-conditioned exploration distribution. This is complemented by a nearly matching upper bound for an explore-then-commit algorithm showing that that O(n^{2/3}) is the optimal rate in the data-poor regime. The results complement existing bounds for the data-rich regime and also provide another example where carefully balancing the trade-off between information and regret is necessary. Finally, we prove a dimension-free O(\sqrt{n}) regret upper bound under an additional assumption on the magnitude of the signal for relevant features.

paragraphs: Sparse linear bandits model sequential decisions with many available features but a sparse underlying structure. The learner must balance collecting information against choosing rewarding actions. This paper studies the unavoidable cost of that balance through regret bounds that do not depend on the ambient dimension.

For the setting it calls data-poor, the abstract specifies a horizon larger than the ambient dimension and feature vectors admitting a well-conditioned exploration distribution. Under these conditions, the authors establish a minimax lower bound with n^(2/3) dependence on the horizon n. An explore-then-commit algorithm provides a nearly matching upper bound, identifying that horizon dependence as optimal in the stated regime.

The paper also proves a dimension-free upper bound of order √n under an additional assumption about the signal magnitude of relevant features. The stronger guarantee therefore depends on extra structure. Together, the results distinguish what is possible under the basic exploration conditions from what becomes possible with a signal-strength assumption, and show why information gathering must be balanced carefully against immediate reward.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes nearly matching dimension-free n^(2/3) regret bounds for a stated sparse-bandit regime and a √n upper bound with an additional signal-strength assumption.

title: High-Dimensional Sparse Linear Bandits

abstract: Domain adaptive object re-ID aims to transfer the learned knowledge from the labeled source domain to the unlabeled target domain to tackle the open-class re-identification problems. Although state-of-the-art pseudo-label-based methods have achieved great success, they did not make full use of all valuable information because of the domain gap and unsatisfying clustering performance. To solve these problems, we propose a novel self-paced contrastive learning framework with hybrid memory. The hybrid memory dynamically generates source-domain class-level, target-domain cluster-level and un-clustered instance-level supervisory signals for learning feature representations. Different from the conventional contrastive learning strategy, the proposed framework jointly distinguishes source-domain classes, and target-domain clusters and un-clustered instances. Most importantly, the proposed self-paced method gradually creates more reliable clusters to refine the hybrid memory and learning targets, and is shown to be the key to our outstanding performance. Our method outperforms state-of-the-arts on multiple domain adaptation tasks of object re-ID and even boosts the performance on the source domain without any extra annotations. Our generalized version on unsupervised object re-ID surpasses state-of-the-art algorithms by considerable 16.7% and 7.9% on Market-1501 and MSMT17 benchmarks.

paragraphs: Domain-adaptive object re-identification transfers knowledge from labeled source images to an unlabeled target domain. Pseudo-labeling can help, but imperfect clustering and differences between domains leave useful information underused. This paper proposes a contrastive learning framework that brings several forms of supervision into a shared training process, including target examples that have not been assigned to clusters.

Its hybrid memory supplies source-class, target-cluster, and individual unclustered-target signals. The model learns to distinguish all three kinds jointly. A self-paced procedure gradually produces more reliable target clusters, updating both the memory and the learning targets. The authors identify this progressive refinement as a key contributor to the method’s performance.

The method outperforms existing approaches on multiple domain-adaptation tasks and also improves source-domain performance without extra annotations. A generalized version for unsupervised re-identification reports improvements of 16.7% on Market-1501 and 7.9% on MSMT17 over state-of-the-art algorithms. These findings support using both grouped and ungrouped target information while improving the reliability of the groups throughout learning.
summary.tldr: Hybrid memory combines labeled source classes, target clusters, and unclustered instances while self-paced refinement improves domain-adaptive re-identification.

title: Self-paced Contrastive Learning with Hybrid Memory for Domain Adaptive Object Re-ID

abstract: Learning matching costs has been shown to be critical to the success of the state-of-the-art deep stereo matching methods, in which 3D convolutions are applied on a 4D feature volume to learn a 3D cost volume. However, this mechanism has never been employed for the optical flow task. This is mainly due to the significantly increased search dimension in the case of optical flow computation, \ie, a straightforward extension would require dense 4D convolutions in order to process a 5D feature volume, which is computationally prohibitive. This paper proposes a novel solution that is able to bypass the requirement of building a 5D feature volume while still allowing the network to learn suitable matching costs from data. Our key innovation is to decouple the connection between 2D displacements and learn the matching costs at each 2D displacement hypothesis independently, \ie, displacement-invariant cost learning. Specifically, we apply the same 2D convolution-based matching net independently on each 2D displacement hypothesis to learn a 4D cost volume. Moreover, we propose a displacement-aware projection layer to scale the learned cost volume, which reconsiders the correlation between different displacement candidates and mitigates the multi-modal problem in the learned cost volume. The cost volume is then projected to optical flow estimation through a 2D soft-argmin layer. Extensive experiments show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on various datasets, and outperforms all published optical flow methods on the Sintel benchmark. The code is available at https://github.com/jytime/DICL-Flow.

paragraphs: Optical flow estimation requires comparing possible two-dimensional movements between images. Learning how to score candidate matches has helped stereo matching, but directly extending that machinery to optical flow would require an expensive five-dimensional feature volume and dense four-dimensional convolutions. This paper develops a way to learn matching costs without building that feature volume.

The method evaluates each candidate displacement independently using the same matching network built from two-dimensional convolutions. These evaluations form a four-dimensional cost volume. Sharing the matching network across displacement hypotheses provides the displacement-invariant component of the approach while avoiding the computationally prohibitive direct extension described in the abstract.

A displacement-aware projection layer then adjusts the costs while considering relationships among candidate movements. This helps address ambiguity when multiple candidates appear plausible. A two-dimensional soft-argmin layer converts the adjusted costs into a flow estimate. The authors report leading accuracy across several datasets and better Sintel performance than all published optical flow methods in their comparison. The result connects a more manageable matching computation with strong reported estimation accuracy.
summary.tldr: Scoring displacements independently with a shared network makes learned optical-flow matching costs computationally manageable and highly accurate in reported evaluations.

title: Displacement-Invariant Matching Cost Learning for Accurate Optical Flow Estimation

abstract: This paper develops a novel and unified framework to analyze the convergence of a large family of Q-learning algorithms from the switching system perspective. We show that the nonlinear ODE models associated with Q-learning and many of its variants can be naturally formulated as affine switching systems. Building on their asymptotic stability, we obtain a number of interesting results: (i) we provide a simple ODE analysis for the convergence of asynchronous Q-learning under relatively weak assumptions; (ii) we establish the first convergence analysis of the averaging Q-learning algorithm; and (iii) we derive a new sufficient condition for the convergence of Q-learning with linear function approximation.
originalAbstract: This paper develops a novel and unified framework to analyze the convergence of a large family of Q-learning algorithms from the switching system perspective. We show that the nonlinear ODE models associated with Q-learning and many of its variants can be naturally formulated as affine switching systems. Building on their asymptotic stability, we obtain a number of interesting results: (i) we provide a simple ODE analysis for the convergence of asynchronous Q-learning under relatively weak assumptions; (ii) we establish the first convergence analysis of the averaging Q-learning algorithm; and (iii) we derive a new sufficient condition for the convergence of Q-learning with linear function approximation.

paragraphs: The paper develops a common mathematical framework for studying whether Q-learning algorithms converge. Its starting point is the nonlinear ordinary differential equations associated with Q-learning and several variants. The authors show that these equations can be represented as affine switching systems, allowing their behavior to be analyzed through a shared dynamical-systems perspective.

The key connection is between asymptotic stability of those systems and convergence of the learning algorithms. This representation supports a simpler differential-equation analysis of asynchronous Q-learning under relatively weak assumptions. The framework also yields what the authors identify as the first convergence analysis for averaging Q-learning, extending the usefulness of the same mathematical viewpoint.

For Q-learning with linear function approximation, the paper derives a new sufficient condition for convergence. That qualification matters: the result provides a condition that guarantees convergence when satisfied, without claiming it is necessary. The contribution is thus both organizational and analytical, bringing multiple variants into one framework while producing distinct convergence results for each.
summary.tldr: A switching-system formulation unifies convergence analysis for several Q-learning variants and yields a new sufficient condition for linear approximation.

title: A Unified Switching System Perspective and Convergence Analysis of Q-Learning Algorithms

abstract: Telehealth and remote health monitoring have become increasingly important during the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic and it is widely expected that this will have a lasting impact on healthcare practices. These tools can help reduce the risk of exposing patients and medical staff to infection, make healthcare services more accessible, and allow providers to see more patients. However, objective measurement of vital signs is challenging without direct contact with a patient. We present a video-based and on-device optical cardiopulmonary vital sign measurement approach. It leverages a novel multi-task temporal shift convolutional attention network (MTTS-CAN) and enables real-time cardiovascular and respiratory measurements on mobile platforms. We evaluate our system on an Advanced RISC Machine (ARM) CPU and achieve state-of-the-art accuracy while running at over 150 frames per second which enables real-time applications. Systematic experimentation on large benchmark datasets reveals that our approach leads to substantial (20%-50%) reductions in error and generalizes well across datasets.

paragraphs: Remote health monitoring needs objective measurements even when a patient cannot be examined through direct contact. This paper presents a video-based approach for measuring cardiovascular and respiratory vital signs on a mobile device. The aim is to combine contactless measurement with computation fast enough for real-time use.

The system uses a multi-task temporal shift convolutional attention network, called MTTS-CAN. Its architecture brings temporal processing and attention into a model serving both cardiovascular and respiratory measurement tasks. Running the approach on the device is central to the contribution, so the evaluation considers processing speed alongside measurement accuracy.

On an ARM CPU, the authors report state-of-the-art accuracy and processing above 150 frames per second, supporting real-time applications in the evaluated setting. Experiments on large benchmark datasets show error reductions of 20%–50% and good generalization across datasets. Together, these findings indicate that the proposed architecture can combine efficient execution with improved measurement performance, addressing two requirements for making video-based vital-sign measurement useful on mobile platforms.
summary.tldr: MTTS-CAN measures cardiovascular and respiratory signals from video on mobile hardware, reporting over 150 frames per second and substantial benchmark error reductions.

title: Multi-Task Temporal Shift Attention Networks for On-Device Contactless Vitals Measurement

abstract: Large pretrained language models (LMs) like BERT have improved performance in many disparate natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, fine tuning such models requires a large number of training examples for each target task. Simultaneously, many realistic NLP problems are "few shot", without a sufficiently large training set. In this work, we propose a novel conditional neural process-based approach for few-shot text classification that learns to transfer from other diverse tasks with rich annotation. Our key idea is to represent each task using gradient information from a base model and to train an adaptation network that modulates a text classifier conditioned on the task representation. While previous task-aware few-shot learners represent tasks by input encoding, our novel task representation is more powerful, as the gradient captures input-output relationships of a task. Experimental results show that our approach outperforms traditional fine-tuning, sequential transfer learning, and state-of-the-art meta learning approaches on a collection of diverse few-shot tasks. We further conducted analysis and ablations to justify our design choices.

paragraphs: Pretrained language models help many language tasks, but adapting them can require more labeled examples than a target task provides. Grad2Task addresses few-shot text classification by learning from other tasks with rich annotations. The goal is to transfer useful adaptation behavior to tasks with only a small training set.

Its central choice is how to represent a task. Instead of using only encodings of the input texts, Grad2Task uses gradient information from a base model. Those gradients capture relationships between inputs and outputs, so the representation reflects what the task asks the classifier to learn. An adaptation network then modulates the classifier according to that task representation.

The approach is based on conditional neural processes and learns across diverse source tasks. Experiments on a collection of varied few-shot classification tasks show improvements over traditional fine-tuning, sequential transfer learning, and state-of-the-art meta-learning approaches. Additional analyses and ablations support the design choices. The findings suggest that information about how a task changes a model can be useful for deciding how to adapt that model.
summary.tldr: Grad2Task represents tasks through model gradients and uses those representations to adapt text classifiers, improving performance on diverse few-shot tasks.

title: Grad2Task: Improved Few-shot Text Classification Using Gradients for Task Representation

abstract: Hierarchical clustering studies a recursive partition of a data set into clusters of successively smaller size, and is a fundamental problem in data analysis. In this work we study the cost function for hierarchical clustering introduced by Dasgupta, and present two polynomial-time approximation algorithms: Our first result is an $O(1)$-approximation algorithm for graphs of high conductance. Our simple construction bypasses complicated recursive routines of finding sparse cuts known in the literature. Our second and main result is an $O(1)$-approximation algorithm for a wide family of graphs that exhibit a well-defined structure of clusters. This result generalises the previous state-of-the-art, which holds only for graphs generated from stochastic models. The significance of our work is demonstrated by the empirical analysis on both synthetic and real-world data sets, on which our presented algorithm outperforms the previously proposed algorithm for graphs with a well-defined cluster structure.

paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering organizes data through repeated divisions into progressively smaller groups. This paper studies that task using Dasgupta's cost function and develops two polynomial-time approximation algorithms. Their constant-factor guarantees mean the resulting hierarchy's cost stays within a fixed multiplicative factor of the optimum for the graph families covered by the results.

The first algorithm applies to high-conductance graphs. Its simple construction avoids the complicated recursive searches for sparse cuts used in earlier work. The main algorithm covers a broad family of graphs with clearly defined cluster structure, extending guarantees that previously applied only to graphs generated by stochastic models.

The contribution therefore broadens the structural conditions under which efficient hierarchical clustering has a strong approximation guarantee. The authors also evaluate their approach on synthetic and real datasets. In those experiments, the proposed algorithm outperforms the earlier algorithm intended for graphs with well-defined clusters, adding empirical support to the theoretical extension beyond stochastic graph-generation assumptions.
summary.tldr: Two efficient hierarchical clustering algorithms achieve constant-factor guarantees for high-conductance and broadly defined well-clustered graphs.

title: Hierarchical Clustering: $O(1)$-Approximation for Well-Clustered Graphs

abstract: Training saliency detection models with weak supervisions, e.g., image-level tags or captions, is appealing as it removes the costly demand of per-pixel annotations. Despite the rapid progress of RGB-D saliency detection in fully-supervised setting, it however remains an unexplored territory when only weak supervision signals are available. This paper is set to tackle the problem of weakly-supervised RGB-D salient object detection. The key insight in this effort is the idea of maintaining per-pixel pseudo-labels with iterative refinements by reconciling the multimodal input signals in our joint semantic mining (JSM). Considering the large variations in the raw depth map and the lack of explicit pixel-level supervisions, we propose spatial semantic modeling (SSM) to capture saliency-specific depth cues from the raw depth and produce depth-refined pseudo-labels. Moreover, tags and captions are incorporated via a fill-in-the-blank training in our textual semantic modeling (TSM) to estimate the confidences of competing pseudo-labels. At test time, our model involves only a light-weight sub-network of the training pipeline, i.e., it requires only an RGB image as input, thus allowing efficient inference. Extensive evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach under the weakly-supervised setting. Importantly, our method could also be adapted to work in both fully-supervised and unsupervised paradigms. In each of these scenarios, superior performance has been attained by our approach with comparing to the state-of-the-art dedicated methods. As a by-product, a CapS dataset is constructed by augmenting existing benchmark training set with additional image tags and captions.

paragraphs: Salient-object detection identifies prominent objects at the pixel level, but collecting pixel annotations is expensive. This paper trains with weaker supervision, including image tags and captions, while using color and depth information. Its central challenge is turning those indirect signals into useful pixel-level training targets.

Joint semantic mining maintains pseudo-labels for individual pixels and repeatedly refines them by reconciling multiple input signals. Spatial semantic modeling extracts saliency-relevant depth cues and uses them to improve those labels. summary.tldr: Joint semantic mining refines pixel pseudo-labels using depth and text during training, producing a lightweight saliency detector that needs only RGB input.

title: Joint Semantic Mining for Weakly Supervised RGB-D Salient Object Detection

abstract: In many machine learning tasks, a common approach for dealing with large-scale data is to build a small summary, {\em e.g.,} coreset, that can efficiently represent the original input. However, real-world datasets usually contain outliers and most existing coreset construction methods are not resilient against outliers (in particular, an outlier can be located arbitrarily in the space by an adversarial attacker). In this paper, we propose a novel robust coreset method for the {\em continuous-and-bounded learning} problems (with outliers) which includes a broad range of popular optimization objectives in machine learning, {\em e.g.,} logistic regression and $ k $-means clustering. Moreover, our robust coreset can be efficiently maintained in fully-dynamic environment. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first robust and fully-dynamic coreset construction method for these optimization problems. Another highlight is that our coreset size can depend on the doubling dimension of the parameter space, rather than the VC dimension of the objective function which could be very large or even challenging to compute. Finally, we conduct the experiments on real-world datasets to evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed robust coreset method.

paragraphs: A coreset is a small summary intended to represent a much larger dataset for an optimization task. Outliers complicate that goal, particularly when an adversary can place them arbitrarily in the data space. This paper develops a robust coreset method for continuous-and-bounded learning problems that explicitly include outliers.

The covered problem class includes objectives such as logistic regression and k-means clustering. The construction can also be maintained efficiently in a fully dynamic environment, where data are inserted or deleted. This combines robustness with the ability to update the summary as the underlying dataset changes.

A further feature is that coreset size can depend on the doubling dimension of the parameter space instead of the objective's VC dimension, which may be large or difficult to compute. The authors evaluate the method on real-world datasets. The contribution is therefore both a robust, maintainable data summary and an alternative way to express its size requirements through the structure of the parameter space.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs outlier-robust coresets that support dynamic updates and can have size governed by the parameter space's doubling dimension.

title: Robust and Fully-Dynamic Coreset for Continuous-and-Bounded Learning (With Outliers) Problems

abstract: For its advantage in GPU acceleration and less dependency on human experts, machine learning has been an emerging tool for solving the placement and routing problems, as two critical steps in modern chip design flow. Being still in its early stage, there are several fundamental issues unresolved: scalability, reward design, and end-to-end learning paradigm etc. To achieve end-to-end placement learning, we first propose a joint learning method for the placement of macros and standard cells, by the integration of reinforcement learning with a gradient based optimization scheme. To further bridge the placement with the subsequent routing task, we also develop a joint learning approach via reinforcement learning. One key design in our (reinforcement) learning paradigm involves a multi-view embedding model to encode both global graph level and local node level information of the input macros. Moreover, the random network distillation is devised to encourage exploration. Experiments on public chip design benchmarks show that our method can effectively learn from experience and also provide high-quality intermediate placement for the post standard cell placement, within few hours for training.

paragraphs: Chip design requires placing components and routing the connections between them. Machine learning offers GPU acceleration and reduced reliance on expert decisions, but connecting these tasks within an effective learning process remains challenging. This paper develops joint learning methods to coordinate placement decisions and better connect placement with the routing stage that follows.

For macros and standard cells, the authors combine reinforcement learning with gradient-based optimization. They also develop a reinforcement-learning approach linking placement to routing. A multi-view embedding represents both the global graph of input macros and information about individual nodes, giving the learning system access to the overall design and its local components.

Random network distillation encourages exploration within this learning process. Experiments on public chip-design benchmarks show that the method learns from experience and produces high-quality intermediate placements for subsequent standard-cell placement, with training taking a few hours. The stated outcome supports useful coordination within the design flow, particularly through the quality of intermediate placements supplied to later processing.
summary.tldr: Joint reinforcement learning and gradient optimization coordinate chip placement and routing, producing useful intermediate placements after a few hours of training.

title: On Joint Learning for Solving Placement and Routing in Chip Design

abstract: Sparse tensors appear frequently in federated deep learning, either as a direct artifact of the deep neural network’s gradients, or as a result of an explicit sparsification process. Existing communication primitives are agnostic to the peculiarities of deep learning; consequently, they impose unnecessary communication overhead. This paper introduces DeepReduce, a versatile framework for the compressed communication of sparse tensors, tailored to federated deep learning. DeepReduce decomposes sparse tensors into two sets, values and indices, and allows both independent and combined compression of these sets. We support a variety of common compressors, such as Deflate for values, or run-length encoding for indices. We also propose two novel compression schemes that achieve superior results: curve fitting-based for values, and bloom filter-based for indices. DeepReduce is orthogonal to existing gradient sparsifiers and can be applied in conjunction with them, transparently to the end-user, to significantly lower the communication overhead. As proof of concept, we implement our approach on TensorFlow and PyTorch. Our experiments with large real models demonstrate that DeepReduce transmits 320% less data than existing sparsifiers, without affecting accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/hangxu0304/DeepReduce.

paragraphs: Federated deep learning often needs to transmit sparse tensors, either because gradients are naturally sparse or because a sparsification method removes entries. Sparsity alone does not eliminate communication overhead: the remaining numerical values and their locations still need to be communicated. DeepReduce targets this additional cost with compression designed specifically for sparse tensors.

The framework separates a tensor into values and indices, allowing the two components to be compressed independently or together. It supports established methods such as Deflate for values and run-length encoding for indices. The authors also introduce value compression based on curve fitting and index compression based on Bloom filters, reporting superior results for these new schemes.

DeepReduce can work alongside existing gradient sparsifiers, making it an additional compression layer rather than requiring a replacement sparsification method. Implementations in TensorFlow and PyTorch demonstrate the approach. Experiments with large real models report substantially lower transmitted data than existing sparsifiers without an observed accuracy loss, showing that exploiting the representation of sparse updates can yield further communication savings.
summary.tldr: DeepReduce compresses sparse tensor values and indices to reduce federated learning communication beyond sparsification alone.

title: DeepReduce: A Sparse-tensor Communication Framework for Federated Deep Learning

abstract: Normalizing flows are bijective mappings between inputs and latent representations with a fully factorized distribution. They are very attractive due to exact likelihood evaluation and efficient sampling. However, their effective capacity is often insufficient since the bijectivity constraint limits the model width. We address this issue by incrementally padding intermediate representations with noise. We precondition the noise in accordance with previous invertible units, which we describe as cross-unit coupling. Our invertible glow-like modules increase the model expressivity by fusing a densely connected block with Nyström self-attention. We refer to our architecture as DenseFlow since both cross-unit and intra-module couplings rely on dense connectivity. Experiments show significant improvements due to the proposed contributions and reveal state-of-the-art density estimation under moderate computing budgets.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows connect observations to a simple latent distribution through invertible transformations. This structure makes likelihood evaluation and sampling attractive, but the requirement of invertibility restricts model width and can limit expressive capacity. DenseFlow addresses that restriction by progressively adding noise to intermediate representations.

The added noise is preconditioned using earlier invertible units, creating what the authors call cross-unit coupling. Within each invertible module, the architecture combines a densely connected block with Nyström self-attention. Dense connections therefore operate both across units and inside modules, giving the model additional ways to combine information as representations pass through the flow.

These changes target the capacity of the transformations used for density modeling. The experiments report significant improvements from the proposed components and state-of-the-art density estimation under moderate computing budgets. The result supports the combination of incremental noise padding and dense coupling as a practical way to strengthen flow models. Its significance lies in improving the flexibility of this structured model family without making a claim that every flow architecture needs the same modifications.
summary.tldr: DenseFlow expands intermediate representations with conditioned noise and dense connections to improve flow-based density estimation.

title: Densely connected normalizing flows

abstract: In this paper, we aim at synthesizing a free-viewpoint video of an arbitrary human performance using sparse multi-view cameras. Recently, several works have addressed this problem by learning person-specific neural radiance fields (NeRF) to capture the appearance of a particular human. In parallel, some work proposed to use pixel-aligned features to generalize radiance fields to arbitrary new scenes and objects. Adopting such generalization approaches to humans, however, is highly challenging due to the heavy occlusions and dynamic articulations of body parts. To tackle this, we propose Neural Human Performer, a novel approach that learns generalizable neural radiance fields based on a parametric human body model for robust performance capture. Specifically, we first introduce a temporal transformer that aggregates tracked visual features based on the skeletal body motion over time. Moreover, a multi-view transformer is proposed to perform cross-attention between the temporally-fused features and the pixel-aligned features at each time step to integrate observations on the fly from multiple views. Experiments on the ZJU-MoCap and AIST datasets show that our method significantly outperforms recent generalizable NeRF methods on unseen identities and poses.

paragraphs: Neural Human Performer aims to render human performance videos from freely chosen viewpoints using sparse multi-camera observations. Generalizing to new people and poses is difficult because body parts move relative to one another and frequently become occluded. The paper addresses these challenges with a generalizable neural radiance field grounded in a parametric human body model.

A temporal transformer aggregates visual features tracked over time using skeletal motion. This connects observations of moving body regions across frames. A second transformer combines the temporally aggregated features with features aligned to image pixels, using cross-attention to integrate the available camera views at each time step.

The approach brings together body structure, temporal evidence, and multiple viewpoints in the representation used for rendering. On ZJU-MoCap and AIST, the authors report significantly better results than recent generalizable NeRF methods for unseen identities and poses. Those evaluations support the value of explicitly organizing observations around human motion when transferring a rendering model beyond the people and poses seen during training.
summary.tldr: Neural Human Performer combines body-guided temporal features and multi-view attention to improve rendering of unseen people and poses.

title: Neural Human Performer: Learning Generalizable Radiance Fields for Human Performance Rendering

abstract: We propose new width-based planning and learning algorithms inspired from a careful analysis of the design decisions made by previous width-based planners. The algorithms are applied over the Atari-2600 games and our best performing algorithm, Novelty guided Critical Path Learning (N-CPL), outperforms the previously introduced width-based planning and learning algorithms $\pi$-IW(1), $\pi$-IW(1)+ and $\pi$-HIW(n, 1). Furthermore, we present a taxonomy of the Atari-2600 games according to some of their defining characteristics. This analysis of the games provides further insight into the behaviour and performance of the algorithms introduced. Namely, for games with large branching factors, and games with sparse meaningful rewards, N-CPL outperforms $\pi$-IW, $\pi$-IW(1)+ and $\pi$-HIW(n, 1).
