paragraphs: This paper develops planning and learning algorithms by examining design choices in earlier width-based planners. The work concerns lookahead methods with learned base policies and heuristics, evaluated on Atari-2600 games. Its strongest reported method is Novelty guided Critical Path Learning, abbreviated N-CPL.

The authors report that N-CPL outperforms the earlier width-based approaches pi-IW(1), pi-IW(1)+, and pi-HIW(n, 1). They also organize Atari games into a taxonomy based on defining characteristics. This adds an explanatory dimension to the evaluation: the comparisons can be examined in relation to the kinds of decision problems the games present.

The analysis highlights games with large branching factors and games where meaningful rewards are sparse. Large branching factors involve many possible continuations, while sparse meaningful rewards provide infrequent useful feedback. N-CPL outperforms the named prior approaches in these categories. The paper therefore contributes both improved algorithms within the evaluated planning family and a characterization of game properties that helps interpret their behavior and performance.
summary.tldr: N-CPL improves on earlier width-based Atari planners, with a game taxonomy clarifying performance in branching and sparse-reward settings.

title: Width-based Lookaheads with Learnt Base Policies and Heuristics Over the Atari-2600 Benchmark

abstract: In contrast to the advances in characterizing the sample complexity for solving Markov decision processes (MDPs), the optimal statistical complexity for solving constrained MDPs (CMDPs) remains unknown. We resolve this question by providing minimax upper and lower bounds on the sample complexity for learning near-optimal policies in a discounted CMDP with access to a generative model (simulator). In particular, we design a model-based algorithm that addresses two settings: (i) relaxed feasibility, where small constraint violations are allowed, and (ii) strict feasibility, where the output policy is required to satisfy the constraint. For (i), we prove that our algorithm returns an $\epsilon$-optimal policy with probability $1 - \delta$, by making $\tilde{O}\left(\frac{S A \log(1/\delta)}{(1 - \gamma)^3 \epsilon^2}\right)$ queries to the generative model, thus matching the sample-complexity for unconstrained MDPs. For (ii), we show that the algorithm's sample complexity is upper-bounded by $\tilde{O} \left(\frac{S A \, \log(1/\delta)}{(1 - \gamma)^5 \, \epsilon^2 \zeta^2} \right)$ where $\zeta$ is the problem-dependent Slater constant that characterizes the size of the feasible region. Finally, we prove a matching lower-bound for the strict feasibility setting, thus obtaining the first near minimax optimal bounds for discounted CMDPs. Our results show that learning CMDPs is as easy as MDPs when small constraint violations are allowed, but inherently more difficult when we demand zero constraint violation.

paragraphs: A constrained Markov decision process asks an agent to achieve high reward while respecting a constraint. This paper determines near-optimal data requirements for learning such policies in discounted problems with access to a simulator. It distinguishes allowing small constraint violations from requiring the returned policy to satisfy the constraint exactly.

The authors develop a model-based algorithm for both settings. With relaxed feasibility, its sample complexity matches that of unconstrained MDPs, up to the factors hidden in the stated bound. With strict feasibility, the bound has a stronger dependence on the discount factor and also depends on a Slater constant describing the size of the feasible region.

A matching lower bound for strict feasibility shows that the additional difficulty is inherent to the setting, rather than just a weakness of the proposed algorithm. Together, the guarantees establish a statistical distinction between approximate and exact constraint satisfaction. Small permitted violations can leave the learning difficulty comparable to ordinary MDPs, whereas demanding zero violation carries an unavoidable additional cost under the studied simulator-access setting.
summary.tldr: Near-optimal bounds show that strict constraint satisfaction makes discounted MDP learning harder than allowing small violations.

title: Near-Optimal Sample Complexity Bounds for Constrained MDPs

abstract: While other areas of machine learning have seen more and more automation, designing a high-performing recommender system still requires a high level of human effort. Furthermore, recent work has shown that modern recommender system algorithms do not always improve over well-tuned baselines. A natural follow-up question is, "how do we choose the right algorithm for a new dataset and performance metric?" In this work, we start by giving the first large-scale study of recommender system approaches by comparing 24 algorithms and 100 sets of hyperparameters across 85 datasets and 315 metrics. We find that the best algorithms and hyperparameters are highly dependent on the dataset and performance metric. However, there is also a strong correlation between the performance of each algorithm and various meta-features of the datasets. Motivated by these findings, we create RecZilla, a meta-learning approach to recommender systems that uses a model to predict the best algorithm and hyperparameters for new, unseen datasets. By using far more meta-training data than prior work, RecZilla is able to substantially reduce the level of human involvement when faced with a new recommender system application. We not only release our code and pretrained RecZilla models, but also all of our raw experimental results, so that practitioners can train a RecZilla model for their desired performance metric: https://github.com/naszilla/reczilla.

paragraphs: Choosing a recommender system requires deciding both which algorithm to use and how to configure it. This paper investigates why that decision remains labor intensive. Its large-scale study compares 24 algorithms and 100 hyperparameter sets across 85 datasets and 315 evaluation metrics, examining how performance changes with the data and the criterion used to judge success.

The study finds that the best algorithm and configuration depend strongly on the dataset and metric. It also finds strong correlations between algorithm performance and measurable characteristics of datasets. Those correlations motivate learning from previous recommendation problems to help choose a system for an unfamiliar one.

The resulting method, RecZilla, predicts an algorithm and hyperparameters for new datasets using meta-learning. The authors report that substantially more meta-training data than prior work helps reduce the human involvement required for new applications. They also release experimental results alongside code and pretrained models, allowing practitioners to train a selector for their preferred metric. The findings support making recommendation-system selection explicitly sensitive to both dataset characteristics and evaluation priorities.
summary.tldr: RecZilla learns from a large comparison of recommendation algorithms to predict suitable algorithms and hyperparameters for new datasets and evaluation goals.

title: On the Generalizability and Predictability of Recommender Systems

abstract: A compositional understanding of the world in terms of objects and their geometry in 3D space is considered a cornerstone of human cognition. Facilitating the learning of such a representation in neural networks holds promise for substantially improving labeled data efficiency. As a key step in this direction, we make progress on the problem of learning 3D-consistent decompositions of complex scenes into individual objects in an unsupervised fashion. We introduce Object Scene Representation Transformer (OSRT), a 3D-centric model in which individual object representations naturally emerge through novel view synthesis. OSRT scales to significantly more complex scenes with larger diversity of objects and backgrounds than existing methods. At the same time, it is multiple orders of magnitude faster at compositional rendering thanks to its light field parametrization and the novel Slot Mixer decoder. We believe this work will not only accelerate future architecture exploration and scaling efforts, but it will also serve as a useful tool for both object-centric as well as neural scene representation learning communities.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a neural network can represent a scene as individual objects arranged in three-dimensional space. Its goal is to learn decompositions that remain consistent across viewpoints without supervised object labels. Such representations are motivated by the possibility of improving labeled-data efficiency, although the reported contribution centers on learning and rendering the scene decomposition.

Object Scene Representation Transformer, or OSRT, learns through novel-view synthesis: generating a scene's appearance from another viewpoint. Individual object representations emerge through this task within a model organized around three-dimensional scenes. The authors report that OSRT handles substantially more complex scenes, with greater variety in objects and backgrounds, than existing approaches.

The model also uses a light-field parameterization and a Slot Mixer decoder to make compositional rendering multiple orders of magnitude faster. This combines a richer range of representable scenes with a large rendering-speed improvement. The authors see that combination as useful for exploring and scaling future architectures. The work advances a representation-learning approach in which predicting views provides the training signal for discovering separate objects.
summary.tldr: OSRT learns object-based scene representations through novel-view synthesis while supporting more complex scenes and much faster compositional rendering.

title: Object Scene Representation Transformer

abstract: Mixup is a commonly adopted data augmentation technique for image classification. Recent advances in mixup methods primarily focus on mixing based on saliency. However, many saliency detectors require intense computation and are especially burdensome for parameter-heavy transformer models. To this end, we propose TokenMixup, an efficient attention-guided token-level data augmentation method that aims to maximize the saliency of a mixed set of tokens. TokenMixup provides ×15 faster saliency-aware data augmentation compared to gradient-based methods. Moreover, we introduce a variant of TokenMixup which mixes tokens within a single instance, thereby enabling multi-scale feature augmentation. Experiments show that our methods significantly improve the baseline models’ performance on CIFAR and ImageNet-1K, while being more efficient than previous methods. We also reach state-of-the-art performance on CIFAR-100 among from-scratch transformer models. Code is available at https://github.com/mlvlab/TokenMixup.

paragraphs: Mixup creates augmented training examples by combining existing examples. Saliency-aware variants try to preserve informative content, but computing saliency can be expensive, especially for large transformers. TokenMixup uses attention to guide augmentation at the token level, aiming to maximize the saliency of the resulting collection of tokens.

The paper also introduces a variant that mixes tokens within a single example, enabling augmentation of features across scales. Both versions make the choice of what to mix central to the augmentation process. The authors report that their saliency-aware augmentation is 15 times faster than gradient-based alternatives, addressing the cost of obtaining the guidance signal.

Experiments on CIFAR and ImageNet-1K show significant improvements over the baseline models while being more efficient than previous methods. The approach also reaches state-of-the-art CIFAR-100 performance among transformers trained from scratch. These findings support attention-guided token mixing as a way to obtain useful content-aware augmentation without the computational burden of the compared gradient-based saliency methods.
summary.tldr: TokenMixup uses attention-guided token mixing to improve transformer classification with saliency-aware augmentation reported to be 15 times faster than gradient-based methods.

title: TokenMixup: Efficient Attention-guided Token-level Data Augmentation for Transformers

abstract: Conditional generative adversarial networks (cGANs) have shown superior results in class-conditional generation tasks. To simultaneously control multiple conditions, cGANs require multi-label training datasets, where multiple labels can be assigned to each data instance. Nevertheless, the tremendous annotation cost limits the accessibility of multi-label datasets in real-world scenarios. Therefore, in this study we explore the practical setting called the single positive setting, where each data instance is annotated by only one positive label with no explicit negative labels. To generate multi-label data in the single positive setting, we propose a novel sampling approach called single-to-multi-label (S2M) sampling, based on the Markov chain Monte Carlo method. As a widely applicable “add-on” method, our proposed S2M sampling method enables existing unconditional and conditional GANs to draw high-quality multi-label data with a minimal annotation cost. Extensive experiments on real image datasets verify the effectiveness and correctness of our method, even when compared to a model trained with fully annotated datasets.

To generate multi-label data in the single positive setting, we propose a novel sampling approach called single-to-multi-label (S2M) sampling, based on the Markov chain Monte Carlo method. As a widely applicable “add-on” method, our proposed S2M sampling method enables existing unconditional and conditional GANs to draw high-quality multi-label data with a minimal annotation cost. Extensive experiments on real image datasets verify the effectiveness and correctness of our method, even when compared to a model trained with fully annotated datasets.

paragraphs: Generating data that satisfies several conditions usually requires training examples annotated with multiple labels. Those annotations can be expensive. This paper considers a more limited setting: each example has one known positive label, and there are no explicit negative labels. An absent annotation therefore does not establish that a condition is absent from the example.

The proposed single-to-multi-label sampling method, S2M, uses Markov chain Monte Carlo to draw samples satisfying multiple labels. It operates as an add-on to existing generative adversarial networks, including both unconditional and conditional GANs. This makes the sampling procedure the central mechanism for obtaining multi-label outputs from the single-positive setting.

Experiments on real image datasets support the method's effectiveness and correctness, including comparisons with a model trained using fully annotated data. The findings suggest that useful control over several output conditions can be obtained with substantially lighter annotation requirements. The paper's contribution is specifically a broadly applicable sampling approach that enables existing GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data.
summary.tldr: S2M uses MCMC sampling to obtain multi-label GAN outputs from data annotated with only one positive label per example.

title: Mining Multi-Label Samples from Single Positive Labels

abstract: We focus on the task of creating a reinforcement learning agent that is inherently explainable---with the ability to produce immediate local explanations by thinking out loud while performing a task and analyzing entire trajectories post-hoc to produce temporally extended explanations. This Hierarchically Explainable Reinforcement Learning agent (HEX-RL), operates in Interactive Fictions, text-based game environments in which an agent perceives and acts upon the world using textual natural language. These games are usually structured as puzzles or quests with long-term dependencies in which an agent must complete a sequence of actions to succeed---providing ideal environments in which to test an agent's ability to explain its actions. Our agent is designed to treat explainability as a first-class citizen, using an extracted symbolic knowledge graph-based state representation coupled with a Hierarchical Graph Attention mechanism that points to the facts in the internal graph representation that most influenced the choice of actions. Experiments show that this agent provides significantly improved explanations over strong baselines, as rated by human participants generally unfamiliar with the environment, while also matching state-of-the-art task performance.

paragraphs: An agent’s actions can be difficult to understand when success depends on a long sequence of decisions. This paper develops HEX-RL, a reinforcement learning agent designed to explain individual choices as it acts and to explain longer stretches of behavior afterward. Its setting is interactive fiction, where observations and actions are expressed in text.

HEX-RL represents the game state using an extracted symbolic knowledge graph. A hierarchical graph attention mechanism identifies facts in that internal representation that most influenced an action choice. This connects explanation generation to information used in the agent’s decision process. Text-based puzzles and quests provide tasks where both immediate actions and longer dependencies matter.

Human participants, generally unfamiliar with the environments, rate HEX-RL’s explanations significantly better than those from strong baselines. The agent also matches state-of-the-art task performance. The findings show that this architecture can combine competitive game-playing ability with explanations people judge more useful, covering both local decisions and extended trajectories rather than only isolated actions.
summary.tldr: HEX-RL connects text-game decisions to knowledge-graph facts, improving human-rated explanations while matching state-of-the-art task performance.

title: Inherently Explainable Reinforcement Learning in Natural Language

abstract: Meta learning has demonstrated tremendous success in few-shot learning with limited supervised data. In those settings, the meta model is usually overparameterized. While the conventional statistical learning theory suggests that overparameterized models tend to overfit, empirical evidence reveals that overparameterized meta learning methods still work well -- a phenomenon often called ``benign overfitting.'' To understand this phenomenon, we focus on the meta learning settings with a challenging bilevel structure that we term the gradient-based meta learning, and analyze its generalization performance under an overparameterized meta linear regression model. While our analysis uses the relatively tractable linear models, our theory contributes to understanding the delicate interplay among data heterogeneity, model adaptation and benign overfitting in gradient-based meta learning tasks. We corroborate our theoretical claims through numerical simulations.

paragraphs: Meta-learning aims to support learning new tasks from limited supervision, and its models are often overparameterized. Such models can still perform well despite having enough flexibility to overfit. This paper investigates that benign-overfitting phenomenon in gradient-based meta-learning, where learning across tasks and adaptation within a task create a coupled, bilevel problem.

The authors analyze generalization using an overparameterized meta linear regression model. The linear setting provides a tractable way to examine how variation among task data interacts with model adaptation. Keeping the bilevel structure in the analysis matters because the learned meta model is evaluated through its ability to adapt, making adaptation part of the generalization question.

The resulting theory contributes to understanding the relationship among data heterogeneity, adaptation, and benign overfitting. Numerical simulations corroborate the theoretical claims. The scope is specifically a linear model, so the contribution is an analytical account within that setting rather than a general characterization of all nonlinear meta-learning systems. It supplies a basis for explaining why excess model capacity and useful performance can coexist in gradient-based meta-learning.
summary.tldr: An overparameterized linear-model analysis connects benign overfitting in gradient-based meta-learning to task heterogeneity and adaptation.

title: Understanding Benign Overfitting in Gradient-Based Meta Learning

abstract: We study a sequential matching problem faced by "large" centralized platforms where "jobs" must be matched to "workers" subject to uncertainty about worker skill proficiencies. Jobs arrive at discrete times with "job-types" observable upon arrival. To capture the "choice overload" phenomenon, we posit an unlimited supply of workers where each worker is characterized by a vector of attributes (aka "worker-types") drawn from an underlying population-level distribution. The distribution as well as mean payoffs for possible worker-job type-pairs are unobservables and the platform's goal is to sequentially match incoming jobs to workers in a way that maximizes its cumulative payoffs over the planning horizon. We establish lower bounds on the "regret" of any matching algorithm in this setting and propose a novel rate-optimal learning algorithm that adapts to aforementioned primitives "online." Our learning guarantees highlight a distinctive characteristic of the problem: achievable performance only has a "second-order" dependence on worker-type distributions; we believe this finding may be of interest more broadly.

paragraphs: The paper studies a platform that must assign arriving jobs to workers while learning which matches are valuable. A job’s type is visible on arrival, but the platform initially lacks knowledge of worker-type frequencies and average rewards for worker–job type combinations. Its objective is to maximize total payoff over a planning horizon.

To model a large market and choice overload, the analysis assumes an unlimited worker supply, with worker attributes drawn from an underlying population distribution. The authors establish lower bounds on regret, measuring the performance cost of learning, and propose an online algorithm that adapts to the unknown distribution and payoffs as matching proceeds.

The algorithm is rate-optimal relative to the established limits. A distinctive theoretical finding is that achievable performance depends only at second order on the worker-type distribution. This identifies a particular way that population composition enters the learning guarantees. The authors suggest that this dependence may have broader relevance, while their demonstrated result concerns the stated sequential matching model.
summary.tldr: A rate-optimal online algorithm learns profitable job–worker matches under unknown worker populations and match payoffs.

title: Dynamic Learning in Large Matching Markets

abstract: This paper studies policy optimization algorithms for multi-agent reinforcement learning. We begin by proposing an algorithm framework for two-player zero-sum Markov Games in the full-information setting, where each iteration consists of a policy update step at each state using a certain matrix game algorithm, and a value update step with a certain learning rate. This framework unifies many existing and new policy optimization algorithms. We show that the \emph{state-wise average policy} of this algorithm converges to an approximate Nash equilibrium (NE) of the game, as long as the matrix game algorithms achieve low weighted regret at each state, with respect to weights determined by the speed of the value updates. Next, we show that this framework instantiated with the Optimistic Follow-The-Regularized-Leader (OFTRL) algorithm at each state (and smooth value updates) can find an $\mathcal{\widetilde{O}}(T^{-5/6})$ approximate NE in $T$ iterations, and a similar algorithm with slightly modified value update rule achieves a faster $\mathcal{\widetilde{O}}(T^{-1})$ convergence rate. These improve over the current best $\mathcal{\widetilde{O}}(T^{-1/2})$ rate of symmetric policy optimization type algorithms. We also extend this algorithm to multi-player general-sum Markov Games and show an $\mathcal{\widetilde{O}}(T^{-3/4})$ convergence rate to Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE). Finally, we provide a numerical example to verify our theory and investigate the importance of smooth value updates, and find that using ''eager'' value updates instead (equivalent to the independent natural policy gradient algorithm) may significantly slow down the convergence, even on a simple game with $H=2$ layers.

The results emphasize that coordinating value updates with policy learning is central to the framework's guarantees and observed behavior.
summary.tldr: A unified policy-optimization framework yields faster equilibrium convergence guarantees through suitable state-wise learning algorithms and value updates.

title: Policy Optimization for Markov Games: Unified Framework and Faster Convergence

abstract: While preference modelling is becoming one of the pillars of machine learning, the problem of preference explanation remains challenging and underexplored. In this paper, we propose \textsc{Pref-SHAP}, a Shapley value-based model explanation framework for pairwise comparison data. We derive the appropriate value functions for preference models and further extend the framework to model and explain \emph{context specific} information, such as the surface type in a tennis game. To demonstrate the utility of \textsc{Pref-SHAP}, we apply our method to a variety of synthetic and real-world datasets and show that richer and more insightful explanations can be obtained over the baseline.

paragraphs: Preference models learn from comparisons, but predicting which option is preferred does not by itself explain that prediction. This paper addresses explanations for pairwise comparison data. Its aim is to make the reasoning represented by a preference model more understandable, including information that depends on the setting in which the comparison occurs.

The proposed framework, Pref-SHAP, builds on Shapley values. The authors derive value functions appropriate for preference models, giving the explanation framework a formulation tailored to comparisons. They then extend it to model and explain context-specific information. A tennis court's surface is the example given: the setting is part of what an explanation may need to account for.

The authors apply Pref-SHAP to synthetic and real-world datasets and report richer, more insightful explanations than the baseline. The stated contribution is explanatory rather than a claim of improved prediction accuracy. It connects a general approach to allocating explanatory credit with the particular structure of preferences and the contexts in which they are expressed.
summary.tldr: Pref-SHAP adapts Shapley-value explanations to pairwise preference models and context-specific information.

title: Explaining Preferences with Shapley Values

abstract: As several industries are moving towards modeling massive 3D virtual worlds, the need for content creation tools that can scale in terms of the quantity, quality, and diversity of 3D content is becoming evident. In our work, we aim to train performant 3D generative models that synthesize textured meshes which can be directly consumed by 3D rendering engines, thus immediately usable in downstream applications. Prior works on 3D generative modeling either lack geometric details, are limited in the mesh topology they can produce, typically do not support textures, or utilize neural renderers in the synthesis process, which makes their use in common 3D software non-trivial. In this work, we introduce GET3D, a Generative model that directly generates Explicit Textured 3D meshes with complex topology, rich geometric details, and high fidelity textures. We bridge recent success in the differentiable surface modeling, differentiable rendering as well as 2D Generative Adversarial Networks to train our model from 2D image collections. GET3D is able to generate high-quality 3D textured meshes, ranging from cars, chairs, animals, motorbikes and human characters to buildings, achieving significant improvements over previous methods.

paragraphs: GET3D addresses the need to create many detailed and varied three-dimensional objects for virtual worlds. Its target output is an explicit textured mesh that a standard rendering engine can consume directly. That output format matters because a generated object needs usable geometry and surface appearance to fit into downstream 3D applications.

The model combines differentiable surface modeling, differentiable rendering, and ideas from two-dimensional generative adversarial networks. This combination enables training from collections of 2D images while producing 3D meshes. The generated shapes can have complex topology, detailed geometry, and high-quality textures, addressing several restrictions identified in previous approaches.

The paper reports high-quality generation across categories including cars, chairs, animals, motorbikes, human characters, and buildings, with significant improvements over earlier methods. The contribution therefore concerns both visual quality and the form in which the generated content is delivered. Learning from images produces assets designed for direct use in rendering software, connecting image-based training to practical 3D content creation.
summary.tldr: GET3D learns from 2D image collections to generate detailed, textured 3D meshes that standard rendering engines can use directly.

title: GET3D: A Generative Model of High Quality 3D Textured Shapes Learned from Images

abstract: The vulnerability of deep neural networks has been widely found in various models as well as tasks where slight perturbations on the inputs could lead to incorrect predictions. These perturbed inputs are known as adversarial examples and one of the intriguing properties of them is Adversarial Transfersability, i.e. the capability of adversarial examples to fool other models. Traditionally, this transferability is always regarded as a critical threat to the defense against adversarial attacks, however, we argue that the network robustness can be significantly boosted by utilizing adversarial transferability from a new perspective. In this work, we first discuss the influence of different popular normalization layers on the adversarial transferability, and then provide both empirical evidence and theoretical analysis to shed light on the relationship between normalization types and transferability. Based on our theoretical analysis, we propose a simple yet effective module named Random Normalization Aggregation (RNA) which replaces the batch normalization layers in the networks and aggregates different selected normalization types to form a huge random space. Specifically, a random path is sampled during each inference procedure so that the network itself can be treated as an ensemble of a wide range of different models. Since the entire random space is designed with low adversarial transferability, it is difficult to perform effective attacks even when the network parameters are accessible. We conduct extensive experiments on various models and datasets, and demonstrate the strong superiority of proposed algorithm. The PyTorch code is available at https://github.com/UniSerj/Random-Norm-Aggregation and the MindSpore code is available at https://gitee.com/mindspore/models/tree/master/research/cv/RNA.

paragraphs: Small input perturbations can cause neural networks to make incorrect predictions, and an attack designed for one model may also fool another. This paper studies how normalization layers influence that transferability. It combines empirical evidence with theoretical analysis to motivate a defense built around making attacks transfer poorly between different model configurations.

Random Normalization Aggregation replaces batch normalization layers with a module that aggregates selected normalization types. Each inference samples a random path through these choices, producing a large space of possible configurations. The network can therefore act like an ensemble of many models while drawing a particular configuration for each prediction.

The intended protection comes from designing that random space to have low adversarial transferability. An attack effective against one configuration may have less success against another sampled configuration. The authors argue that this makes effective attacks difficult even when model parameters are accessible, and report strong experimental performance across multiple models and datasets. These findings support the defense empirically without establishing that every possible attack must fail.
summary.tldr: Random Normalization Aggregation strengthens adversarial defense by sampling normalization configurations designed to have low attack transferability.

title: Random Normalization Aggregation for Adversarial Defense

abstract: Additive Noise Models (ANMs) are a common model class for causal discovery from observational data. Due to a lack of real-world data for which an underlying ANM is known, ANMs with randomly sampled parameters are commonly used to simulate data for the evaluation of causal discovery algorithms. While some parameters may be fixed by explicit assumptions, fully specifying an ANM requires choosing all parameters. Reisach et al. (2021) show that, for many ANM parameter choices, sorting the variables by increasing variance yields an ordering close to a causal order and introduce ‘var-sortability’ to quantify this alignment. Since increasing variances may be unrealistic and cannot be exploited when data scales are arbitrary, ANM data are often rescaled to unit variance in causal discovery benchmarking.We show that synthetic ANM data are characterized by another pattern that is scale-invariant and thus persists even after standardization: the explainable fraction of a variable’s variance, as captured by the coefficient of determination $R^2$, tends to increase along the causal order. The result is high ‘$R^2$-sortability’, meaning that sorting the variables by increasing $R^2$ yields an ordering close to a causal order. We propose a computationally efficient baseline algorithm termed ‘$R^2$-SortnRegress’ that exploits high $R^2$-sortability and that can match and exceed the performance of established causal discovery algorithms. We show analytically that sufficiently high edge weights lead to a relative decrease of the noise contributions along causal chains, resulting in increasingly deterministic relationships and high $R^2$. We characterize $R^2$-sortability on synthetic data with different simulation parameters and find high values in common settings. Our findings reveal high $R^2$-sortability as an assumption about the data generating process relevant to causal discovery and implicit in many ANM sampling schemes. It should be made explicit, as its prevalence in real-world data is an open question. For causal discovery benchmarking, we provide implementations of $R^2$-sortability, the $R^2$-SortnRegress algorithm, and ANM simulation procedures in our library CausalDisco at https://causaldisco.github.io/CausalDisco/.

paragraphs: Causal discovery algorithms are often evaluated on simulated additive noise models, where variables depend on their causes plus noise. These simulations can contain shortcuts: ordering variables by variance may already approximate their causal order. Standardizing every variable removes that particular clue, but the paper identifies another clue that survives changes in scale.

The new clue is the fraction of a variable’s variance that can be explained, measured by R². In common simulation settings, this fraction tends to increase along the causal order. The authors quantify this pattern as R²-sortability and introduce R²-SortnRegress, an efficient baseline that exploits it and can match or outperform established causal discovery algorithms.

Their analysis shows that sufficiently large edge weights reduce the relative contribution of noise along causal chains, producing increasingly deterministic relationships. Experiments characterize how simulation choices affect this pattern. The implication is that benchmark performance can depend on an implicit property of the data generator. Whether similarly high R²-sortability is common in real data remains an open question.
summary.tldr: A scale-invariant pattern in synthetic causal data provides a strong sorting baseline and exposes an implicit assumption in common benchmarks.

title: A Scale-Invariant Sorting Criterion to Find a Causal Order in Additive Noise Models

abstract: The recent success of transformer-based image generative models in object-centric learning highlights the importance of powerful image generators for handling complex scenes. However, despite the high expressiveness of diffusion models in image generation, their integration into object-centric learning remains largely unexplored in this domain. In this paper, we explore the feasibility and potential of integrating diffusion models into object-centric learning and investigate the pros and cons of this approach. We introduce Latent Slot Diffusion (LSD), a novel model that serves dual purposes: it is the first object-centric learning model to replace conventional slot decoders with a latent diffusion model conditioned on object slots, and it is also the first unsupervised compositional conditional diffusion model that operates without the need for supervised annotations like text. Through experiments on various object-centric tasks, including the first application of the FFHQ dataset in this field, we demonstrate that LSD significantly outperforms state-of-the-art transformer-based decoders, particularly in more complex scenes, and exhibits superior unsupervised compositional generation quality. In addition, we conduct a preliminary investigation into the integration of pre-trained diffusion models in LSD and demonstrate its effectiveness in real-world image segmentation and generation. Project page is available at https://latentslotdiffusion.github.io

paragraphs: Object-centric learning aims to organize visual information into representations associated with objects. This paper asks whether the expressive image-generation capabilities of diffusion models can improve that process, especially for complex scenes. It introduces Latent Slot Diffusion, or LSD, which conditions a latent diffusion image generator on learned object slots.

The diffusion model replaces the conventional decoder that reconstructs images from those slots. This makes the generator part of the object-centric learning system while also enabling compositional conditional generation without supervised annotations such as text. The shared design connects learning object-based representations with generating images from those representations.

Across the evaluated object-centric tasks, LSD significantly outperforms compared state-of-the-art Transformer decoders, particularly on more complex scenes, and produces stronger unsupervised compositional generations. The experiments also bring FFHQ into this evaluation setting. A separate preliminary investigation incorporates pretrained diffusion models and demonstrates effectiveness for real-world image segmentation and generation. Those initial results support further integration, while the principal evidence concerns the proposed slot-conditioned diffusion architecture.
summary.tldr: Latent Slot Diffusion uses object slots to condition diffusion generation, improving evaluated object-centric learning and unsupervised compositional generation.

title: Object-Centric Slot Diffusion

abstract: In this work, we study the implications of the implicit bias of gradient flow on generalization and adversarial robustness in ReLU networks. We focus on a setting where the data consists of clusters and the correlations between cluster means are small, and show that in two-layer ReLU networks gradient flow is biased towards solutions that generalize well, but are vulnerable to adversarial examples. Our results hold even in cases where the network is highly overparameterized. Despite the potential for harmful overfitting in such settings, we prove that the implicit bias of gradient flow prevents it. However, the implicit bias also leads to non-robust solutions (susceptible to small adversarial $\ell_2$-perturbations), even though robust networks that fit the data exist.
originalAbstract: In this work, we study the implications of the implicit bias of gradient flow on generalization and adversarial robustness in ReLU networks. We focus on a setting where the data consists of clusters and the correlations between cluster means are small, and show that in two-layer ReLU networks gradient flow is biased towards solutions that generalize well, but are vulnerable to adversarial examples. Our results hold even in cases where the network is highly overparameterized. Despite the potential for harmful overfitting in such settings, we prove that the implicit bias of gradient flow prevents it. However, the implicit bias also leads to non-robust solutions (susceptible to small adversarial $\ell_2$-perturbations), even though robust networks that fit the data exist.

paragraphs: Training can favor particular solutions even without an explicit penalty specifying which solution to choose. This implicit bias may help a network generalize, but the paper asks whether it also supports resistance to adversarial changes. It studies gradient flow in two-layer ReLU networks under a specific clustered-data setting.

The analysis assumes that correlations between cluster means are small. Within this setting, gradient flow favors solutions that generalize well and avoids harmful overfitting, even when the network has many more parameters than might be needed to fit the data. This establishes a benefit of the optimization dynamics despite the network's capacity to fit undesirable solutions.

The same dynamics nevertheless lead to vulnerability to small adversarial perturbations measured in the ℓ2 norm. Robust networks fitting the data do exist, so the vulnerability is associated with the solutions favored by training rather than their absence from the model class. The result separates ordinary generalization from adversarial robustness under the stated assumptions: successful prediction on new data does not ensure resistance to deliberately chosen small changes.
summary.tldr: For clustered data with weakly correlated means, gradient flow favors two-layer ReLU networks that generalize well but remain adversarially vulnerable.

title: The Double-Edged Sword of Implicit Bias: Generalization vs. Robustness in ReLU Networks

abstract: Trending topic diffusion and prediction analysis is an important problem and has been well studied in social networks. Representation learning is an effective way to extract node embeddings, which can help for topic propagation analysis by completing downstream tasks such as link prediction and node classification. In real world, there are often several trending topics or opinion leaders in public opinion space at the same time and they can be regarded as different centers of public opinion. A public opinion field will be formed surrounding every center. These public opinion fields compete for public's attention and it will potentially affect the development of public opinion. However, the existing methods do not consider public opinion field effect for trending topics diffusion. In this paper, we introduce three well-known observations about public opinion field effect in media and communication studies, and propose a novel and effective heterogeneous representation learning framework to incorporate public opinion field effect and social circle influence effect. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to consider these effects in representation learning for trending topic diffusion. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets validate the superiority of our model.

paragraphs: Several trending topics or opinion leaders can attract attention at the same time. This paper treats each as a center of a public-opinion field, with the surrounding fields competing for public attention. Such competition can potentially influence how topics spread, yet the authors argue that existing representation-learning approaches overlook this effect.

The proposed heterogeneous representation-learning framework incorporates both public-opinion field effects and social-circle influence. It draws on three observations from media and communication studies to guide that design. The learned node representations are intended to support downstream analysis of topic propagation, including tasks such as link prediction and node classification.

Experiments on real-world datasets report stronger performance than the compared methods. The findings support incorporating interactions among attention centers and social circles into representations used for diffusion analysis. The authors qualify their novelty claim as the first such treatment to their knowledge. The contribution is a modeling approach with empirical support; the idea that competing fields may shape opinion development remains distinct from claiming a universal causal law for how every topic spreads.
summary.tldr: A representation-learning framework incorporates competition among public-opinion centers and social-circle influence to improve trending-topic diffusion analysis.

title: Public Opinion Field Effect Fusion in Representation Learning for Trending Topics Diffusion

abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models have recently received a lot of interest for their astonishing ability to produce high-fidelity images from text only. However, achieving one-shot generation that aligns with the user’s intent is nearly impossible, yet small changes to the input prompt often result in very different images. This leaves the user with little semantic control. To put the user in control, we show how to interact with the diffusion process to flexibly steer it along semantic directions. This semantic guidance (SEGA) generalizes to any generative architecture using classifier-free guidance. More importantly, it allows for subtle and extensive edits, composition and style changes, and optimizing the overall artistic conception. We demonstrate SEGA’s effectiveness on both latent and pixel-based diffusion models such as Stable Diffusion, Paella, and DeepFloyd-IF using a variety of tasks, thus providing strong evidence for its versatility and flexibility.

paragraphs: SEGA addresses the difficulty of controlling text-to-image generation through prompt wording alone. A generated image may miss the user's intent, while a small prompt change can produce a substantially different result. The paper introduces semantic guidance as a way to interact with the generation process and steer it along meaningful directions.

The method supports both subtle and extensive edits, as well as changes in composition, style, and overall artistic conception. Its stated scope extends to generative architectures that use classifier-free guidance. This architectural condition is central to the claimed generality: the steering mechanism builds on that form of guidance.

The authors demonstrate SEGA across varied tasks using latent and pixel-based diffusion models, including Stable Diffusion, Paella, and DeepFloyd-IF. These experiments provide evidence of versatility across the tested models and editing needs. The contribution is a more flexible interface to the diffusion process, allowing semantic control during generation rather than relying entirely on finding a prompt that yields the intended image.
summary.tldr: SEGA steers image generation along semantic directions and applies to generative architectures using classifier-free guidance.

title: SEGA: Instructing Text-to-Image Models using Semantic Guidance

abstract: The recent explosion of interest in multimodal applications has resulted in a wide selection of datasets and methods for representing and integrating information from different modalities. Despite these empirical advances, there remain fundamental research questions: How can we quantify the interactions that are necessary to solve a multimodal task? Subsequently, what are the most suitable multimodal models to capture these interactions? To answer these questions, we propose an information-theoretic approach to quantify the degree of redundancy, uniqueness, and synergy relating input modalities with an output task. We term these three measures as the PID statistics of a multimodal distribution (or PID for short), and introduce two new estimators for these PID statistics that scale to high-dimensional distributions. To validate PID estimation, we conduct extensive experiments on both synthetic datasets where the PID is known and on large-scale multimodal benchmarks where PID estimations are compared with human annotations. Finally, we demonstrate their usefulness in (1) quantifying interactions within multimodal datasets, (2) quantifying interactions captured by multimodal models, (3) principled approaches for model selection, and (4) three real-world case studies engaging with domain experts in pathology, mood prediction, and robotic perception where our framework helps to recommend strong multimodal models for each application.

paragraphs: Multimodal models combine different kinds of input, but their usefulness depends on how those inputs relate to the prediction task. Some information may be repeated across modalities, some may be available from only one, and some may emerge from their combination. This paper develops an information-theoretic framework for quantifying these forms of interaction.

The framework measures redundancy, uniqueness, and synergy through partial information decomposition, or PID. The authors introduce two estimators that scale to high-dimensional distributions. They evaluate estimation on synthetic datasets with known PID values and on large multimodal benchmarks, where estimates are compared with human annotations. These tests examine whether the measures capture meaningful interaction structure.

The authors then use PID to characterize both datasets and the interactions learned by models, supporting principled model selection. Three case studies involve domain experts in pathology, mood prediction, and robotic perception. In those applications, the framework helps recommend strong multimodal models. Its contribution is to make interaction requirements measurable and connect them to choices about how modalities should be modeled together.
summary.tldr: Scalable information-decomposition estimates quantify multimodal interactions and help guide model selection.

title: Quantifying & Modeling Multimodal Interactions: An Information Decomposition Framework

abstract: Audio-Visual Source Localization (AVSL) aims to locate sounding objects within video frames given the paired audio clips. Existing methods predominantly rely on self-supervised contrastive learning of audio-visual correspondence. Without any bounding-box annotations, they struggle to achieve precise localization, especially for small objects, and suffer from blurry boundaries and false positives. Moreover, the naive semi-supervised method is poor in effectively utilizing the abundance of unlabeled audio-visual pairs. In this paper, we propose a novel Semi-Supervised Learning framework for AVSL, namely Dual Mean-Teacher (DMT), comprising two teacher-student structures to circumvent the confirmation bias issue. Specifically, two teachers, pre-trained on limited labeled data, are employed to filter out noisy samples via the consensus between their predictions, and then generate high-quality pseudo-labels by intersecting their confidence maps. The optimal utilization of both labeled and unlabeled data combined with this unbiased framework enable DMT to outperform current state-of-the-art methods by a large margin, with CIoU of $\textbf{90.4\%}$ and $\textbf{48.8\%}$ on Flickr-SoundNet and VGG-Sound Source, obtaining $\textbf{8.9\%}$ and $\textbf{9.6\%}$ improvements respectively, given only $3\%$ of data positional-annotated. We also extend our framework to some existing AVSL methods and consistently boost their performance. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/gyx-gloria/DMT.

Learning only from audio-image correspondence can leave imprecise boundaries, false detections, and difficulty with small objects. The paper investigates how a small amount of positional annotation can help exploit a much larger collection of unlabeled pairs.

Dual Mean-Teacher uses two teacher-student structures to address confirmation bias, where a model reinforces its own incorrect predictions. Both teachers are initially trained with limited labeled data. Agreement between their predictions filters noisy samples, and intersections of their confidence maps provide pseudo-labels for further learning.

The abstract reports improvements of 8.9% and 9.6%, respectively. Applying the framework to existing localization methods also consistently improves their performance, supporting the usefulness of teacher agreement for making unlabeled audio-visual examples more informative.
summary.tldr: Two cooperating teacher models produce cleaner pseudo-labels, improving audio-visual localization with only a small amount of positional annotation.

title: Dual Mean-Teacher: An Unbiased Semi-Supervised Framework for Audio-Visual Source Localization

abstract: In this paper, we present Neural k-Opt (NeuOpt), a novel learning-to-search (L2S) solver for routing problems. It learns to perform flexible k-opt exchanges based on a tailored action factorization method and a customized recurrent dual-stream decoder. As a pioneering work to circumvent the pure feasibility masking scheme and enable the autonomous exploration of both feasible and infeasible regions, we then propose the Guided Infeasible Region Exploration (GIRE) scheme, which supplements the NeuOpt policy network with feasibility-related features and leverages reward shaping to steer reinforcement learning more effectively. Additionally, we equip NeuOpt with Dynamic Data Augmentation (D2A) for more diverse searches during inference. Extensive experiments on the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) and Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP) demonstrate that our NeuOpt not only significantly outstrips existing (masking-based) L2S solvers, but also showcases superiority over the learning-to-construct (L2C) and learning-to-predict (L2P) solvers. Notably, we offer fresh perspectives on how neural solvers can handle VRP constraints. Our code is available: https://github.com/yining043/NeuOpt.

paragraphs: Routing solvers search for good routes while respecting problem constraints. Neural search methods often mask out moves that would violate those constraints, restricting where the search can go. This paper introduces NeuOpt and a guided strategy that allows exploration of both feasible and infeasible regions.

NeuOpt learns flexible k-opt exchanges, which modify routes through exchanges involving multiple connections. A tailored action factorization and recurrent dual-stream decoder represent these moves. The Guided Infeasible Region Exploration scheme adds feasibility information to the policy network and shapes reinforcement-learning rewards to steer exploration. Dynamic Data Augmentation further diversifies searches at inference time.

Experiments on the Traveling Salesman Problem and Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem report substantial gains over existing masking-based learning-to-search methods. The authors also report superiority over the evaluated learning-to-construct and learning-to-predict solvers. The findings support treating constraint handling as part of a learned search strategy, with explicit guidance for exploring infeasible regions, rather than limiting the search entirely through feasibility masks.
summary.tldr: NeuOpt learns flexible route exchanges and uses feasibility-aware rewards to search both feasible and infeasible regions effectively.

title: Learning to Search Feasible and Infeasible Regions of Routing Problems with Flexible Neural k-Opt

abstract: A popular benchmark for intra-patient lung registration is provided by the DIR-LAB COPDgene dataset consisting of large-motion in- and expiratory breath-hold CT pairs. This dataset alone, however, does not provide enough samples to properly train state-of-the-art deep learning methods. Other public datasets often also provide only small sample sizes or include primarily small motions between scans that do not translate well to larger deformations. For point-based geometric registration, the PVT1010 dataset provides a large number of vessel point clouds without any correspondences and a labeled test set corresponding to the COPDgene cases. However, the absence of correspondences for supervision complicates training, and a fair comparison with image-based algorithms is infeasible, since CT scans for the training data are not publicly available.We here provide a combined benchmark for image- and point-based registration approaches. We curated a total of 248 public multi-centric in- and expiratory lung CT scans from 124 patients, which show large motion between scans, processed them to ensure sufficient homogeneity between the data and generated vessel point clouds that are well distributed even deeper inside the lungs. For supervised training, we provide vein and artery segmentations of the vessels and multiple thousand image-derived keypoint correspondences for each pair. For validation, we provide multiple scan pairs with manual landmark annotations. Finally, as first baselines on our new benchmark, we evaluate several image and point cloud registration methods on the dataset.

paragraphs: Lung registration aligns scans of the same patient taken at different breathing stages. Large breathing-related motion makes this challenging, and existing public resources have limitations for training and comparing modern methods. Some contain too few examples or mostly small motions; a large vessel point-cloud dataset lacks training correspondences and publicly available matching CT scans.

Lung250M-4B brings image-based and point-based registration into a combined benchmark. The authors curate 248 public CT scans from 124 patients across multiple centers, pairing inhalation and exhalation scans with large motion. They process the scans for sufficient homogeneity and generate vessel point clouds that also cover regions deeper inside the lungs.

For supervised training, the dataset includes vein and artery segmentations and several thousand image-derived keypoint correspondences per pair. Validation pairs include manually annotated landmarks. The authors also evaluate several image and point-cloud registration methods as initial baselines. The central contribution is a shared data resource that supports supervised learning and more direct comparison of approaches operating on different representations of lung anatomy.
summary.tldr: Lung250M-4B combines paired lung CT scans, vessel point clouds, and correspondence annotations to support training and comparison of registration methods.

title: Lung250M-4B: A Combined 3D Dataset for CT- and Point Cloud-Based Intra-Patient Lung Registration

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) aims to learn optimal policies from offline datasets, where the parameterization of policies is crucial but often overlooked. Recently, Diffsuion-QL significantly boosts the performance of offline RL by representing a policy with a diffusion model, whose success relies on a parametrized Markov Chain with hundreds of steps for sampling. However, Diffusion-QL suffers from two critical limitations. 1) It is computationally inefficient to forward and backward through the whole Markov chain during training. 2) It is incompatible with maximum likelihood-based RL algorithms (e.g., policy gradient methods) as the likelihood of diffusion models is intractable. Therefore, we propose efficient diffusion policy (EDP) to overcome these two challenges. EDP approximately constructs actions from corrupted ones at training to avoid running the sampling chain. We conduct extensive experiments on the D4RL benchmark. The results show that EDP can reduce the diffusion policy training time from 5 days to 5 hours on gym-locomotion tasks. Moreover, we show that EDP is compatible with various offline RL algorithms (TD3, CRR, and IQL) and achieves new state-of-the-art on D4RL by large margins over previous methods.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns action-selection policies from existing datasets. Diffusion models offer an effective policy representation, but the earlier Diffusion-QL approach requires a sampling chain with hundreds of steps. Passing through that chain during training is expensive, and the intractable likelihood of diffusion models complicates compatibility with likelihood-based reinforcement learning methods.

Efficient Diffusion Policy, or EDP, addresses these obstacles by approximately constructing actions from corrupted actions during training. This avoids running the full sampling chain for that training operation. The contribution concerns how diffusion policies are trained and incorporated into offline learning algorithms, preserving their usefulness while reducing a major computational burden.

On D4RL gym-locomotion tasks, the authors report a training-time reduction from five days to five hours. They also demonstrate compatibility with TD3, CRR, and IQL, and report state-of-the-art D4RL performance with large improvements over earlier methods. These findings indicate that the tested efficiency gains accompany strong policy performance, making diffusion policies more practical within several offline reinforcement learning approaches.
summary.tldr: EDP avoids full diffusion sampling chains during training, sharply reducing reported training time while improving offline reinforcement learning performance.

title: Efficient Diffusion Policies For Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Traditional federated learning (FL) algorithms operate under the assumption that the data distributions at training (source domains) and testing (target domain) are the same. The fact that domain shifts often occur in practice necessitates equipping FL methods with a domain generalization (DG) capability. However, existing DG algorithms face fundamental challenges in FL setups due to the lack of samples/domains in each client’s local dataset. In this paper, we propose StableFDG, a style and attention based learning strategy for accomplishing federated domain generalization, introducing two key contributions. The first is style-based learning, which enables each client to explore novel styles beyond the original source domains in its local dataset, improving domain diversity based on the proposed style sharing, shifting, and exploration strategies. Our second contribution is an attention-based feature highlighter, which captures the similarities between the features of data samples in the same class, and emphasizes the important/common characteristics to better learn the domain-invariant characteristics of each class in data-poor FL scenarios. Experimental results show that StableFDG outperforms existing baselines on various DG benchmark datasets, demonstrating its efficacy.

paragraphs: Federated learning becomes harder when the data encountered after training differ from the training domains. Domain-generalization methods seek to handle that shift, but each federated client may have too few examples or too little domain variety to apply them effectively. StableFDG addresses both local diversity and the learning of characteristics shared across domains.

Its first component expands the styles a client can learn from through style sharing, shifting, and exploration. This allows training to consider styles beyond those originally present in the client's data. Its second component is an attention-based feature highlighter. It compares features of examples from the same class and emphasizes their important common characteristics, helping the model learn class information that is less tied to a particular domain.

The two components address complementary difficulties: restricted exposure to variation and limited evidence about what should remain stable across that variation. Experiments show that StableFDG outperforms existing baselines on multiple domain-generalization benchmarks. These results support the combination of style diversity and attention to shared class features in the evaluated federated settings with limited local data.
summary.tldr: StableFDG combines expanded style diversity with attention to shared class features to improve federated generalization across domains.

title: StableFDG: Style and Attention Based Learning for Federated Domain Generalization

abstract: Biases with respect to socially-salient attributes of individuals have been well documented in evaluation processes used in settings such as admissions and hiring. We view such an evaluation process as a transformation of a distribution of the true utility of an individual for a task to an observed distribution and model it as a solution to a loss minimization problem subject to an information constraint. Our model has two parameters that have been identified as factors leading to biases: the resource-information trade-off parameter in the information constraint and the risk-averseness parameter in the loss function. We characterize the distributions that arise from our model and study the effect of the parameters on the observed distribution. The outputs of our model enrich the class of distributions that can be used to capture variation across groups in the observed evaluations. We empirically validate our model by fitting real-world datasets and use it to study the effect of interventions in a downstream selection task. These results contribute to an understanding of the emergence of bias in evaluation processes and provide tools to guide the deployment of interventions to mitigate biases.

paragraphs: Evaluations in hiring or admissions can differ systematically across socially salient groups. This paper models the evaluation process as a transformation from a distribution of individuals' true usefulness for a task into a distribution of observed evaluations. That perspective separates the underlying quantity being assessed from the scores that an evaluation process ultimately produces.

The transformation is described as minimizing a loss while operating under an information constraint. Two parameters capture proposed contributors to bias: the trade-off between resources and available information, and the evaluator's aversion to risk. The authors characterize the resulting distributions and examine how changing these parameters affects observed evaluations.

The model expands the range of distributions available for representing differences in evaluations across groups. The authors fit it to real-world datasets and use it to examine interventions in a subsequent selection task. These findings support the model as a tool for studying how evaluation processes can generate bias and how interventions may change selection outcomes. They do not establish that either parameter alone explains every real evaluation disparity.
summary.tldr: An optimization model connects information constraints and risk aversion to biased evaluations and downstream selection outcomes.

title: Bias in Evaluation Processes: An Optimization-Based Model

abstract: Phased releases are a common strategy in the technology industry for gradually releasing new products or updates through a sequence of A/B tests in which the number of treated units gradually grows until full deployment or deprecation. Performing phased releases in a principled way requires selecting the proportion of units assigned to the new release in a way that balances the risk of an adverse effect with the need to iterate and learn from the experiment rapidly. In this paper, we formalize this problem and propose an algorithm that automatically determines the release percentage at each stage in the schedule, balancing the need to control risk while maximizing ramp-up speed. Our framework models the challenge as a constrained batched bandit problem that ensures that our pre-specified experimental budget is not depleted with high probability. Our proposed algorithm leverages an adaptive Bayesian approach in which the maximal number of units assigned to the treatment is determined by the posterior distribution, ensuring that the probability of depleting the remaining budget is low. Notably, our approach analytically solves the ramp sizes by inverting probability bounds, eliminating the need for challenging rare-event Monte Carlo simulation. It only requires computing means and variances of outcome subsets, making it highly efficient and parallelizable.

Our proposed algorithm leverages an adaptive Bayesian approach in which the maximal number of units assigned to the treatment is determined by the posterior distribution, ensuring that the probability of depleting the remaining budget is low. Notably, our approach analytically solves the ramp sizes by inverting probability bounds, eliminating the need for challenging rare-event Monte Carlo simulation. It only requires computing means and variances of outcome subsets, making it highly efficient and parallelizable.

paragraphs: A phased release exposes increasing numbers of users or other units to a new product through successive A/B tests. Increasing exposure quickly can accelerate learning, but it also increases exposure to a potentially harmful change. This paper formalizes the choice of release percentages as a constrained batched bandit problem, making the trade-off between speed and risk explicit.

The algorithm uses an adaptive Bayesian approach to choose the largest treatment group permitted by its risk calculation at each stage. Its posterior distribution informs how much additional exposure the remaining experimental budget can support. The framework aims to keep the probability of exhausting that budget low; its protection is a high-probability guarantee rather than a claim that adverse outcomes cannot occur.

A key computational contribution is solving for release sizes analytically by inverting probability bounds. This avoids relying on rare-event Monte Carlo simulations to estimate budget-depletion risk. The required calculations use means and variances of outcome subsets, which makes the procedure efficient and parallelizable. The result is a principled way to adapt a rollout schedule as experimental evidence accumulates.
summary.tldr: An adaptive Bayesian algorithm chooses phased-release sizes to accelerate rollout while keeping experimental budget depletion unlikely.

title: Balancing Risk and Reward: A Batched-Bandit Strategy for Automated Phased Release

abstract: Denoising diffusion generative models are capable of generating high-quality data, but suffers from the computation-costly generation process, due to a iterative noise estimation using full-precision networks. As an intuitive solution, quantization can significantly reduce the computational and memory consumption by low-bit parameters and operations. However, low-bit noise estimation networks in diffusion models (DMs) remain unexplored yet and perform much worse than the full-precision counterparts as observed in our experimental studies. In this paper, we first identify that the bottlenecks of low-bit quantized DMs come from a large distribution oscillation on activations and accumulated quantization error caused by the multi-step denoising process. To address these issues, we first develop a Timestep-aware Quantization (TaQ) method and a Noise-estimating Mimicking (NeM) scheme for low-bit quantized DMs (Q-DM) to effectively eliminate such oscillation and accumulated error respectively, leading to well-performed low-bit DMs. In this way, we propose an efficient Q-DM to calculate low-bit DMs by considering both training and inference process in the same framework. We evaluate our methods on popular DDPM and DDIM models. Extensive experimental results show that our method achieves a much better performance than the prior arts. For example, the 4-bit Q-DM theoretically accelerates the 1000-step DDPM by 7.8x and achieves a FID score of 5.17, on the unconditional CIFAR-10 dataset.

paragraphs: Diffusion generation repeatedly runs a noise-estimation network, making full-precision computation expensive. Low-bit quantization can reduce computation and memory use, but the authors observe a substantial quality loss when applying it to these networks. They identify changing activation distributions and quantization error accumulated over denoising steps as the central obstacles.

Q-DM addresses these problems through two components. Timestep-aware Quantization handles activation-distribution oscillation, while Noise-estimating Mimicking targets accumulated error. The framework considers both training and inference so that low-bit operation is supported throughout the proposed approach, rather than treated only as a change to numerical precision.

For unconditional CIFAR-10 generation, a four-bit Q-DM achieves a FID score of 5.17 and a theoretical 7.8-fold acceleration of a 1,000-step DDPM. The acceleration is explicitly theoretical, rather than a measured wall-clock claim. The results support accounting for the changing, multistep nature of denoising when designing diffusion-model quantization.
summary.tldr: Q-DM addresses timestep-dependent activations and accumulated quantization error to improve low-bit diffusion generation.

title: Q-DM: An Efficient Low-bit Quantized Diffusion Model

abstract: Reinforcement learning presents an attractive paradigm to reason about several distinct aspects of sequential decision making, such as specifying complex goals, planning future observations and actions, and critiquing their utilities. However, the combined integration of these capabilities poses competing algorithmic challenges in retaining maximal expressivity while allowing for flexibility in modeling choices for efficient learning and inference. We present Decision Stacks, a generative framework that decomposes goal-conditioned policy agents into 3 generative modules. These modules simulate the temporal evolution of observations, rewards, and actions via independent generative models that can be learned in parallel via teacher forcing. Our framework guarantees both expressivity and flexibility in designing individual modules to account for key factors such as architectural bias, optimization objective and dynamics, transferrability across domains, and inference speed. Our empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of Decision Stacks for offline policy optimization for several MDP and POMDP environments, outperforming existing methods and enabling flexible generative decision making.

paragraphs: Sequential decision making combines several jobs: representing a goal, anticipating observations and actions, and assessing their utility. Combining all of them creates competing demands on model expressivity, training, and inference. Decision Stacks addresses this design problem by separating a goal-conditioned agent into three generative modules.

The modules model the evolution of observations, rewards, and actions. They can be trained independently and in parallel through teacher forcing, using supplied sequences during learning. This modular organization lets designers make different architectural and optimization choices for the different components. The framework guarantees expressivity while allowing flexibility around factors such as transfer across domains and inference speed.

The authors evaluate Decision Stacks for offline policy optimization in several environments, including both fully and partially observable settings. They report improvements over existing methods. The significance is that the separation into modules supports effective decision making while preserving room to choose how each part is modeled. The experiments demonstrate that this flexibility can coexist with strong performance in the evaluated environments.
summary.tldr: Decision Stacks separates goal-conditioned decision making into generative observation, reward, and action modules, enabling flexible design and effective offline learning.

title: Decision Stacks: Flexible Reinforcement Learning via Modular Generative Models

abstract: Radar signal interpretation plays a crucial role in remote detection and ranging. With the gradual display of the advantages of neural network technology in signal processing, learning-based radar signal interpretation is becoming a research hot-spot and made great progress. And since radar semantic segmentation (RSS) can provide more fine-grained target information, it has become a more concerned direction in this field. However, the temporal information, which is an important clue for analyzing radar data, has not been exploited sufficiently in present RSS frameworks. In this work, we propose a novel temporal information learning paradigm, i.e., data-driven temporal information aggregation with learned target-history relations. Following this idea, a flexible learning module, called Temporal Relation-Aware Module (TRAM) is carefully designed. TRAM contains two main blocks: i) an encoder for capturing the target-history temporal relations (TH-TRE) and ii) a learnable temporal relation attentive pooling (TRAP) for aggregating temporal information. Based on TRAM, an end-to-end Temporal-Aware RSS Network (TARSS-Net) is presented, which has outstanding performance on publicly available and our collected real-measured datasets. Code and supplementary materials are available at https://github.com/zlw9161/TARSS-Net.
