paragraphs: Orientation maps organize neurons according to the edge directions they respond to most strongly. Such maps have long been associated with the layered visual cortex of mammals. This paper asks whether similar organization can emerge in a visual system without that cortical structure, using the fruit fly brain as the system to investigate.

The authors combine a complete fruit fly brain wiring map with biologically grounded models of spiking neurons. They stimulate the resulting network with visual inputs at different orientations and examine responses farther along the visual pathway. This ties the simulated processing to measured connectivity while allowing the researchers to study how the network’s dynamics organize responses.

The simulations show that coherent orientation maps can emerge from dynamics constrained by the connectome. This supports the possibility that cortical architecture is not required for such organization in the modeled setting. The authors suggest that independently originating species could evolve similar visual structures. That evolutionary interpretation remains a suggestion drawn from the computational result, which concerns map formation in the simulated fly visual system.
summary.tldr: A spiking model constrained by the fruit fly connectome produces coherent orientation maps, suggesting similar visual organization can emerge without a cortex.

title: Connectome-Based Modelling Reveals Orientation Maps in the Drosophila Optic Lobe

abstract: We introduce InfinityStar, a unified spacetime autoregressive framework for high-resolution image and dynamic video synthesis. Building on the recent success of autoregressive modeling in both vision and language, our purely discrete approach jointly captures spatial and temporal dependencies within a single architecture. This unified design naturally supports a variety of generation tasks such as text-to-image, text-to-video, image-to-video, and long-duration video synthesis via straightforward temporal autoregression. Through extensive experiments, InfinityStar scores 83.74 on VBench, outperforming all autoregressive models by large margins, even surpassing diffusion competitors like HunyuanVideo. Without extra optimizations, our model generates a 5s, 720p video approximately 10$\times$ faster than leading diffusion-based methods. To our knowledge, InfinityStar is the first discrete autoregressive video generator capable of producing industrial-level 720p videos. We release all code and models to foster further research in efficient, high-quality video generation.

paragraphs: InfinityStar uses one discrete autoregressive architecture to generate both images and videos. Its central idea is to model spatial relationships within imagery and temporal relationships across video together. This gives a common framework for text-to-image, text-to-video, image-to-video, and longer video generation.

For extended videos, the framework continues generation through temporal autoregression: later content is generated in sequence. The unified design connects still-image synthesis and dynamic video synthesis through the same modeling approach. The paper presents this as a route to high-resolution visual generation using a purely discrete representation.

The authors report a VBench score of 83.74, exceeding all autoregressive models in their comparison and diffusion competitors including HunyuanVideo. They also report generating a five-second, 720p video roughly ten times faster than leading diffusion methods without additional optimization. These results support the approach’s combination of quality and speed. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first discrete autoregressive video generator capable of industrial-level 720p output and release its code and models.
summary.tldr: InfinityStar unifies discrete autoregressive image and video generation, reporting strong quality and substantially faster video synthesis.

title: InfinityStar: Uniﬁed Spacetime AutoRegressive Modeling for Visual Generation

abstract: Real world systems often have parameterized controllers which can be tuned to improve performance. Bayesian optimization methods provide for efficient optimization of these controllers, so as to reduce the number of required experiments on the expensive physical system. In this paper we address Bayesian optimization in the setting where performance is only observed through a stochastic binary outcome – success or failure of the experiment. Unlike bandit problems, the goal is to maximize the system performance after this offline training phase rather than minimize regret during training. In this work we define the stochastic binary optimization problem and propose an approach using an adaptation of Gaussian Processes for classification that presents a Bayesian optimization framework for this problem. We propose an experiment selection metric for this setting based on expected improvement. We demonstrate the algorithm’s performance on synthetic problems and on a real snake robot learning to move over an obstacle.

paragraphs: Tuning a physical controller can require expensive experiments, and an experiment may reveal only success or failure. The paper studies optimization under this stochastic binary feedback. Its objective is to obtain a strong controller after an offline training phase, so the value of an experiment comes from helping select the final controller.

The authors define this optimization problem and develop a Bayesian optimization framework using an adaptation of Gaussian processes for classification. This accommodates binary observations while supporting decisions about which controller settings to try next. They also propose an experiment-selection metric based on expected improvement, tailored to the success-or-failure setting.

The approach is demonstrated on synthetic problems and a real snake robot learning to cross an obstacle. These applications show how binary experimental feedback can guide controller optimization even when no graded performance measurement is observed. The paper's contribution is the combination of a problem formulation, a probabilistic modeling approach, and a criterion for selecting informative experiments.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian optimization framework tunes expensive controllers using only stochastic success-or-failure observations.

title: Expensive Function Optimization with Stochastic Binary Outcomes

abstract: The stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD) algorithm is appealing for large scale Bayesian learning. The SGLD algorithm seamlessly transit stochastic optimization and Bayesian posterior sampling. However, solid theories, such as convergence proof, have not been developed. We theoretically analyze the SGLD algorithm with constant stepsize in two ways. First, we show by using the Fokker-Planck equation that the probability distribution of random variables generated by the SGLD algorithm converges to the Bayesian posterior. Second, we analyze the convergence of the SGLD algorithm by using the Ito process, which reveals that the SGLD algorithm does not strongly but weakly converges. This result indicates that the SGLD algorithm can be an approximation method for posterior averaging.

First, we show by using the Fokker-Planck equation that the probability distribution of random variables generated by the SGLD algorithm converges to the Bayesian posterior. paragraphs: Stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics, or SGLD, connects stochastic optimization with sampling from a Bayesian posterior. This makes it appealing for Bayesian learning at large scale, but the paper addresses a gap in its theoretical foundations. The authors focus specifically on the behavior of SGLD with a constant step size.

They analyze the algorithm through two mathematical perspectives. Using the Fokker-Planck equation, they show convergence of the distribution of the generated random variables to the Bayesian posterior. Using an Ito process, they examine the type of convergence and report weak convergence rather than strong convergence. These are distinct statements about the behavior of the algorithm.

The distinction matters for how the generated samples can be used. Weak convergence concerns distributional behavior rather than strong agreement of individual random trajectories. The authors interpret their result as supporting SGLD as an approximation method for posterior averaging. The stated implication is therefore about estimating posterior averages within the analyzed constant-step-size setting.
summary.tldr: Two analyses of constant-step-size SGLD establish distributional and weak convergence results supporting its use for approximate posterior averaging.

title: Approximation Analysis of Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics by using Fokker-Planck Equation and Ito Process

abstract: Sequence prediction and classification are ubiquitous and challenging problems in machine learning that can require identifying complex dependencies between temporally distant inputs. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have the ability, in theory, to cope with these temporal dependencies by virtue of the short-term memory implemented by their recurrent (feedback) connections. However, in practice they are difficult to train successfully when long-term memory is required. This paper introduces a simple, yet powerful modification to the simple RNN (SRN) architecture, the Clockwork RNN (CW-RNN), in which the hidden layer is partitioned into separate modules, each processing inputs at its own temporal granularity, making computations only at its prescribed clock rate. Rather than making the standard RNN models more complex, CW-RNN reduces the number of SRN parameters, improves the performance significantly in the tasks tested, and speeds up the network evaluation. The network is demonstrated in preliminary experiments involving three tasks: audio signal generation, TIMIT spoken word classification, where it outperforms both SRN and LSTM networks, and online handwriting recognition, where it outperforms SRNs.

paragraphs: Sequence tasks often require connecting information separated by many time steps. Recurrent neural networks can theoretically retain relevant information through feedback connections, but training them to use long-term memory is difficult in practice. This paper introduces the Clockwork RNN, an architectural modification that gives different parts of the network different schedules for processing a sequence.

The hidden layer is divided into modules, with each module computing only at its assigned clock rate. This lets the architecture process inputs at multiple temporal granularities instead of requiring every hidden unit to operate at the same pace. The paper reports that this design reduces the number of parameters relative to a simple RNN and makes network evaluation faster.

Preliminary experiments cover audio signal generation, spoken word classification on TIMIT, and online handwriting recognition. The Clockwork RNN outperforms both simple RNNs and LSTMs on the spoken word task, and simple RNNs on handwriting recognition. These findings support the usefulness of scheduled hidden modules on the tested tasks; they do not establish superiority across all sequence problems.
summary.tldr: Clockwork RNNs update hidden modules at different rates, reducing parameters and evaluation cost while improving performance on the tested sequence tasks.

title: A Clockwork RNN

abstract: k-means++ seeding has become a de facto standard for hard clustering algorithms. In this paper, our first contribution is a two-way generalisation of this seeding, k-variates++, that includes the sampling of general densities rather than just a discrete set of Dirac densities anchored at the point locations, *and* a generalisation of the well known Arthur-Vassilvitskii (AV) approximation guarantee, in the form of a *bias+variance* approximation bound of the *global* optimum. This approximation exhibits a reduced dependency on the "noise" component with respect to the optimal potential — actually approaching the statistical lower bound. We show that k-variates++ *reduces* to efficient (biased seeding) clustering algorithms tailored to specific frameworks; these include distributed, streaming and on-line clustering, with *direct* approximation results for these algorithms. Finally, we present a novel application of k-variates++ to differential privacy. For either the specific frameworks considered here, or for the differential privacy setting, there is little to no prior results on the direct application of k-means++ and its approximation bounds — state of the art contenders appear to be significantly more complex and / or display less favorable (approximation) properties. We stress that our algorithms can still be run in cases where there is *no* closed form solution for the population minimizer. We demonstrate the applicability of our analysis via experimental evaluation on several domains and settings, displaying competitive performances vs state of the art.

paragraphs: Choosing initial cluster centers is an important part of hard clustering. This paper generalizes k-means++ seeding so that sampling can use general probability densities rather than only probability masses located at observed data points. The resulting method, k-variates++, broadens the kinds of sampling procedures that can fit within the seeding framework.

The theoretical contribution also generalizes the usual approximation guarantee. The authors derive a bias-plus-variance bound relative to the global optimum, with reduced dependence on the noise component and behavior approaching a statistical lower bound. They show how the framework specializes to efficient clustering algorithms for distributed, streaming, and online settings, supplying direct approximation results for those algorithms.

The paper additionally applies k-variates++ to differential privacy. The algorithms remain usable when the population minimizer has no closed-form expression, so an explicit solution to that population problem is not required to run them. Experiments across several domains and settings show competitive performance against leading alternatives. The contribution combines a broader seeding rule with analysis that carries into several computational settings.
summary.tldr: k-variates++ extends k-means++ to general sampling densities and supplies approximation guarantees for distributed, streaming, online, and private clustering settings.

title: k-variates++: more pluses in the k-means++

abstract: Subspace clustering with missing data (SCMD) is a useful tool for analyzing incomplete datasets. Let d be the ambient dimension, and r the dimension of the subspaces. Existing theory shows that Nk = O(r d) columns per subspace are necessary for SCMD, and Nk =O(min d^(log d), d^(r+1) ) are sufficient. We close this gap, showing that Nk =O(r d) is also sufficient. To do this we derive deterministic sampling conditions for SCMD, which give precise information theoretic requirements and determine sampling regimes. These results explain the performance of SCMD algorithms from the literature. Finally, we give a practical algorithm to certify the output of any SCMD method deterministically.

paragraphs: Subspace clustering with missing data groups incomplete observations according to their underlying subspaces. The paper asks how much observed information is sufficient for this task. With ambient dimension d and subspace dimension r, earlier theory left a large gap between the stated necessary number of columns per subspace and the known sufficient number.

The authors close that gap by showing that O(rd) columns per subspace are sufficient, matching the necessary scale described in the abstract. They derive deterministic sampling conditions that specify information-theoretic requirements and distinguish sampling regimes. These conditions make the pattern of available information part of the analysis, alongside the number of columns.

The results also explain the performance of existing subspace-clustering methods. Beyond the sample requirements, the paper supplies a practical algorithm for deterministically certifying the output of any method for this problem. This connects a theoretical account of when the data contains enough information with a separate procedure for checking a proposed clustering result.
summary.tldr: Deterministic sampling conditions close the sample-requirement gap for subspace clustering with missing data and enable output certification.

title: The Information-Theoretic Requirements of Subspace Clustering with Missing Data

abstract: Archetypal Analysis is the method of choice to compute interpretable matrix factorizations. Every data point is represented as a convex combination of factors, i.e., points on the boundary of the convex hull of the data. This renders computation inefficient. In this paper, we show that the set of vertices of a convex hull, the so-called frame, can be efficiently computed by a quadratic program. We provide theoretical and empirical results for our proposed approach and make use of the frame to accelerate Archetypal Analysis. The novel method yields similar reconstruction errors as baseline competitors but is much faster to compute.

paragraphs: Archetypal Analysis seeks interpretable matrix factorizations by representing each data point as a convex combination of factors. Such combinations use nonnegative weights that sum to one. The factors lie on the boundary of the data’s convex hull, tying the representation to the outer geometry of the observed data while making computation expensive.

This paper focuses on the frame, the set of vertices defining that convex hull. The authors show that it can be computed efficiently using a quadratic program and provide both theoretical and empirical results for their approach. They then use the computed frame to accelerate Archetypal Analysis.

The resulting method achieves reconstruction errors similar to those of the baseline competitors while taking much less time to compute. That comparison matters because speed alone would be less useful if the factorization stopped representing the data well. The stated results indicate that exploiting the frame can preserve comparable reconstruction quality while reducing the computational burden of this interpretable factorization approach.
summary.tldr: Computing convex-hull vertices with a quadratic program accelerates Archetypal Analysis while retaining comparable reconstruction error.

title: Frame-based Data Factorizations

abstract: Hierarchical architectures are critical to the scalability of reinforcement learning methods. Most current hierarchical frameworks execute actions serially, with macro-actions comprising sequences of primitive actions. We propose a novel alternative to these control hierarchies based on concurrent execution of many actions in parallel. Our scheme exploits the guaranteed concurrent compositionality provided by the linearly solvable Markov decision process (LMDP) framework, which naturally enables a learning agent to draw on several macro-actions simultaneously to solve new tasks. We introduce the Multitask LMDP module, which maintains a parallel distributed representation of tasks and may be stacked to form deep hierarchies abstracted in space and time.

Many existing frameworks execute those actions serially, with each macro-action corresponding to a sequence of simpler actions. This paper proposes a different organization in which an agent can draw on several macro-actions concurrently when solving a new task.

The construction uses linearly solvable Markov decision processes, or LMDPs. Their guaranteed concurrent compositionality provides the mathematical basis for combining multiple actions in parallel. That property is central to the proposal: the ability to combine behaviors follows from the chosen framework, rather than being asserted for arbitrary reinforcement-learning systems.

The authors introduce a Multitask LMDP module that holds a parallel, distributed representation of tasks. Modules may be stacked to create deeper hierarchies with abstraction across both space and time. The contribution is an architectural route to hierarchy through composition, making simultaneous use of multiple macro-actions part of the representation and control scheme. It broadens how hierarchical behavior can be organized within the LMDP setting.
summary.tldr: Multitask LMDP modules build control hierarchies by composing several macro-actions concurrently.

title: Hierarchy Through Composition with Multitask LMDPs

abstract: A common practice in statistics and machine learning is to assume that the statistical data types (e.g., ordinal, categorical or real-valued) of variables, and usually also the likelihood model, is known. However, as the availability of real-world data increases, this assumption becomes too restrictive. Data are often heterogeneous, complex, and improperly or incompletely documented. Surprisingly, despite their practical importance, there is still a lack of tools to automatically discover the statistical types of, as well as appropriate likelihood (noise) models for, the variables in a dataset. In this paper, we fill this gap by proposing a Bayesian method, which accurately discovers the statistical data types in both synthetic and real data.

paragraphs: Statistical analysis commonly starts by deciding what kind of variable each dataset column represents. A variable might describe an unordered category, an ordered category, or a real-valued measurement. Those choices affect how a model interprets observations and represents noise. This paper treats those choices as something to learn from the data.

The motivation is practical: real datasets often mix different kinds of variables and arrive with incomplete or unreliable documentation. Assuming that their statistical types and suitable likelihood models are already known can therefore be restrictive. The authors propose a Bayesian method to address the discovery of these modeling ingredients automatically.

The reported results show accurate identification of statistical data types on both synthetic and real datasets. The contribution is a way to support a decision that usually precedes model fitting but is often taken for granted. By making variable interpretation part of inference, the approach addresses uncertainty about how heterogeneous data should be modeled.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian method automatically identifies statistical variable types in heterogeneous, incompletely documented datasets.

title: Automatic Discovery of the Statistical Types of Variables in a Dataset

abstract: Boolean tensor decomposition approximates data of multi-way binary relationships as product of interpretable low-rank binary factors, following the rules Boolean algebra. Here, we present its first probabilistic treatment. We facilitate scalable sampling-based posterior inference by exploitation of the combinatorial structure of the factor conditionals. Maximum a posteriori estimates consistently outperform existing non-probabilistic approaches. We show that our performance gains can partially be explained by convergence to solutions that occupy relatively large regions of the parameter space, as well as by implicit model averaging. Moreover, the Bayesian treatment facilitates model selection with much greater accuracy than the previously suggested minimum description length based approach. We investigate three real-world data sets. First, temporal interaction networks and behavioural data of university students demonstrate the inference of instructive latent patterns. Next, we decompose a tensor with more than 10 Billion data points, indicating relations of gene expression in cancer patients. Not only does this demonstrate scalability, it also provides an entirely novel perspective on relational properties of continuous data and, in the present example, on the molecular heterogeneity of cancer. Our implementation is available on GitHub: https://github.com/TammoR/LogicalFactorisationMachines

paragraphs: Boolean tensor decomposition summarizes multiway binary relationships through a small set of interpretable binary factors combined using Boolean algebra. This paper introduces a probabilistic treatment of that decomposition. It uses the combinatorial structure of conditional distributions over factors to make sampling-based posterior inference scalable.

The authors report that maximum a posteriori estimates consistently outperform existing nonprobabilistic approaches. They partly attribute these gains to finding solutions occupying larger regions of parameter space and to implicit model averaging. The Bayesian formulation also improves model selection accuracy relative to a previously proposed minimum-description-length approach, addressing both how factors are fitted and how a model is selected.

Three real-world datasets illustrate the method. Student interaction and behavioral data reveal informative latent patterns, while a cancer gene-expression application involves a tensor exceeding ten billion entries. That larger example demonstrates scalability and offers a relational view of continuous data. In the cancer setting, this perspective exposes structure relevant to molecular heterogeneity rather than treating the measurements only as isolated numerical values.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian approach to Boolean tensor decomposition improves reported factor estimation and model selection while scaling to billions of entries.

title: Probabilistic Boolean Tensor Decomposition

abstract: Gaussian mixture models (GMM) are the most widely used statistical model for the k-means clustering problem and form a popular framework for clustering in machine learning and data analysis. In this paper, we propose a natural robust model for k-means clustering that generalizes the Gaussian mixture model, and that we believe will be useful in identifying robust algorithms. Our first contribution is a polynomial time algorithm that provably recovers the ground-truth up to small classification error w.h.p., assuming certain separation between the components. Perhaps surprisingly, the algorithm we analyze is the popular Lloyd’s algorithm for k-means clustering that is the method-of-choice in practice. Our second result complements the upper bound by giving a nearly matching lower bound on the number of misclassified points incurred by any k-means clustering algorithm on the semi-random model.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a semi-random model for k-means clustering that generalizes Gaussian mixture models. The aim is to provide a setting for studying robust clustering algorithms while retaining enough structure for mathematical analysis. The central question is how accurately an algorithm can recover the underlying groups in this more general model.

The authors show that a polynomial-time algorithm recovers the true grouping with only a small classification error, with high probability, provided the components have the required separation. The analyzed method is Lloyd’s algorithm, a widely used approach to k-means. This connects a familiar practical procedure to a recovery guarantee under the proposed model.

A complementary lower bound establishes that any k-means clustering algorithm can incur a certain number of misclassified points in this setting. Because this bound nearly matches the upper bound, the analysis also characterizes how much improvement remains possible. The recovery claim depends on component separation and permits a small error rather than requiring perfect clustering.
summary.tldr: Lloyd’s algorithm receives recovery guarantees for a semi-random Gaussian-mixture generalization, with a nearly matching error lower bound.

title: Clustering Semi-Random Mixtures of Gaussians

abstract: An important question that arises in the study of high dimensional vector representations learned from data is: given a set D of vectors and a query q, estimate the number of points within a specified distance threshold of q. Our algorithm uses locality sensitive hashing to preprocess the data to accurately and efficiently estimate the answers to such questions via an unbiased estimator that uses importance sampling. A key innovation is the ability to maintain a small number of hash tables via preprocessing data structures and algorithms that sample from multiple buckets in each hash table. We give bounds on the space requirements and query complexity of our scheme, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm by experiments on a standard word embedding dataset.
originalAbstract: An important question that arises in the study of high dimensional vector representations learned from data is: given a set D of vectors and a query q, estimate the number of points within a specified distance threshold of q. Our algorithm uses locality sensitive hashing to preprocess the data to accurately and efficiently estimate the answers to such questions via an unbiased estimator that uses importance sampling. A key innovation is the ability to maintain a small number of hash tables via preprocessing data structures and algorithms that sample from multiple buckets in each hash table. We give bounds on the space requirements and query complexity of our scheme, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm by experiments on a standard word embedding dataset.

paragraphs: The paper studies a local counting problem for high-dimensional vector data: given a query vector and a distance threshold, estimate how many stored vectors fall within that distance. Such a count describes how densely populated the query's neighborhood is. The goal is to answer these queries accurately and efficiently.

The algorithm preprocesses the vectors with locality sensitive hashing and constructs an unbiased estimator using importance sampling. Unbiasedness means that the estimator is correct on average over its sampling randomness, rather than that every individual estimate equals the true count. The sampling procedure provides the statistical basis for estimating the neighborhood population.

A central design feature is sampling from multiple buckets within each hash table. Supporting data structures and preprocessing allow the method to operate with a small number of tables. The authors provide bounds on storage requirements and query complexity, linking this design to computational costs. Experiments on a standard word-embedding dataset demonstrate effectiveness for the kind of learned vector representations that motivate the problem.
summary.tldr: The method combines locality sensitive hashing and importance sampling to estimate neighborhood counts using few hash tables.

title: Local Density Estimation in High Dimensions

abstract: Neural density estimators are flexible families of parametric models which have seen widespread use in unsupervised machine learning in recent years. Maximum-likelihood training typically dictates that these models be constrained to specify an explicit density. However, this limitation can be overcome by instead using a neural network to specify an energy function, or unnormalized density, which can subsequently be normalized to obtain a valid distribution. The challenge with this approach lies in accurately estimating the normalizing constant of the high-dimensional energy function. We propose the Autoregressive Energy Machine, an energy-based model which simultaneously learns an unnormalized density and computes an importance-sampling estimate of the normalizing constant for each conditional in an autoregressive decomposition. The Autoregressive Energy Machine achieves state-of-the-art performance on a suite of density-estimation tasks.
originalAbstract: Neural density estimators are flexible families of parametric models which have seen widespread use in unsupervised machine learning in recent years. However, this limitation can be overcome by instead using a neural network to specify an energy function, or unnormalized density, which can subsequently be normalized to obtain a valid distribution. The challenge with this approach lies in accurately estimating the normalizing constant of the high-dimensional energy function. We propose the Autoregressive Energy Machine, an energy-based model which simultaneously learns an unnormalized density and computes an importance-sampling estimate of the normalizing constant for each conditional in an autoregressive decomposition. The Autoregressive Energy Machine achieves state-of-the-art performance on a suite of density-estimation tasks.

paragraphs: A density estimator learns how probability is distributed across possible observations. Neural versions are flexible, but maximum-likelihood training usually requires an explicitly specified probability density. An energy-based model instead learns an unnormalized score, allowing the network to describe a distribution before calculating the adjustment needed to make its probabilities sum or integrate to one.

That adjustment, the normalizing constant, is difficult to estimate for a high-dimensional energy function. The Autoregressive Energy Machine addresses this challenge by decomposing the distribution into conditional distributions. It learns an unnormalized density while using importance sampling to estimate the normalizing constant for each conditional. The autoregressive organization therefore provides a way to handle normalization through the individual conditional components.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on a collection of density-estimation tasks. These findings support combining the flexibility of energy-based modeling with conditional normalization estimates. A central distinction is that normalization is estimated through sampling; the approach does not depend on requiring every learned conditional density to arrive already normalized.
summary.tldr: Autoregressive Energy Machines learn flexible energy-based densities and estimate each conditional distribution’s normalization through importance sampling.

title: Autoregressive Energy Machines

abstract: We propose a stochastic gradient framework for solving stochastic composite convex optimization problems with (possibly) infinite number of linear inclusion constraints that need to be satisfied almost surely. We use smoothing and homotopy techniques to handle constraints without the need for matrix-valued projections. We show for our stochastic gradient algorithm $\mathcal{O}(\log(k)/\sqrt{k})$ convergence rate for general convex objectives and $\mathcal{O}(\log(k)/k)$ convergence rate for restricted strongly convex objectives. These rates are known to be optimal up to logarithmic factor, even without constraints. We conduct numerical experiments on basis pursuit, hard margin support vector machines and portfolio optimization problems and show that our algorithm achieves state-of-the-art practical performance.

We show for our stochastic gradient algorithm $\mathcal{O}(\log(k)/\sqrt{k})$ convergence rate for general convex objectives and $\mathcal{O}(\log(k)/k)$ convergence rate for restricted strongly convex objectives. These rates are known to be optimal up to logarithmic factor, even without constraints. We conduct numerical experiments on basis pursuit, hard margin support vector machines and portfolio optimization problems and show that our algorithm achieves state-of-the-art practical performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies convex optimization when both the objective and the constraints involve randomness. The constraints must hold almost surely, meaning with probability one, and there may be infinitely many linear inclusion constraints. This makes satisfying the constraints a central part of learning, rather than something that can be checked against a short, fixed list.

The authors propose a stochastic gradient framework that combines smoothing with homotopy techniques. Smoothing makes the constraint treatment more manageable for gradient updates, while homotopy changes that treatment progressively. Together, these techniques let the method handle the constraints without requiring matrix-valued projections.

The analysis gives convergence rates of O(log(k)/sqrt(k)) for general convex objectives and O(log(k)/k) for restricted strongly convex objectives. These match known optimal rates up to a logarithmic factor, even compared with problems without constraints. Experiments on basis pursuit, hard-margin support vector machines, and portfolio optimization report state-of-the-art practical performance, supporting the usefulness of the framework across these tested problems.
summary.tldr: A stochastic gradient framework handles potentially infinitely many almost-sure constraints while achieving convergence rates optimal up to logarithmic factors.

title: Almost surely constrained convex optimization

abstract: Many applications in machine learning require optimizing a function whose true gradient is unknown or computationally expensive, but where surrogate gradient information, directions that may be correlated with the true gradient, is cheaply available. For example, this occurs when an approximate gradient is easier to compute than the full gradient (e.g. in meta-learning or unrolled optimization), or when a true gradient is intractable and is replaced with a surrogate (e.g. in reinforcement learning or training networks with discrete variables). We propose Guided Evolutionary Strategies (GES), a method for optimally using surrogate gradient directions to accelerate random search. GES defines a search distribution for evolutionary strategies that is elongated along a subspace spanned by the surrogate gradients and estimates a descent direction which can then be passed to a first-order optimizer. We analytically and numerically characterize the tradeoffs that result from tuning how strongly the search distribution is stretched along the guiding subspace and use this to derive a setting of the hyperparameters that works well across problems. We evaluate GES on several example problems, demonstrating an improvement over both standard evolutionary strategies and first-order methods that directly follow the surrogate gradient.

paragraphs: Optimization sometimes offers a cheap approximate gradient even when the true gradient is unavailable or expensive. Such surrogate directions may correlate with the direction that would improve the objective, but following them directly can be imperfect. Guided Evolutionary Strategies uses these directions to inform random search.

The method stretches its search distribution along the subspace spanned by surrogate gradients. It then estimates a descent direction that can be supplied to a first-order optimizer. This lets surrogate information shape where the algorithm searches while retaining an evolutionary-strategy estimate of how to update the parameters. The strength of the stretching controls how much emphasis the guiding subspace receives.

The authors analyze this tradeoff mathematically and numerically, using it to derive hyperparameter settings that work well across problems. Evaluations on several example problems show improvements over both standard evolutionary strategies and methods that directly follow surrogate gradients. These results support using approximate gradients as structured guidance for search when their information is useful but does not fully substitute for a true gradient.
summary.tldr: Guided Evolutionary Strategies uses surrogate-gradient directions to shape random search and improves on unguided search and direct surrogate updates in example problems.

title: Guided evolutionary strategies: augmenting random search with surrogate gradients

abstract: We investigate online convex optimization in changing environments, and choose the adaptive regret as the performance measure. The goal is to achieve a small regret over every interval so that the comparator is allowed to change over time. Different from previous works that only utilize the convexity condition, this paper further exploits smoothness to improve the adaptive regret. To this end, we develop novel adaptive algorithms for convex and smooth functions, and establish problem-dependent regret bounds over any interval. Our regret bounds are comparable to existing results in the worst case, and become much tighter when the comparator has a small loss.

The goal is to achieve a small regret over every interval so that the comparator is allowed to change over time. Different from previous works that only utilize the convexity condition, this paper further exploits smoothness to improve the adaptive regret. To this end, we develop novel adaptive algorithms for convex and smooth functions, and establish problem-dependent regret bounds over any interval. paragraphs: This paper considers online optimization in environments that change over time. Performance is measured through adaptive regret, which asks how well a learner performs over every time interval relative to a comparator for that interval. This makes the evaluation sensitive to changing conditions: good performance over the full sequence alone does not establish good performance during each shorter period.

The authors develop adaptive algorithms for loss functions that are both convex and smooth. Earlier work used convexity, while this approach also exploits smoothness to obtain stronger guarantees. The resulting bounds depend on properties of the particular problem and apply over any interval. In particular, they account for how much loss the comparator incurs.

In the worst case, the new regret guarantees remain comparable to existing results. When the comparator achieves a small loss, the bounds become substantially tighter. The benefit is therefore conditional on the difficulty of the interval being evaluated. The work shows how smoothness can support more informative guarantees for changing environments without claiming an improvement of the same size on every sequence.
summary.tldr: Exploiting smoothness yields adaptive regret bounds that improve when the interval's comparator has low loss while remaining competitive in the worst case.

title: Adaptive Regret of Convex and Smooth Functions

abstract: The change-point detection problem seeks to identify distributional changes in streams of data. Increasingly, tools for change-point detection are applied in settings where data may be highly sensitive and formal privacy guarantees are required, such as identifying disease outbreaks based on hospital records, or IoT devices detecting activity within a home. Differential privacy has emerged as a powerful technique for enabling data analysis while preventing information leakage about individuals. Much of the prior work on change-point detection{—}including the only private algorithms for this problem{—}requires complete knowledge of the pre-change and post-change distributions, which is an unrealistic assumption for many practical applications of interest. This work develops differentially private algorithms for solving the change-point detection problem when the data distributions are unknown. Additionally, the data may be sampled from distributions that change smoothly over time, rather than fixed pre-change and post-change distributions. We apply our algorithms to detect changes in the linear trends of such data streams. Finally, we also provide experimental results to empirically validate the performance of our algorithms.

paragraphs: Change-point detection seeks to identify when the distribution generating a data stream changes. In applications involving hospital records or activity inside a home, detecting a shift must also respect the sensitivity of individual observations. This paper develops detection algorithms with differential privacy guarantees for settings where the underlying distributions are unknown.

The unknown-distribution setting is central to the contribution. Much prior work described in the abstract, including the existing private methods, assumes complete knowledge of the distributions before and after a change. Removing that requirement addresses situations where the detector must work without being given both sides of the transition in advance.

The proposed setting also allows distributions to evolve smoothly over time, rather than remaining fixed on either side of a single abrupt change. The authors apply their algorithms to detecting changes in linear trends and provide experiments validating their performance. The work thus broadens private change detection along two dimensions: incomplete distributional knowledge and streams whose ordinary behavior can itself vary over time.
summary.tldr: The paper develops differentially private change detectors for unknown distributions, including streams with smoothly evolving behavior and changing linear trends.

title: Privately detecting changes in unknown distributions

abstract: Random Features (RF) models are used as efficient parametric approximations of kernel methods. We investigate, by means of random matrix theory, the connection between Gaussian RF models and Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR). For a Gaussian RF model with $P$ features, $N$ data points, and a ridge $\lambda$, we show that the average (i.e. expected) RF predictor is close to a KRR predictor with an \emph{effective ridge} $\tilde{\lambda}$. We show that $\tilde{\lambda} > \lambda$ and $\tilde{\lambda} \searrow \lambda$ monotonically as $P$ grows, thus revealing the \emph{implicit regularization effect} of finite RF sampling. We then compare the risk (i.e. test error) of the $\tilde{\lambda}$-KRR predictor with the average risk of the $\lambda$-RF predictor and obtain a precise and explicit bound on their difference. Finally, we empirically find an extremely good agreement between the test errors of the average $\lambda$-RF predictor and $\tilde{\lambda}$-KRR predictor.

For a Gaussian RF model with $P$ features, $N$ data points, and a ridge $\lambda$, we show that the average (i.e. expected) RF predictor is close to a KRR predictor with an \emph{effective ridge} $\tilde{\lambda}$. We show that $\tilde{\lambda} > \lambda$ and $\tilde{\lambda} \searrow \lambda$ monotonically as $P$ grows, thus revealing the \emph{implicit regularization effect} of finite RF sampling. We then compare the risk (i.e. test error) of the $\tilde{\lambda}$-KRR predictor with the average risk of the $\lambda$-RF predictor and obtain a precise and explicit bound on their difference. Finally, we empirically find an extremely good agreement between the test errors of the average $\lambda$-RF predictor and $\tilde{\lambda}$-KRR predictor.

paragraphs: Random-feature models approximate kernel methods using a finite collection of features. This paper examines how that approximation changes the predictor, beyond simply making computation more manageable. Using random matrix theory, the authors relate Gaussian random-feature regression to kernel ridge regression, which explicitly regularizes the fitted model through a ridge parameter.

For a model with P features, N observations, and ridge parameter lambda, the expected random-feature predictor is close to a kernel predictor with an effective ridge larger than lambda. As the number of features increases, that effective ridge decreases monotonically toward lambda. Finite feature sampling therefore introduces additional regularization even when the explicit ridge setting stays fixed.

The authors also derive an explicit bound comparing the effective-ridge kernel predictor’s test error with the average risk of the random-feature predictor. Empirically, they find very close agreement between the test errors of the averaged random-feature predictor and the corresponding kernel predictor. The distinction between an expected predictor and an individual random realization matters to interpreting these results.
summary.tldr: Finite Gaussian random-feature sampling acts like additional ridge regularization, with its strength decreasing as more features are used.

title: Implicit Regularization of Random Feature Models

abstract: We introduce a new way of learning to encode position information for non-recurrent models, such as Transformer models. Unlike RNN and LSTM, which contain inductive bias by loading the input tokens sequentially, non-recurrent models are less sensitive to position. The main reason is that position information among input units is not encoded inherently, i.e., they are permutation equivalent, this problem justifies why all of the existing models are accompanied by position encoding/embedding layer at the input. However, this solution has clear limitations: the sinusoidal position encoding is not flexible enough as it is manually designed and does not contain any learnable parameters, whereas the position embedding restricts the maximum length of input sequences. It is thus desirable to design a new position layer that contains learnable parameters to adjust to different datasets and different architectures. At the same time, we would also like it to extrapolate in accordance with the variable length of inputs. In our proposed solution, we borrow from the recent Neural ODE approach, which may be viewed as a versatile continuous version of a ResNet. This model is capable of modeling many kinds of dynamical systems. We model the evolution of encoded results along position index by such a dynamical system, thereby overcoming the above limitations of existing methods. We evaluate our new position layers on a variety of neural machine translation and language understanding tasks, the experimental results show consistent improvements over the baselines.

However, this solution has clear limitations: the sinusoidal position encoding is not flexible enough as it is manually designed and does not contain any learnable parameters, whereas the position embedding restricts the maximum length of input sequences. It is thus desirable to design a new position layer that contains learnable parameters to adjust to different datasets and different architectures. At the same time, we would also like it to extrapolate in accordance with the variable length of inputs. In our proposed solution, we borrow from the recent Neural ODE approach, which may be viewed as a versatile continuous version of a ResNet. This model is capable of modeling many kinds of dynamical systems. We model the evolution of encoded results along position index by such a dynamical system, thereby overcoming the above limitations of existing methods. We evaluate our new position layers on a variety of neural machine translation and language understanding tasks, the experimental results show consistent improvements over the baselines.

paragraphs: Models such as Transformers need an explicit way to represent token position because they do not process inputs sequentially like recurrent networks. Common choices create a trade-off: fixed sinusoidal encodings have no learnable parameters, while position embeddings restrict the maximum sequence length. The paper seeks a position representation that is both adaptable and able to extend across input lengths.

Its solution models the evolution of positional encodings as a continuous dynamical system. Drawing on Neural ODEs, the authors learn how the encoding changes along the position index. This provides parameters that can adapt to different datasets and architectures while supporting extrapolation as the input length varies.

Experiments on neural machine translation and language understanding tasks report consistent improvements over the evaluated baselines. The contribution places a learned continuous process inside the position layer, connecting flexibility and variable-length encoding in one design. The reported task improvements support that design without establishing that extrapolation will succeed equally well for every possible sequence length.
summary.tldr: A learned continuous dynamical system encodes token positions and improves results on translation and language understanding tasks.

title: Learning to Encode Position for Transformer with Continuous Dynamical Model

abstract: We consider the study of a classification model whose properties are impossible to estimate using a validation set, either due to the absence of such a set or because access to the classifier, even as a black-box, is impossible. Instead, only aggregate statistics on the rate of positive predictions in each of several sub-populations are available, as well as the true rates of positive labels in each of these sub-populations. We show that these aggregate statistics can be used to lower-bound the discrepancy of a classifier, which is a measure that balances inaccuracy and unfairness. To this end, we define a new measure of unfairness, equal to the fraction of the population on which the classifier behaves differently, compared to its global, ideally fair behavior, as defined by the measure of equalized odds. We propose an efficient and practical procedure for finding the best possible lower bound on the discrepancy of the classifier, given the aggregate statistics, and demonstrate in experiments the empirical tightness of this lower bound, as well as its possible uses on various types of problems, ranging from estimating the quality of voting polls to measuring the effectiveness of patient identification from internet search queries. The code and data are available at https://github.com/sivansabato/bfa.

paragraphs: Evaluating a classifier usually requires more access than is available in this paper’s setting. There may be no validation set, or the classifier itself may be inaccessible even for queries. Instead, the available evidence consists of each subpopulation’s positive prediction rate and its true positive-label rate.

The authors show how these aggregate statistics can establish a lower bound on discrepancy, a measure combining inaccuracy and unfairness. They introduce an unfairness measure based on the fraction of the population where the classifier’s behavior differs from its globally fair behavior under equalized odds. This turns population-level information into a constraint on how favorable the classifier’s combined accuracy and fairness could be.

An efficient procedure computes the strongest discrepancy lower bound supported by the supplied aggregate statistics. Experiments demonstrate empirical tightness and illustrate applications involving voting polls and patient identification from internet searches. A lower bound identifies a minimum amount of discrepancy consistent with the evidence; it does not recover every individual prediction or fully determine the classifier’s behavior. That makes the method useful when direct evaluation is unavailable.
summary.tldr: Aggregate prediction and label rates can yield tight lower bounds on a classifier’s combined inaccuracy and unfairness without direct classifier access.

title: Bounding the fairness and accuracy of classifiers from population statistics

abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation is used in many machine learning applications where, during training, a model has access to unlabeled data in the target domain, and a related labeled dataset. In this paper, we introduce a novel and general domain-adversarial framework. Specifically, we derive a novel generalization bound for domain adaptation that exploits a new measure of discrepancy between distributions based on a variational characterization of f-divergences. It recovers the theoretical results from Ben-David et al. (2010a) as a special case and supports divergences used in practice. Based on this bound, we derive a new algorithmic framework that introduces a key correction in the original adversarial training method of Ganin et al. (2016). We show that many regularizers and ad-hoc objectives introduced over the last years in this framework are then not required to achieve performance comparable to (if not better than) state-of-the-art domain-adversarial methods. Experimental analysis conducted on real-world natural language and computer vision datasets show that our framework outperforms existing baselines, and obtains the best results for f-divergences that were not considered previously in domain-adversarial learning.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation learns from labeled source data while also using unlabeled data from a related target domain. The challenge is to make source supervision useful despite differences between the distributions. This paper introduces a domain-adversarial framework grounded in a new generalization bound that measures those differences using a variational characterization of f-divergences.

The bound includes an earlier theoretical result as a special case and supports divergences already used in practice. From it, the authors derive a corrected adversarial training framework. They show that many additional regularizers and improvised objectives used in previous approaches are unnecessary for obtaining comparable or better performance within their framework.

Experiments on natural language and computer vision datasets report improvements over existing baselines. The best results arise from f-divergences that had not previously been considered in domain-adversarial learning. The findings link a broader theoretical treatment of distribution discrepancy to useful algorithmic choices. They also suggest that revising the training objective itself can reduce the need for added components in the evaluated adaptation methods.
summary.tldr: An f-divergence generalization bound motivates corrected domain-adversarial training that improves benchmark performance without many previously added regularizers.

title: f-Domain Adversarial Learning: Theory and Algorithms

abstract: We consider the zeroth-order optimization problem in the huge-scale setting, where the dimension of the problem is so large that performing even basic vector operations on the decision variables is infeasible. In this paper, we propose a novel algorithm, coined ZO-BCD, that exhibits favorable overall query complexity and has a much smaller per-iteration computational complexity. In addition, we discuss how the memory footprint of ZO-BCD can be reduced even further by the clever use of circulant measurement matrices. As an application of our new method, we propose the idea of crafting adversarial attacks on neural network based classifiers in a wavelet domain, which can result in problem dimensions of over one million. In particular, we show that crafting adversarial examples to audio classifiers in a wavelet domain can achieve the state-of-the-art attack success rate of 97.9% with significantly less distortion.

In addition, we discuss how the memory footprint of ZO-BCD can be reduced even further by the clever use of circulant measurement matrices. paragraphs: Black-box optimization must improve an objective without directly accessing its gradients. This paper considers an especially demanding regime: the decision vector is so large that even basic operations over all its entries are infeasible. In this setting, reducing the number of objective queries alone does not resolve the computational problem.

The proposed method, ZO-BCD, uses zeroth-order block coordinate descent to obtain favorable overall query complexity alongside much lower computation per iteration. The authors also discuss reducing memory use with circulant measurement matrices. These contributions address separate practical constraints: how often the objective is queried, how much work each update requires, and how much information must be stored.

As an application, the paper constructs adversarial examples for neural classifiers in a wavelet representation, producing optimization problems with more than one million dimensions. For audio classifiers, the reported attacks reach a state-of-the-art success rate of 97.9% with significantly less distortion. This application illustrates why computationally manageable updates matter when black-box optimization operates over extremely large representations.
summary.tldr: ZO-BCD reduces per-iteration computation for enormous black-box optimization problems and supports effective wavelet-domain adversarial attacks.

title: A Zeroth-Order Block Coordinate Descent Algorithm for Huge-Scale Black-Box Optimization

abstract: Bayesian persuasion studies how an informed sender should partially disclose information to influence the behavior of a self-interested receiver. Classical models make the stringent assumption that the sender knows the receiver’s utility. This can be relaxed by considering an online learning framework in which the sender repeatedly faces a receiver of an unknown, adversarially selected type. We study, for the first time, an online Bayesian persuasion setting with multiple receivers. We focus on the case with no externalities and binary actions, as customary in offline models. Our goal is to design no-regret algorithms for the sender with polynomial per-iteration running time. First, we prove a negative result: for any 0 < $\alpha$ $\leq$ 1, there is no polynomial-time no-$\alpha$-regret algorithm when the sender’s utility function is supermodular or anonymous. Then, we focus on the setting of submodular sender’s utility functions and we show that, in this case, it is possible to design a polynomial-time no-(1-1/e)-regret algorithm. To do so, we introduce a general online gradient descent framework to handle online learning problems with a finite number of possible loss functions. This requires the existence of an approximate projection oracle. We show that, in our setting, there exists one such projection oracle which can be implemented in polynomial time.

paragraphs: Bayesian persuasion studies how an informed sender can influence self-interested receivers by selectively disclosing information. This paper moves to repeated interactions with multiple receivers whose types are unknown and selected adversarially. It considers binary actions and no externalities, and seeks learning algorithms with polynomial computation per iteration.

The results depend on the structure of the sender’s utility. For supermodular or anonymous utilities, the authors establish that polynomial-time no-alpha-regret algorithms are unavailable for any approximation factor alpha between zero and one, including one. For submodular utilities, they instead construct a polynomial-time algorithm with a no-(1-1/e)-regret guarantee. This is an approximation-based regret result, not an unqualified exact no-regret guarantee.

The construction uses a general online gradient descent framework for problems with finitely many possible loss functions. It requires an approximate projection oracle, which the authors show can be implemented in polynomial time for their setting. The paper thereby identifies both computational barriers and a utility structure that permits efficient learning.
summary.tldr: For multiple-receiver online persuasion, submodular sender utilities permit efficient approximate no-regret learning, while supermodular or anonymous utilities face impossibility results.

title: Multi-Receiver Online Bayesian Persuasion

abstract: We present a probabilistic model where the latent variable respects both the distances and the topology of the modeled data. The model leverages the Riemannian geometry of the generated manifold to endow the latent space with a well-defined stochastic distance measure, which is modeled locally as Nakagami distributions. These stochastic distances are sought to be as similar as possible to observed distances along a neighborhood graph through a censoring process. The model is inferred by variational inference based on observations of pairwise distances. We demonstrate how the new model can encode invariances in the learned manifolds.

The model is inferred by variational inference based on observations of pairwise distances. We demonstrate how the new model can encode invariances in the learned manifolds.

paragraphs: The paper develops a probabilistic latent-variable model for data described through pairwise dissimilarities. Its aim is to learn a representation that respects both observed distances and the data's topology, meaning its underlying pattern of connectivity. The representation is tied to the geometry of the manifold generated by the model.

The authors use Riemannian geometry to define a stochastic distance measure in latent space. Locally, those uncertain distances are modeled with Nakagami distributions. Through a censoring process, the model seeks agreement between these stochastic distances and observed distances along a neighborhood graph, linking geometric uncertainty to the relationships supplied by the data.

Inference uses a variational method based on pairwise distance observations. This makes the dissimilarity information central to learning the latent representation, while the neighborhood graph supplies the local relationships used for distance matching. The authors demonstrate that the resulting manifolds can encode invariances. The contribution brings distance preservation, topology, and probabilistic geometric modeling into one latent-variable framework.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic latent-variable model uses manifold geometry and uncertain distances to represent dissimilarity data while respecting topology and encoding invariances.

title: Isometric Gaussian Process Latent Variable Model for Dissimilarity Data

abstract: Production systems operating on a growing domain of analytic services often require generating warm-start solution models for emerging tasks with limited data. One potential approach to address this warm-start challenge is to adopt meta learning to generate a base model that can be adapted to solve unseen tasks with minimal fine-tuning. This however requires the training processes of previous solution models of existing tasks to be synchronized. This is not possible if these models were pre-trained separately on private data owned by different entities and cannot be synchronously re-trained. To accommodate for such scenarios, we develop a new personalized learning framework that synthesizes customized models for unseen tasks via fusion of independently pre-trained models of related tasks. We establish performance guarantee for the proposed framework and demonstrate its effectiveness on both synthetic and real datasets.

paragraphs: When a new task has little data, a useful starting model can reduce the burden of learning from scratch. Meta-learning offers one approach by training a base model for later adaptation. This paper addresses a different practical situation: relevant models already exist, but they were trained independently on private data held by separate entities.

In that situation, synchronizing and repeating the earlier training processes may be impossible. The proposed personalized learning framework instead synthesizes a model for an unseen task by fusing independently pretrained models from related tasks. It makes the existing collection of models the basis for constructing a customized starting solution.

The authors establish a performance guarantee for the framework and demonstrate its effectiveness on synthetic and real datasets. The significance is its fit to an existing, decentralized collection of trained models, where coordinated retraining is unavailable. It provides a route to warm-start personalization that draws on related task solutions while accommodating how those solutions were originally produced.
summary.tldr: Model fusion builds customized models for data-limited new tasks from related models that were pretrained independently.

title: Model Fusion for Personalized Learning

abstract: With the development of deep networks on various large-scale datasets, a large zoo of pretrained models are available. When transferring from a model zoo, applying classic single-model-based transfer learning methods to each source model suffers from high computational cost and cannot fully utilize the rich knowledge in the zoo. We propose \emph{Zoo-Tuning} to address these challenges, which learns to adaptively transfer the parameters of pretrained models to the target task. With the learnable channel alignment layer and adaptive aggregation layer, Zoo-Tuning \emph{adaptively aggregates channel aligned pretrained parameters to derive the target model}, which simultaneously promotes knowledge transfer and adapts source models to downstream tasks. The adaptive aggregation substantially reduces the computation cost at both training and inference. We further propose lite Zoo-Tuning with the temporal ensemble of batch average gating values to reduce the storage cost at the inference time. We evaluate our approach on a variety of tasks, including reinforcement learning, image classification, and facial landmark detection. Experiment results demonstrate that the proposed adaptive transfer learning approach can more effectively and efficiently transfer knowledge from a zoo of models.

paragraphs: A collection of pretrained models contains knowledge learned from different large-scale datasets. Applying ordinary transfer learning separately to every model can be expensive and does not fully combine that knowledge. Zoo-Tuning addresses this by learning how to transfer parameters from multiple source models into a model for the target task.

The method first uses a learnable channel alignment layer, then adaptively aggregates the aligned pretrained parameters. Alignment and aggregation jointly support combining source information while adapting it to the downstream problem. The authors report that this adaptive aggregation substantially reduces computation during both training and inference.

A lighter version further reduces inference storage by using a temporal ensemble of batch-average gating values. The approach is evaluated on reinforcement learning, image classification, and facial landmark detection. The reported experiments show more effective and efficient transfer from the model collection. Its contribution is to make the collection itself a source of learnable, combined parameters, rather than treating transfer as a separate exercise for each pretrained model.
summary.tldr: Zoo-Tuning aligns and adaptively combines pretrained model parameters to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of transfer learning.

title: Zoo-Tuning: Adaptive Transfer from A Zoo of Models

abstract: The Laplacian representation recently gains increasing attention for reinforcement learning as it provides succinct and informative representation for states, by taking the eigenvectors of the Laplacian matrix of the state-transition graph as state embeddings. Such representation captures the geometry of the underlying state space and is beneficial to RL tasks such as option discovery and reward shaping. To approximate the Laplacian representation in large (or even continuous) state spaces, recent works propose to minimize a spectral graph drawing objective, which however has infinitely many global minimizers other than the eigenvectors. As a result, their learned Laplacian representation may differ from the ground truth. To solve this problem, we reformulate the graph drawing objective into a generalized form and derive a new learning objective, which is proved to have eigenvectors as its unique global minimizer. It enables learning high-quality Laplacian representations that faithfully approximate the ground truth. We validate this via comprehensive experiments on a set of gridworld and continuous control environments. Moreover, we show that our learned Laplacian representations lead to more exploratory options and better reward shaping.

paragraphs: Laplacian representations describe reinforcement-learning states using eigenvectors of the state-transition graph’s Laplacian matrix. These embeddings capture the geometry of the state space and can support option discovery and reward shaping. For large or continuous spaces, learning an approximation is useful because the desired representation must be obtained without directly handling every state.

The paper identifies an ambiguity in an existing spectral graph-drawing objective: it has infinitely many global minimizers besides the intended eigenvectors. Consequently, optimizing that objective can produce a representation different from the target. The authors generalize the graph-drawing formulation and derive a new objective for which they prove that the eigenvectors form the unique global minimizer.

Experiments in gridworld and continuous-control environments validate the improved approximation of the target representation. The learned embeddings also produce more exploratory options and better reward shaping. The contribution links an objective-level guarantee to downstream usefulness: making the intended representation uniquely optimal addresses a source of ambiguity in training and improves the representations used by the evaluated reinforcement-learning methods.
summary.tldr: A generalized graph-drawing objective uniquely targets Laplacian eigenvectors and yields representations that improve exploration and reward shaping in experiments.

title: Towards Better Laplacian Representation in Reinforcement Learning with Generalized Graph Drawing

abstract: We introduce a unified framework for group equivariant networks on homogeneous spaces derived from a Fourier perspective. We consider tensor-valued feature fields, before and after a convolutional layer. We present a unified derivation of kernels via the Fourier domain by leveraging the sparsity of Fourier coefficients of the lifted feature fields. The sparsity emerges when the stabilizer subgroup of the homogeneous space is a compact Lie group. We further introduce a nonlinear activation, via an elementwise nonlinearity on the regular representation after lifting and projecting back to the field through an equivariant convolution. We show that other methods treating features as the Fourier coefficients in the stabilizer subgroup are special cases of our activation. Experiments on $SO(3)$ and $SE(3)$ show state-of-the-art performance in spherical vector field regression, point cloud classification, and molecular completion.

paragraphs: Equivariant networks are designed so that transformations of their inputs produce corresponding transformations of their features. This paper presents a unified Fourier-based framework for such networks on homogeneous spaces, considering tensor-valued feature fields before and after convolution. It addresses both convolutional kernels and nonlinear activations, two components that must fit the desired transformation behavior.

The kernel derivation uses sparsity in the Fourier coefficients of lifted feature fields. This sparsity arises when the space’s stabilizer subgroup is a compact Lie group. For nonlinear processing, the framework lifts features to the regular representation, applies an elementwise nonlinearity, and projects back through an equivariant convolution. The authors show that other activations using Fourier coefficients in the stabilizer subgroup are special cases.

Experiments involving SO(3) and SE(3) report state-of-the-art results in spherical vector-field regression, point-cloud classification, and molecular completion. These results accompany the framework’s unifying mathematical contribution. By deriving kernels and activations through a common perspective, the paper connects previously separate design choices and demonstrates their usefulness on several geometric learning tasks.
summary.tldr: A Fourier-based framework unifies equivariant convolution kernels and nonlinear activations, with strong reported results across geometric learning tasks.

title: Unified Fourier-based Kernel and Nonlinearity Design for Equivariant Networks on Homogeneous Spaces

abstract: Subgraphs of a larger global graph may be distributed across multiple devices, and only locally accessible due to privacy restrictions, although there may be links between subgraphs. Recently proposed subgraph Federated Learning (FL) methods deal with those missing links across local subgraphs while distributively training Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on them. However, they have overlooked the inevitable heterogeneity between subgraphs comprising different communities of a global graph, consequently collapsing the incompatible knowledge from local GNN models. To this end, we introduce a new subgraph FL problem, personalized subgraph FL, which focuses on the joint improvement of the interrelated local GNNs rather than learning a single global model, and propose a novel framework, FEDerated Personalized sUBgraph learning (FED-PUB), to tackle it. Since the server cannot access the subgraph in each client, FED-PUB utilizes functional embeddings of the local GNNs using random graphs as inputs to compute similarities between them, and use the similarities to perform weighted averaging for server-side aggregation. Further, it learns a personalized sparse mask at each client to select and update only the subgraph-relevant subset of the aggregated parameters. We validate our FED-PUB for its subgraph FL performance on six datasets, considering both non-overlapping and overlapping subgraphs, on which it significantly outperforms relevant baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/JinheonBaek/FED-PUB.

To this end, we introduce a new subgraph FL problem, personalized subgraph FL, which focuses on the joint improvement of the interrelated local GNNs rather than learning a single global model, and propose a novel framework, FEDerated Personalized sUBgraph learning (FED-PUB), to tackle it. Further, it learns a personalized sparse mask at each client to select and update only the subgraph-relevant subset of the aggregated parameters.
