paragraphs: When different devices hold private pieces of a larger graph, their local graph neural networks may learn from quite different communities. Combining them into a single global model can mix incompatible knowledge. This paper formulates personalized subgraph federated learning around improving the related local models together, while allowing their differences to remain meaningful.

Its FED-PUB framework estimates model similarity without giving the server access to clients’ subgraphs. It feeds random graphs into local models and uses their responses as functional embeddings. These similarities determine how the server weights models during aggregation. Each client then learns a sparse personalized mask that selects which aggregated parameters are relevant enough to update locally.

The two mechanisms address personalization at complementary stages: aggregation emphasizes similar models, and local masks select useful parts of the combined parameters. On six datasets containing both overlapping and non-overlapping subgraphs, FED-PUB significantly outperforms relevant baselines. The results support accounting for differences between graph communities alongside the missing cross-subgraph links that earlier methods had emphasized.
summary.tldr: FED-PUB personalizes federated graph learning through behavior-based model similarity and client-specific sparse parameter masks.

title: Personalized Subgraph Federated Learning

abstract: The study of collaborative multi-agent bandits has attracted significant attention recently. In light of this, we initiate the study of a new collaborative setting, consisting of $N$ agents such that each agent is learning one of $M$ stochastic multi-armed bandits to minimize their group cumulative regret. We develop decentralized algorithms which facilitate collaboration between the agents under two scenarios. We characterize the performance of these algorithms by deriving the per agent cumulative regret and group regret upper bounds. We also prove lower bounds for the group regret in this setting, which demonstrates the near-optimal behavior of the proposed algorithms.

In light of this, we initiate the study of a new collaborative setting, consisting of $N$ agents such that each agent is learning one of $M$ stochastic multi-armed bandits to minimize their group cumulative regret. We develop decentralized algorithms which facilitate collaboration between the agents under two scenarios. We characterize the performance of these algorithms by deriving the per agent cumulative regret and group regret upper bounds. We also prove lower bounds for the group regret in this setting, which demonstrates the near-optimal behavior of the proposed algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper studies collaboration among agents that are learning potentially different stochastic bandit problems. There are N agents and M bandits, with each agent assigned to one bandit. The collective objective is to reduce group cumulative regret: the total reward lost through learning decisions compared with choosing the best available actions.

The authors develop decentralized algorithms for two collaboration scenarios. Decentralization places collaboration within the agents' learning process, and the analysis tracks its consequences at two levels. Per-agent regret bounds describe the performance guarantees for individual learners, while group regret bounds describe the combined cost across the population. Both perspectives matter when the overall objective is shared but the underlying learning problems are heterogeneous.

The paper also establishes lower bounds on group regret, giving a theoretical reference for how well algorithms can perform in this setting. Comparing these limits with the proposed algorithms' upper bounds demonstrates near-optimal behavior. The resulting contribution is both a formulation of heterogeneous collaborative bandits and a set of algorithms whose collective performance is supported by matching-style theoretical evidence.
summary.tldr: Decentralized collaboration algorithms achieve near-optimal group regret when agents learn different stochastic bandit problems.

title: Collaborative Multi-Agent Heterogeneous Multi-Armed Bandits

abstract: We introduce the problem of active causal structure learning with advice. In the typical well-studied setting, the learning algorithm is given the essential graph for the observational distribution and is asked to recover the underlying causal directed acyclic graph (DAG) $G^*$ while minimizing the number of interventions made. In our setting, we are additionally given side information about $G^*$ as advice, e.g. a DAG $G$ purported to be $G^*$. We ask whether the learning algorithm can benefit from the advice when it is close to being correct, while still having worst-case guarantees even when the advice is arbitrarily bad. Our work is in the same space as the growing body of research on algorithms with predictions . When the advice is a DAG $G$, we design an adaptive search algorithm to recover $G^*$ whose intervention cost is at most $\mathcal{O}(\max\{1, \log \psi\})$ times the cost for verifying $G^*$; here, $\psi$ is a distance measure between $G$ and $G^*$ that is upper bounded by the number of variables $n$, and is exactly 0 when $G=G^*$. Our approximation factor matches the state-of-the-art for the advice-less setting.

paragraphs: Observational data can leave several causal graphs consistent with the same evidence. Active causal discovery uses interventions to resolve that ambiguity. This paper studies a setting where the learner also receives advice about the true causal graph, such as a proposed directed acyclic graph, and must decide how to benefit from it without relying on its correctness.

The authors design an adaptive search algorithm whose intervention cost depends on how far the advised graph is from the true graph. Its cost is bounded relative to the cost of verifying the true graph. The approximation factor grows logarithmically with a defined distance measure, with a constant floor; that distance is zero for correct advice and never exceeds the number of variables.

This dependence makes the guarantee responsive to advice quality while retaining protection against arbitrarily poor advice. In the worst case, the approximation factor matches the best stated result for learning without advice. The contribution is therefore a way to incorporate a proposed causal structure into intervention planning with a guarantee that remains meaningful when the proposal is unreliable.
summary.tldr: An adaptive causal discovery algorithm uses accurate graph advice to improve its intervention guarantee while retaining worst-case protection against bad advice.

title: Active causal structure learning with advice

abstract: Deep ensembles (DE) have been successful in improving model performance by learning diverse members via the stochasticity of random initialization. While recent works have attempted to promote further diversity in DE via hyperparameters or regularizing loss functions, these methods primarily still rely on a stochastic approach to explore the hypothesis space. In this work, we present Multi-Symmetry Ensembles (MSE), a framework for constructing diverse ensembles by capturing the multiplicity of hypotheses along symmetry axes, which explore the hypothesis space beyond stochastic perturbations of model weights and hyperparameters. We leverage recent advances in contrastive representation learning to create models that separately capture opposing hypotheses of invariant and equivariant functional classes and present a simple ensembling approach to efficiently combine appropriate hypotheses for a given task. We show that MSE effectively captures the multiplicity of conflicting hypotheses that is often required in large, diverse datasets like ImageNet. As a result of their inherent diversity, MSE improves classification performance, uncertainty quantification, and generalization across a series of transfer tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/clott3/multi-sym-ensem

paragraphs: Deep ensembles combine multiple models whose differences often come from random initialization. Other approaches encourage diversity through hyperparameters or loss regularization, but still largely explore alternatives stochastically. This paper introduces Multi-Symmetry Ensembles, which construct diversity around different assumptions about how predictions should respond to transformations.

The framework uses contrastive representation learning to build models belonging to opposing invariant and equivariant functional classes. Invariant hypotheses preserve outputs under the relevant transformations, while equivariant hypotheses allow outputs to change in a corresponding way. A simple ensemble procedure combines hypotheses appropriate to the task, making these differing responses an explicit source of model diversity.

The authors show that the framework captures conflicting hypotheses needed in large, varied datasets such as ImageNet. They report improvements in classification, uncertainty quantification, and generalization across transfer tasks. The significance is that useful ensemble diversity can come from structured differences in learned behavior, extending the exploration of possible solutions beyond random changes to weights and hyperparameters. The reported benefits concern the evaluated tasks and transfers.
summary.tldr: Multi-Symmetry Ensembles combine opposing transformation behaviors to improve ensemble diversity, classification, uncertainty estimates, and transfer.

title: Multi-Symmetry Ensembles: Improving Diversity and Generalization via Opposing Symmetries

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) so far has limited real-world applications. One key challenge is that typical RL algorithms heavily rely on a reset mechanism to sample proper initial states; these reset mechanisms, in practice, are expensive to implement due to the need for human intervention or heavily engineered environments. To make learning more practical, we propose a generic no-regret reduction to systematically design reset-free RL algorithms. Our reduction turns the reset-free RL problem into a two-player game. We show that achieving sublinear regret in this two-player game would imply learning a policy that has both sublinear performance regret and sublinear total number of resets in the original RL problem. This means that the agent eventually learns to perform optimally and avoid resets. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this reduction, we design an instantiation for linear Markov decision processes, which is the first provably correct reset-free RL algorithm.

paragraphs: Many reinforcement learning algorithms assume that the environment can repeatedly be reset to suitable starting states. In practical systems, providing those resets may require human intervention or substantial engineering. This paper develops a general way to design algorithms that learn good behavior while reducing their dependence on resets over time.

The proposed reduction transforms the original learning problem into a two-player game. The authors show that sublinear regret in this game implies both sublinear performance regret and a sublinear total number of resets in the original problem. The guarantee is conditional on achieving the required game regret. Sublinear reset growth means resets become less frequent relative to the amount of learning.

To demonstrate the reduction, the authors construct an algorithm for linear Markov decision processes and present it as the first provably correct reset-free reinforcement learning algorithm. The result gives a concrete setting in which performance improvement and diminishing reset dependence can be guaranteed together. Here, reset-free learning permits resets during learning while controlling their cumulative growth.
summary.tldr: A two-player-game reduction yields conditional guarantees for learning good policies while making resets increasingly infrequent.

title: Provable Reset-free Reinforcement Learning by No-Regret Reduction

abstract: In this paper, we consider the problem of the high computational complexity of video-based facial expression recognition. A novel sequential procedure is proposed with an adaptive frame rate selection in a short video fragment to speed up decision-making. We automatically adjust the frame rate and process fewer frames with a low frame rate for more straightforward videos and more frames for complex ones. To determine the frame rate at which an inference is sufficiently reliable, the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure from multiple comparisons theory is employed to control the false discovery rate. The main advantages of our method are an improvement of the trustworthiness of decision-making by maintaining only one hyper-parameter (false acceptance rate) and its applicability with arbitrary neural network models used as facial feature extractors without the need to re-train these models. An experimental study on datasets from ABAW and EmotiW challenges proves the superior performance (1.5-40 times faster) of the proposed approach compared to processing all frames and existing techniques with early exiting and adaptive frame selection.

paragraphs: Video-based facial expression recognition can be expensive when a model processes every frame. This paper proposes a sequential procedure that adjusts how many frames it examines within a short video fragment. Straightforward videos receive a lower processing frame rate, while more complex videos receive a higher one.

The central question is when the available frames provide sufficiently reliable evidence for a decision. The method uses the Benjamini-Hochberg multiple-testing procedure to control the false discovery rate when making this assessment. It maintains a single false-acceptance-rate hyperparameter, giving the adaptive selection process an explicit statistical criterion rather than relying only on a fixed frame budget.

The procedure can work with arbitrary neural networks used to extract facial features without retraining those networks. This makes frame selection an addition to an existing recognition system. Experiments on ABAW and EmotiW challenge datasets report speedups of 1.5 to 40 times relative to the evaluated full-frame, early-exit, and adaptive-selection techniques, showing the computational benefit of allocating more processing to difficult clips.
summary.tldr: Statistically guided frame selection speeds up facial expression recognition by processing fewer frames in easier videos.

title: Facial Expression Recognition with Adaptive Frame Rate based on Multiple Testing Correction

abstract: Heterogeneity and comorbidity are two interwoven challenges associated with various healthcare problems that greatly hampered research on developing effective treatment and understanding of the underlying neurobiological mechanism. Very few studies have been conducted to investigate heterogeneous causal effects (HCEs) in graphical contexts due to the lack of statistical methods. To characterize this heterogeneity, we first conceptualize heterogeneous causal graphs (HCGs) by generalizing the causal graphical model with confounder-based interactions and multiple mediators. Such confounders with an interaction with the treatment are known as moderators. This allows us to flexibly produce HCGs given different moderators and explicitly characterize HCEs from the treatment or potential mediators on the outcome. We establish the theoretical forms of HCEs and derive their properties at the individual level in both linear and nonlinear models. An interactive structural learning is developed to estimate the complex HCGs and HCEs with confidence intervals provided. Our method is empirically justified by extensive simulations and its practical usefulness is illustrated by exploring causality among psychiatric disorders for trauma survivors. Code implementing the proposed algorithm is open-source and publicly available at: https://github.com/richard-watson/ISL.

paragraphs: Treatment effects can differ between individuals, and multiple interacting conditions make those differences difficult to study. This paper develops a graphical framework for representing heterogeneous causal effects. Its motivation includes healthcare problems where both variation among people and the coexistence of disorders complicate causal analysis.

The framework extends causal graphs with multiple mediators and interactions between treatment and confounders. Confounders participating in those interactions act as moderators, allowing the represented effects to vary with their values. The authors derive individual-level forms and properties of heterogeneous effects in both linear and nonlinear models, covering effects from treatment or potential mediators to an outcome.

An interactive structural learning method estimates the graphs and effects and supplies confidence intervals. Extensive simulations support the method empirically, and an application explores causal relationships among psychiatric disorders in trauma survivors. The contribution combines a representation of effect variation, theoretical characterization, and an estimation procedure, allowing heterogeneity to be studied explicitly within a causal graph rather than only through a single overall treatment effect.
summary.tldr: The paper develops causal graphs and estimation methods that represent individual differences in treatment and mediator effects through moderators and multiple mediators.

title: On Heterogeneous Treatment Effects in Heterogeneous Causal Graphs

abstract: In this paper, we consider the problem of Iterative Machine Teaching (IMT), where the teacher provides examples to the learner iteratively such that the learner can achieve fast convergence to a target model. However, existing IMT algorithms are solely based on parameterized families of target models. They mainly focus on convergence in the parameter space, resulting in difficulty when the target models are defined to be functions without dependency on parameters. To address such a limitation, we study a more general task – Nonparametric Iterative Machine Teaching (NIMT), which aims to teach nonparametric target models to learners in an iterative fashion. Unlike parametric IMT that merely operates in the parameter space, we cast NIMT as a functional optimization problem in the function space. To solve it, we propose both random and greedy functional teaching algorithms. We obtain the iterative teaching dimension (ITD) of the random teaching algorithm under proper assumptions, which serves as a uniform upper bound of ITD in NIMT. Further, the greedy teaching algorithm has a significantly lower ITD, which reaches a tighter upper bound of ITD in NIMT. Finally, we verify the correctness of our theoretical findings with extensive experiments in nonparametric scenarios.

paragraphs: Iterative machine teaching studies how a teacher can supply examples over time to help a learner reach a target model quickly. Existing approaches focus on parameterized model families and measure progress in parameter space. That focus becomes awkward when the desired target is specified directly as a function rather than through a parameter vector.

This paper formulates nonparametric iterative machine teaching as optimization in function space. It proposes both random and greedy functional teaching algorithms. The change of viewpoint allows the teaching objective to concern the function the learner should acquire, extending the setting beyond the parameter-based formulation used by earlier methods.

The theory analyzes iterative teaching dimension, a measure of the teaching effort required. Under appropriate assumptions, the random algorithm gives a uniform upper bound for the nonparametric setting. The greedy algorithm has a significantly lower teaching dimension and yields a tighter bound. Experiments in nonparametric scenarios support the theoretical findings, linking the broader formulation to a measurable advantage from choosing teaching examples greedily.
summary.tldr: A function-space formulation extends iterative machine teaching to nonparametric targets and gives greedy teaching tighter effort bounds than random teaching.

title: Nonparametric Iterative Machine Teaching

abstract: Mixup, a simple data augmentation method that randomly mixes two data points via linear interpolation, has been extensively applied in various deep learning applications to gain better generalization. However, its theoretical explanation remains largely unclear. In this work, we aim to seek a fundamental understanding of the benefits of Mixup. We first show that Mixup using different linear interpolation parameters for features and labels can still achieve similar performance as standard Mixup. This indicates that the intuitive linearity explanation in Zhang et al., (2018) may not fully explain the success of Mixup. Then, we perform a theoretical study of Mixup from the feature learning perspective. We consider a feature-noise data model and show that Mixup training can effectively learn the rare features (appearing in a small fraction of data) from its mixture with the common features (appearing in a large fraction of data). In contrast, standard training can only learn the common features but fails to learn the rare features, thus suffering from bad generalization performance. Moreover, our theoretical analysis also shows that the benefits of Mixup for feature learning are mostly gained in the early training phase, based on which we propose to apply early stopping in Mixup. Experimental results verify our theoretical findings and demonstrate the effectiveness of the early-stopped Mixup training.

paragraphs: Mixup creates training examples by interpolating between pairs of data points and their labels. A common explanation for its success emphasizes matching linear behavior between inputs and labels. This paper finds that using different interpolation parameters for features and labels can still produce similar performance, suggesting that this explanation does not fully account for Mixup’s benefits.

The authors study an alternative explanation through a feature-noise data model. Within that model, Mixup can learn features that appear rarely by mixing them with features that occur frequently. Standard training learns the common features but misses the rare ones, leading to poor generalization in the analyzed setting. The result ties the benefit to what the model learns from the data.

The analysis further indicates that most of these feature-learning benefits arise early in training. This motivates an early-stopped version of Mixup. Experiments support the theoretical findings and the effectiveness of that approach. The paper therefore offers both a conditional account of why mixing helps and a training modification derived from the timing of those benefits.
summary.tldr: Under a feature-noise model, Mixup helps learn rare features, with most benefits arising early enough to motivate early stopping.

title: The Benefits of Mixup for Feature Learning

abstract: Selective labels occur when label observations are subject to a decision-making process; e.g., diagnoses that depend on the administration of laboratory tests. We study a clinically-inspired selective label problem called disparate censorship, where labeling biases vary across subgroups and unlabeled individuals are imputed as “negative” (i.e., no diagnostic test = no illness). Machine learning models naively trained on such labels could amplify labeling bias. Inspired by causal models of selective labels, we propose Disparate Censorship Expectation-Maximization (DCEM), an algorithm for learning in the presence of disparate censorship. We theoretically analyze how DCEM mitigates the effects of disparate censorship on model performance. We validate DCEM on synthetic data, showing that it improves bias mitigation (area between ROC curves) without sacrificing discriminative performance (AUC) compared to baselines. We achieve similar results in a sepsis classification task using clinical data.

paragraphs: A diagnosis can enter a dataset only after someone decides to order a test. If untested people are then recorded as disease-free, the labels mix health status with testing decisions. This paper studies disparate censorship, where that labeling process differs across subgroups. Training directly on these labels can amplify the bias already present in who receives testing.

The authors propose Disparate Censorship Expectation-Maximization, or DCEM, to learn under this specific form of biased observation. The algorithm is motivated by causal models of selective labels. Its purpose is to account for the decision process behind observed labels rather than treating every recorded negative as equally informative about the underlying outcome.

The paper theoretically analyzes how DCEM mitigates effects on model performance. On synthetic data, it reduces bias measured by the area between ROC curves while maintaining discriminative performance measured by AUC relative to baselines. A clinical sepsis-classification task produces similar results. These findings support addressing unequal label observation without necessarily sacrificing the model’s ability to distinguish outcomes.
summary.tldr: DCEM addresses subgroup-dependent missing labels, reducing measured bias without sacrificing discrimination in synthetic and clinical sepsis experiments.

title: From Biased Selective Labels to Pseudo-Labels: An Expectation-Maximization Framework for Learning from Biased Decisions

abstract: Graph clustering is a central topic in unsupervised learning with a multitude of practical applications. In recent years, multi-view graph clustering has gained a lot of attention for its applicability to real-world instances where one often has access to multiple data sources. In this paper we formalize a new family of models, called multi-view stochastic block models that capture this setting. For this model, we first study efficient algorithms that naively work on the union of multiple graphs. Then, we introduce a new efficient algorithm that provably outperforms previous approaches by analyzing the structure of each graph separately. Finally, we complement our results with an information-theoretic lower bound studying the limits of what can be done in this model.

paragraphs: Graph clustering often has access to several data sources, each providing a different graph view. The paper formalizes this situation through a family of multi-view stochastic block models. This supplies a mathematical setting for studying how multiple graphs can contribute to recovering community structure and what algorithms can achieve from the available information.

The authors first analyze efficient methods that combine the graphs by taking their union. They then introduce an efficient algorithm that examines each graph’s structure separately. Under the proposed model, this algorithm provably outperforms earlier approaches. The result establishes a benefit from retaining information about individual views during analysis.

The paper also gives an information-theoretic lower bound, addressing limits imposed by the model rather than just the speed or design of a particular algorithm. This complements the positive algorithmic result with a statement about what is achievable at all. Together, the model, algorithm, and lower bound provide a theoretical basis for understanding the value and limits of multiple graph sources.
summary.tldr: A new multi-view graph model supports an efficient clustering algorithm that provably benefits from analyzing graph views separately.

title: Multi-View Stochastic Block Models

abstract: Deep learning with differential privacy (DP) has garnered significant attention over the past years, leading to the development of numerous methods aimed at enhancing model accuracy and training efficiency. This paper delves into the problem of training Transformer models with differential privacy. Our treatment is modular: the logic is to ’reduce’ the problem of training DP Transformer to the more basic problem of training DP vanilla neural nets. The latter is better understood and amenable to many model-agnostic methods. Such ’reduction’ is done by first identifying the hardness unique to DP Transformer training: the attention distraction phenomenon and a lack of compatibility with existing techniques for efficient gradient clipping. To deal with these two issues, we propose the Re-Attention Mechanism and Phantom Clipping, respectively. We believe that our work not only casts new light on training DP Transformers but also promotes a modular treatment to advance research in the field of differentially private deep learning.

paragraphs: Training Transformers with differential privacy presents obstacles beyond those encountered in ordinary neural networks. This paper takes a modular approach: address the difficulties specific to Transformers so that methods developed for more basic private neural-network training become applicable. The goal is to connect Transformer training to an existing body of model-agnostic techniques.

The authors identify two particular difficulties. One is an attention distraction phenomenon, which concerns the attention mechanism in private Transformer training. The other is incompatibility with existing methods for efficient gradient clipping. These are treated as distinct problems, allowing the proposed solutions to target separate parts of the training process.

The paper introduces Re-Attention to address attention distraction and Phantom Clipping to address the clipping issue. Its contribution is an approach to organizing private Transformer training around these specific obstacles and their corresponding remedies. The authors argue that this modular treatment can also help advance differentially private deep learning by making progress on general neural-network methods easier to carry over to Transformers.
summary.tldr: Re-Attention and Phantom Clipping address two Transformer-specific obstacles to applying general differentially private training methods.

title: Delving into Differentially Private Transformer

abstract: We model real-world data markets, where sellers post fixed prices and buyers are free to purchase from any set of sellers, as a simultaneous game. A key component here is the negative externality buyers induce on one another due to data purchases. Starting with a simple setting where buyers know their valuations a priori, we characterize both the existence and welfare properties of the pure Nash equilibrium in the presence of such externality. While the outcomes are bleak without any intervention, mirroring the limitations of current data markets, we prove that for a standard class of externality functions, platforms intervening through a transaction cost can lead to a pure equilibrium with strong welfare guarantees. We next consider a more realistic setting where buyers learn their valuations over time through market interactions. Our intervention is feasible here as well, and we consider learning algorithms to achieve low regret concerning both individual and cumulative utility metrics. Lastly, we analyze the promises of this intervention under a much richer externality model.

paragraphs: Buying data can affect more than the buyer’s own payoff: one buyer’s purchase may reduce another buyer’s utility. This paper studies data markets with such negative externalities. Sellers post fixed prices, buyers choose any set of sellers to purchase from, and the market is modeled as a simultaneous game.

The authors first assume that buyers already know their valuations. They analyze whether pure Nash equilibria exist and how much welfare those equilibria deliver. Outcomes without intervention are unfavorable, but the paper proves that a platform-imposed transaction cost can produce a pure equilibrium with strong welfare guarantees for a standard class of externality functions.

The study then allows buyers to learn their valuations through repeated market interactions. The intervention remains feasible in that setting, and the authors consider learning algorithms with low regret for both individual and cumulative utility measures. They also examine a richer externality model. The central contribution is a conditional case for transaction costs as a market-design tool, with guarantees tied to the externality structure being analyzed.
summary.tldr: Platform transaction costs can support stable, high-welfare data markets under specified negative-externality models, including when buyers learn their valuations.

title: Equilibrium of Data Markets with Externality

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) is crucial for real-world applications where exploration can be costly or unsafe. However, offline learned policies are often suboptimal, and further online fine-tuning is required. In this paper, we tackle the fundamental dilemma of offline-to-online fine-tuning: if the agent remains pessimistic, it may fail to learn a better policy, while if it becomes optimistic directly, performance may suffer from a sudden drop. We show that Bayesian design principles are crucial in solving such a dilemma. Instead of adopting optimistic or pessimistic policies, the agent should act in a way that matches its belief in optimal policies. Such a probability-matching agent can avoid a sudden performance drop while still being guaranteed to find the optimal policy. Based on our theoretical findings, we introduce a novel algorithm that outperforms existing methods on various benchmarks, demonstrating the efficacy of our approach. Overall, the proposed approach provides a new perspective on offline-to-online RL that has the potential to enable more effective learning from offline data.

paragraphs: An agent trained on previously collected data may still need further interaction to improve its policy. That transition creates a dilemma: continued pessimism can prevent useful exploration, while an abrupt move toward optimism can cause performance to fall. This paper studies how to make the transition from offline learning to online fine-tuning more effective.

The proposed design principle is probability matching. The agent chooses behavior in accordance with its beliefs about which policies are optimal. This makes uncertainty about good policies part of the decision rule, instead of committing to a uniformly optimistic or pessimistic approach. The theoretical analysis shows that such an agent can avoid a sudden performance drop while retaining a guarantee of finding the optimal policy.

The authors translate these findings into an algorithm and report that it outperforms existing methods on several benchmarks. The contribution connects a Bayesian principle for choosing actions with the practical problem of improving an offline policy. Its stated results combine theoretical support for the transition strategy with empirical evidence for the resulting algorithm.
summary.tldr: Matching behavior to beliefs about optimal policies offers a theoretically supported way to improve offline policies through online interaction without an abrupt performance drop.

title: Bayesian Design Principles for Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Sparse Neural Networks (SNNs) have received voluminous attention for mitigating the explosion in computational costs and memory footprints of modern deep neural networks. Despite their popularity, most state-of-the-art training approaches seek to find a single high-quality sparse subnetwork with a preset sparsity pattern and ratio, making them inadequate to satiate platform and resource variability. Recently proposed approaches attempt to jointly train multiple subnetworks (we term as “sparse co-training") with a fixed sparsity pattern, to allow switching sparsity ratios subject to resource requirements. In this work, we take one more step forward and expand the scope of sparse co-training to cover diverse sparsity patterns and multiple sparsity ratios at once. We introduce Sparse Cocktail, the first sparse co-training framework that co-trains a suite of sparsity patterns simultaneously, loaded with multiple sparsity ratios which facilitate harmonious switch across various sparsity patterns and ratios at inference depending on the hardware availability. More specifically, Sparse Cocktail alternatively trains subnetworks generated from different sparsity patterns with a gradual increase in sparsity ratios across patterns and relies on an unified mask generation process and the Dense Pivot Co-training to ensure the subnetworks of different patterns orchestrate their shared parameters without canceling each other’s performance. Experiment results on image classification, object detection, and instance segmentation illustrate the favorable effectiveness and flexibility of Sparse Cocktail, pointing to a promising direction for sparse co-training. Codes will be released.

paragraphs: Sparse neural networks reduce computational and memory demands, but many training methods produce only one subnetwork with a fixed sparsity pattern and ratio. That restricts adaptation to different hardware or resource budgets. Sparse Cocktail broadens joint subnetwork training to include multiple patterns and multiple ratios within the same framework.

The method alternates training among subnetworks with different sparsity patterns while gradually increasing sparsity ratios across patterns. A unified mask-generation process and Dense Pivot Co-training coordinate the parameters shared by those subnetworks. These components are intended to prevent training for one pattern from canceling the performance of another pattern that uses overlapping parameters.

At inference, the trained collection supports switching between sparsity patterns and ratios according to available hardware. Experiments on image classification, object detection, and instance segmentation illustrate the framework's effectiveness and flexibility. The contribution expands the range of deployment choices supported by sparse co-training: resource adaptation can involve both how much of the network is retained and the structural pattern of what remains.
summary.tldr: Sparse Cocktail jointly trains subnetworks with multiple sparsity patterns and ratios so deployment can adapt to available hardware.

title: Sparse Cocktail: Every Sparse Pattern Every Sparse Ratio All At Once

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have exhibited prominent performance in learning graph-structured data. Considering node classification task, based on the i.i.d assumption among node labels, the traditional supervised learning simply sums up cross-entropy losses of the independent training nodes and applies the average loss to optimize GNNs’ weights. But different from other data formats, the nodes are naturally connected. It is found that the independent distribution modeling of node labels restricts GNNs’ capability to generalize over the entire graph and defend adversarial attacks. In this work, we propose a new framework, termed joint-cluster supervised learning, to model the joint distribution of each node with its corresponding cluster. We learn the joint distribution of node and cluster labels conditioned on their representations, and train GNNs with the obtained joint loss. In this way, the data-label reference signals extracted from the local cluster explicitly strengthen the discrimination ability on the target node. The extensive experiments demonstrate that our joint-cluster supervised learning can effectively bolster GNNs’ node classification accuracy. Furthermore, being benefited from the reference signals which may be free from spiteful interference, our learning paradigm significantly protects the node classification from being affected by the adversarial attack.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks classify nodes using connected data, yet their training objectives commonly sum losses that treat node labels independently. The paper argues that this mismatch restricts generalization and resistance to adversarial attacks. It proposes changing the supervision objective so that a node's label is learned together with information from its local cluster.

The resulting framework, joint-cluster supervised learning, models the joint distribution of node and cluster labels conditioned on their representations. It trains the network using the associated joint loss. This gives the target node explicit reference signals from its surrounding cluster, strengthening the information used to distinguish its class.

Experiments show improved node-classification accuracy and substantial protection against the evaluated adversarial attacks. The proposed explanation is that cluster reference signals may remain unaffected when malicious interference targets other information used for classification. That qualification matters: the framework benefits from potentially cleaner contextual signals. Its contribution is therefore a way to incorporate graph relationships directly into supervision, with reported gains in both prediction accuracy and robustness.
summary.tldr: Joint-cluster supervision trains graph networks on node and cluster labels together, improving reported classification accuracy and adversarial robustness.

title: Rethinking Independent Cross-Entropy Loss For Graph-Structured Data

abstract: Distribution matching methods for language model alignment such as Generation with Distributional Control (GDC) and Distributional Policy Gradient (DPG) have not received the same level of attention in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) as contrastive methods such as Sequence Likelihood Calibration (SLiC), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and its variants. We identify high variance of the gradient estimate as the primary reason for the lack of success of these methods and propose a self-normalized baseline to reduce the variance. We further generalize the target distribution in DPG, GDC and DPO by using Bayes’ rule to define the reward-conditioned posterior. The resulting approach, referred to as BRAIn - Bayesian Reward-conditioned Amortized Inference acts as a bridge between distribution matching methods and DPO and significantly outperforms prior art in summarization and Antropic HH tasks.

paragraphs: Language model alignment can be approached by training a model to match a desired distribution of responses. The paper examines why these distribution matching approaches have received less attention and achieved less success than contrastive methods such as Direct Preference Optimization. It identifies high variance in gradient estimates as the primary obstacle.

The authors introduce a self-normalized baseline to reduce that variance, making the estimated training signal less variable. They also broaden how the target response distribution is defined. Using Bayes' rule, they construct a posterior conditioned on reward, giving the alignment objective an explicit probabilistic interpretation tied to the feedback signal.

The resulting method, BRAIn, connects distribution matching approaches with DPO through this reward-conditioned formulation. The authors report significant improvements over prior methods on summarization and Anthropic HH tasks. The contribution combines a practical change to gradient estimation with a more general target distribution, showing that revisiting both can make distribution matching more competitive for language generation from feedback.
summary.tldr: BRAIn combines lower-variance training with a Bayesian reward-conditioned target distribution to improve language model alignment on the reported tasks.

title: BRAIn: Bayesian Reward-conditioned Amortized Inference for natural language generation from feedback

abstract: What makes large language models (LLMs) impressive is also what makes them hard to evaluate: their diversity of uses. To evaluate these models, we must understand the purposes they will be used for. We consider a setting where these deployment decisions are made by people, and in particular, people’s beliefs about where an LLM will perform well. We model such beliefs as the consequence of a human generalization function: having seen what an LLM gets right or wrong, people generalize to where else it might succeed. We collect a dataset of 19K examples of how humans make generalizations across 79 tasks from the MMLU and BIG-Bench benchmarks. We show that the human generalization function can be predicted using NLP methods: people have consistent structured ways to generalize. We then evaluate LLM alignment with the human generalization function. Our results show that – especially for cases where the cost of mistakes is high – more capable models (e.g. GPT-4) can do worse on the instances people choose to use them for, exactly because they are not aligned with the human generalization function.

paragraphs: People decide when to use a language model partly by extrapolating from its previous successes and failures. A good answer on one task may encourage them to trust it on another. This paper studies that extrapolation as a human generalization function, connecting model evaluation to the beliefs that shape actual deployment decisions.

The authors collect 19,000 examples of human generalizations across 79 tasks from MMLU and BIG-Bench. They find that NLP methods can predict these judgments, suggesting that people's expectations follow consistent patterns. They then evaluate how well language model performance aligns with those expectations, rather than considering capability independently of the tasks people choose to delegate.

The results show that more capable models, including GPT-4, can perform worse on the instances people select for them when performance does not align with human generalization. This issue is especially pronounced when mistakes are costly. The finding makes user expectations part of the evaluation problem: broader capability alone does not guarantee better outcomes under human-directed use.
summary.tldr: More capable language models can fare worse on human-selected tasks when their abilities diverge from users' expectations.

title: Do Large Language Models Perform the Way People Expect? Measuring the Human Generalization Function

abstract: Sample labeling is the most primary and fundamental step of semi-supervised learning. In literature, most existing methods randomly label samples with a given ratio, but achieve unpromising and unstable results due to the randomness, especially in multi-view settings. To address this issue, we propose a Dynamic Multi-view Labeling Strategy with Shared and Specific Information. To be brief, by building two classifiers with existing labels to utilize decoupled shared and specific information, we select the samples of low classification confidence and label them in high priorities. The newly generated labels are also integrated to update the classifiers adaptively. The two processes are executed alternatively until a satisfying classification performance. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed method, we conduct extensive experiments on popular benchmarks, achieving promising performance. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/wanxinhang/ICML2024_decouple_then_classify.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning depends partly on which examples receive labels. Randomly labeling a fixed proportion can produce disappointing or unstable results, especially when each example has multiple views. This paper focuses on making that selection responsive to what the current classifiers find uncertain, rather than leaving the initial allocation of labels entirely to chance.

The method separates information shared across views from information specific to individual views. It builds two classifiers using existing labels and these decoupled sources of information. Examples classified with low confidence receive higher priority for labeling. Newly obtained labels then update the classifiers, allowing the next round of selection to reflect what has already been learned.

Selection and classifier updating alternate until classification performance is satisfactory. The approach therefore links the labeling process to an evolving model instead of treating labeling as a single preliminary step. Experiments on established benchmarks produce promising performance. The stated findings support combining shared and view-specific information to guide label acquisition, while the abstract does not claim a universal performance guarantee for this iterative strategy.
summary.tldr: An adaptive labeling strategy separates shared and view-specific information, prioritizes uncertain examples, and updates its classifiers as labels arrive.

title: Decouple then Classify: A Dynamic Multi-view Labeling Strategy with Shared and Specific Information

abstract: Recent LLM-driven visual agents mainly focus on solving image-based tasks, which limits their ability to understand dynamic scenes, making it far from real-life applications like guiding students in laboratory experiments and identifying their mistakes. Hence, this paper explores DoraemonGPT, a comprehensive and conceptually elegant system driven by LLMs to understand dynamic scenes. Considering the video modality better reflects the ever-changing nature of real-world scenarios, we exemplify DoraemonGPT as a video agent. Given a video with a question/task, DoraemonGPT begins by converting the input video into a symbolic memory that stores task-related attributes. This structured representation allows for spatial-temporal querying and reasoning by well-designed sub-task tools, resulting in concise intermediate results. Recognizing that LLMs have limited internal knowledge when it comes to specialized domains (e.g., analyzing the scientific principles underlying experiments), we incorporate plug-and-play tools to assess external knowledge and address tasks across different domains. Moreover, a novel LLM-driven planner based on Monte Carlo Tree Search is introduced to explore the large planning space for scheduling various tools. The planner iteratively finds feasible solutions by backpropagating the result’s reward, and multiple solutions can be summarized into an improved final answer. We extensively evaluate DoraemonGPT’s effectiveness on three benchmarks and several in-the-wild scenarios. Project page: https://z-x-yang.github.io/doraemon-gpt.

paragraphs: DoraemonGPT is an LLM-driven system for understanding scenes that change over time, demonstrated as a video agent. Given a video and a question or task, it first converts relevant video information into a symbolic memory. This structured representation stores attributes that can support reasoning about both spatial relationships and temporal changes.

Specialized tools query that memory and return concise intermediate results. Additional plug-and-play tools provide access to external knowledge when a task requires expertise beyond the language model’s internal knowledge. The system therefore combines information extracted from the video with tools that help interpret what that information means for a particular task.

An LLM-driven planner uses Monte Carlo Tree Search to explore possible sequences of tool use. It feeds rewards from results back through the search to find feasible solutions, and can combine multiple solutions into an improved final answer. Evaluation covers three benchmarks and several in-the-wild scenarios. The contribution is an integrated approach to video representation, knowledge access, and tool planning for dynamic-scene understanding.
summary.tldr: DoraemonGPT combines structured video memory, external tools, and tree-search planning to answer questions about dynamic scenes.

title: DoraemonGPT: Toward Understanding Dynamic Scenes with Large Language Models (Exemplified as A Video Agent)

abstract: We propose a novel model-based reinforcement learning algorithm—Dynamics Learning and predictive control with Parameterized Actions (DLPA)—for Parameterized Action Markov Decision Processes (PAMDPs). The agent learns a parameterized-action-conditioned dynamics model and plans with a modified Model Predictive Path Integral control. We theoretically quantify the difference between the generated trajectory and the optimal trajectory during planning in terms of the value they achieved through the lens of Lipschitz Continuity. Our empirical results on several standard benchmarks show that our algorithm achieves superior sample efficiency and asymptotic performance than state-of-the-art PAMDP methods.

The agent learns a parameterized-action-conditioned dynamics model and plans with a modified Model Predictive Path Integral control. We theoretically quantify the difference between the generated trajectory and the optimal trajectory during planning in terms of the value they achieved through the lens of Lipschitz Continuity. Our empirical results on several standard benchmarks show that our algorithm achieves superior sample efficiency and asymptotic performance than state-of-the-art PAMDP methods.

paragraphs: Parameterized-action reinforcement learning involves choosing actions together with the parameters that specify them. This paper introduces Dynamics Learning and predictive control with Parameterized Actions, or DLPA, for that setting. Its central approach is to learn how the environment responds to parameterized actions and use that learned dynamics model when planning.

The agent conditions its dynamics model on the parameterized action, then plans using a modified form of Model Predictive Path Integral control. Learning and planning therefore have complementary roles: the model represents predicted environment behavior, while the controller uses predictions to choose actions. This makes the parameterized action structure part of both the predictive model and the planning procedure.

The authors also analyze the value difference between a generated trajectory and an optimal trajectory through Lipschitz continuity. This provides a theoretical account of planning quality in terms of achieved value. On several standard benchmarks, DLPA delivers better sample efficiency and asymptotic performance than the compared state-of-the-art parameterized-action methods, supporting the proposed model-based approach.
summary.tldr: DLPA learns parameterized-action dynamics and plans with predictive control, improving sample efficiency and final performance on evaluated benchmarks.

title: Model-based Reinforcement Learning for Parameterized Action Spaces

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning policies, which are integral to modern control systems, represent valuable intellectual property. The development of these policies demands considerable resources, such as domain expertise, simulation fidelity, and real-world validation. These policies are potentially vulnerable to model stealing attacks, which aim to replicate their functionality using only black-box access. In this paper, we propose Stealthy Imitation, the first attack designed to steal policies without access to the environment or knowledge of the input range. This setup has not been considered by previous model stealing methods. Lacking access to the victim’s input states distribution, Stealthy Imitation fits a reward model that allows to approximate it. We show that the victim policy is harder to imitate when the distribution of the attack queries matches that of the victim. We evaluate our approach across diverse, high-dimensional control tasks and consistently outperform prior data-free approaches adapted for policy stealing. Lastly, we propose a countermeasure that significantly diminishes the effectiveness of the attack.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning policies can embody expensive simulation, expertise, and real-world validation. This paper examines whether their behavior can be copied through black-box access under unusually restricted conditions. Stealthy Imitation is presented as the first policy-stealing attack that requires neither access to the environment nor knowledge of the input range.

Without access to the states normally encountered by the target policy, the method fits a reward model to approximate the missing input-state distribution. The authors also report a counterintuitive finding: the victim becomes harder to imitate when the attack-query distribution matches the victim's distribution. This makes the relationship between query selection and successful imitation an important part of the study.

Across diverse high-dimensional control tasks, Stealthy Imitation consistently outperforms earlier data-free approaches adapted to policy stealing. The paper also proposes a countermeasure that substantially reduces the attack's effectiveness. Together, the results identify a policy-copying threat under limited attacker knowledge and demonstrate that its success can be meaningfully reduced by a defense in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: Stealthy Imitation copies control policies without environment access or known input ranges, while a proposed defense substantially reduces its effectiveness.

title: Stealthy Imitation: Reward-guided Environment-free Policy Stealing

abstract: Transformer-based Large Language Models rely critically on the KV cache to efficiently handle extended contexts during the decode phase. Yet, the size of the KV cache grows proportionally with the input length, burdening both memory bandwidth and capacity as decoding progresses. To address this challenge, we present RocketKV, a training-free KV cache compression strategy containing two consecutive stages. In the first stage, it performs coarse-grain permanent KV cache eviction on the input sequence tokens. In the second stage, it adopts a hybrid sparse attention method to conduct fine-grain top-k sparse attention, approximating the attention scores by leveraging both head and sequence dimensionality reductions. We show that RocketKV provides a compression ratio of up to 400$\times$, end-to-end speedup of up to 3.7$\times$ as well as peak memory reduction of up to 32.6% in the decode phase on an NVIDIA A100 GPU compared to the full KV cache baseline, while achieving negligible accuracy loss on a variety of long-context tasks. We also propose a variant of RocketKV for multi-turn scenarios, which consistently outperforms other existing methods and achieves accuracy nearly on par with an oracle top-k attention scheme. The source code is available here: https://github.com/NVlabs/RocketKV.

paragraphs: Long-context transformers retain a key-value cache so they can reuse information during decoding. That cache grows with input length, increasing memory capacity and bandwidth demands. RocketKV addresses these costs through a training-free compression method that combines permanent cache reduction with finer selection during attention.

The first stage evicts cached information for input tokens at a coarse level. The second stage applies hybrid sparse attention, selecting a top-k set using approximate attention scores. Those approximations reduce both head and sequence dimensions. The two stages therefore address different parts of the problem: how much information remains cached and how much of it attention uses.

Compared with a full-cache baseline on an NVIDIA A100, the paper reports up to 400-fold compression, up to 3.7-fold end-to-end speedup, and up to 32.6% lower peak memory during decoding, with negligible accuracy loss across varied long-context tasks. These are reported maxima. A multi-turn variant also consistently outperforms the compared methods and approaches oracle top-k attention accuracy, supporting the approach’s usefulness beyond a single interaction.
summary.tldr: RocketKV combines cache eviction and sparse attention to accelerate long-context inference with negligible accuracy loss in the reported evaluations.

title: RocketKV: Accelerating Long-Context LLM Inference via Two-Stage KV Cache Compression

abstract: Bayesian optimization is a widely used method for optimizing expensive black-box functions, with Expected Improvement being one of the most commonly used acquisition functions. In contrast, information-theoretic acquisition functions aim to reduce uncertainty about the function’s optimum and are often considered fundamentally distinct from EI. In this work, we challenge this prevailing perspective by introducing a unified theoretical framework, Variational Entropy Search, which reveals that EI and information-theoretic acquisition functions are more closely related than previously recognized. We demonstrate that EI can be interpreted as a variational inference approximation of the popular information-theoretic acquisition function, named Max-value Entropy Search. Building on this insight, we propose VES-Gamma, a novel acquisition function that balances the strengths of EI and MES. Extensive empirical evaluations across both low- and high-dimensional synthetic and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that VES-Gamma is competitive with state-of-the-art acquisition functions and in many cases outperforms EI and MES.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization chooses which expensive function evaluation to perform next. Expected Improvement favors evaluations with promising potential to improve the best result, while information-based methods seek to reduce uncertainty about the optimum. These objectives are often treated as fundamentally different ways to guide the search.

The paper introduces Variational Entropy Search, a theoretical framework that connects these approaches. It shows that Expected Improvement can be understood as a variational inference approximation to Max-value Entropy Search. This interpretation makes the relationship mathematically explicit: a familiar improvement-based rule can arise as an approximation within an information-based formulation.

The authors use this connection to develop VES-Gamma, an acquisition function intended to combine strengths of both methods. Evaluations cover synthetic and real-world benchmarks in low and high dimensions. VES-Gamma is competitive with state-of-the-art acquisition functions and often outperforms Expected Improvement and Max-value Entropy Search. The contribution therefore includes both a reinterpretation of existing methods and an empirically useful search rule derived from that reinterpretation.
summary.tldr: Variational Entropy Search connects Expected Improvement to information-based Bayesian optimization and yields a competitive acquisition function.

title: A Unified Framework for Entropy Search and Expected Improvement in Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Diffusion models generate high-quality synthetic data. They operate by defining a continuous-time forward process which gradually adds Gaussian noise to data until fully corrupted. The corresponding reverse process progressively “denoises" a Gaussian sample into a sample from the data distribution. However, generating high-quality outputs requires many discretization steps to obtain a faithful approximation of the reverse process. This is expensive and has motivated the development of many acceleration methods. We propose to speed up sample generation by learning the posterior distribution of clean data samples given their noisy versions, instead of only the mean of this distribution. This allows us to sample from the probability transitions of the reverse process on a coarse time scale, significantly accelerating inference with minimal degradation of the quality of the output. This is accomplished by replacing the standard regression loss used to estimate conditional means with a scoring rule. We validate our method on image and robot trajectory generation, where we consistently outperform standard diffusion models at few discretization steps.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate samples by reversing a process that gradually adds Gaussian noise to data. Accurately following that reverse process usually requires many small steps, making generation expensive. This paper changes what the model learns so that it can take larger steps while retaining useful information about possible clean outputs.

Instead of predicting only the average clean sample associated with a noisy input, the method learns the full conditional distribution of clean samples. The authors replace the usual regression objective with a scoring rule, allowing training to target a distribution rather than just its mean. That distribution supports sampling the reverse process’s transitions over a coarser time scale.

The approach is evaluated on image generation and robot trajectory generation. With few discretization steps, it consistently outperforms standard diffusion models in the reported experiments. The authors describe substantial acceleration with minimal output-quality degradation. The central finding is that learning uncertainty over clean samples can make larger reverse-process steps more useful, reducing the need for many fine-grained denoising updates.
summary.tldr: Learning distributions of clean samples instead of conditional means enables faster diffusion generation with strong results at few sampling steps.

title: Distributional Diffusion Models with Scoring Rules

abstract: Graph State Space Models (SSMs) have recently been introduced to enhance Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in modeling long-range interactions. Despite their success, existing methods either compromise on permutation equivariance or limit their focus to pairwise interactions rather than sequences. Building on the connection between Autoregressive Moving Average (ARMA) and SSM, in this paper, we introduce GRAMA, a Graph Adaptive method based on a learnable ARMA framework that addresses these limitations. By transforming from static to sequential graph data, GRAMA leverages the strengths of the ARMA framework, while preserving permutation equivariance. Moreover, GRAMA incorporates a selective attention mechanism for dynamic learning of ARMA coefficients, enabling efficient and flexible long-range information propagation. We also establish theoretical connections between GRAMA and Selective SSMs, providing insights into its ability to capture long-range dependencies. Experiments on 26 synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that GRAMA consistently outperforms backbone models and performs competitively with state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks need ways to connect information from distant parts of a graph. Graph state space models offer one route, but the paper identifies two shortcomings in existing approaches: some lose consistency under node relabeling, while others emphasize pairs of nodes rather than sequences. GRAMA addresses these issues through a learnable autoregressive moving average framework.

The method transforms static graph data into a sequential form so it can use the strengths of ARMA modeling. It preserves permutation equivariance: relabeling nodes produces the corresponding relabeling of outputs. A selective attention mechanism dynamically learns the ARMA coefficients, allowing long-range information propagation to adapt rather than relying entirely on fixed coefficients.

The authors establish theoretical connections between GRAMA and selective state space models to explain its ability to capture distant dependencies. Across 26 synthetic and real-world datasets, GRAMA consistently improves over the backbone models and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods. The findings support combining sequence modeling with the structural consistency required for graph data.
summary.tldr: GRAMA uses adaptive ARMA sequence modeling to capture long-range graph dependencies while preserving permutation equivariance.

title: Graph Adaptive Autoregressive Moving Average Models

abstract: We propose FACTER, a fairness-aware framework for LLM-based recommendation systems that integrates conformal prediction with dynamic prompt engineering. By introducing an adaptive semantic variance threshold and a violation-triggered mechanism, FACTER automatically tightens fairness constraints whenever biased patterns emerge. We further develop an adversarial prompt generator that leverages historical violations to reduce repeated demographic biases without retraining the LLM. Empirical results on MovieLens and Amazon show that FACTER substantially reduces fairness violations (up to 95.5%) while maintaining strong recommendation accuracy, revealing semantic variance as a potent proxy of bias.

paragraphs: FACTER addresses demographic bias in recommendation systems powered by large language models. Its approach combines conformal prediction with prompts that change in response to fairness problems. This creates a mechanism for adjusting recommendation behavior without retraining the underlying language model, making the treatment of observed violations part of the recommendation process.

The framework uses an adaptive threshold on semantic variance as a signal of biased patterns. When a violation is detected, a dedicated mechanism tightens the fairness constraints. An adversarial prompt generator also draws on the history of violations to reduce recurrence of demographic biases. The approach therefore combines a response to current problems with prompt changes informed by previously observed failures.

Experiments on MovieLens and Amazon report reductions in fairness violations of up to 95.5% while maintaining strong recommendation accuracy. That figure describes the largest reported reduction, rather than a uniform outcome across settings. The results support semantic variance as a useful proxy for bias in these evaluations and show how dynamic prompting can improve measured fairness without requiring model retraining.
summary.tldr: FACTER dynamically adjusts fairness thresholds and prompts, reducing recommendation fairness violations by up to 95.5% without retraining the LLM.

title: FACTER: Fairness-Aware Conformal Thresholding and Prompt Engineering for Enabling Fair LLM-Based Recommender Systems

abstract: Graphics rendering applications increasingly leverage neural networks in tasks such as denoising, supersampling, and frame extrapolation to improve image quality while maintaining frame rates. The temporal coherence inherent in these tasks presents an opportunity to reuse intermediate results from previous frames and avoid redundant computations. Recent work has shown that caching intermediate features to be reused in subsequent inferences is an effective method to reduce latency in diffusion models. We extend this idea to real-time rendering and present ReFrame, which explores different caching policies to optimize trade-offs between quality and performance in rendering workloads. ReFrame can be applied to a variety of encoder-decoder style networks commonly found in rendering pipelines. Experimental results show that we achieve 1.4$\times$ speedup on average with negligible quality loss in three real-time rendering tasks. Code available: https://ubc-aamodt-group.github.io/reframe-layer-caching/

paragraphs: Real-time rendering increasingly uses neural networks to improve images through denoising, supersampling, and frame extrapolation. These workloads must balance visual quality with tight frame-time requirements. Because consecutive frames share information, some intermediate neural computations can potentially be reused instead of repeated for every frame.

ReFrame applies layer caching to this setting, extending an idea previously shown useful for diffusion-model inference. It investigates different caching policies to manage the trade-off between reusing intermediate features and preserving output quality. The approach applies to a variety of encoder-decoder networks commonly used in rendering pipelines, making the caching decision relevant across several rendering workloads.

Across three real-time rendering tasks, the experiments report an average 1.4-fold speedup with negligible quality loss. The result indicates that temporal coherence can provide computational savings inside the neural network itself. Its practical significance lies in using similarities between successive frames to reduce inference latency while retaining the image quality expected from the underlying rendering task.
summary.tldr: ReFrame reuses intermediate neural features across rendered frames, achieving an average 1.4-fold speedup with negligible quality loss in three tasks.

title: ReFrame: Layer Caching for Accelerated Inference in Real-Time Rendering

abstract: Visual prompting techniques are widely used to efficiently fine-tune pretrained Vision Transformers (ViT) by learning a small set of shared prompts for all tokens. However, existing methods overlook the unique roles of different tokens in conveying discriminative information and interact with all tokens using the same prompts, thereby limiting the representational capacity of ViT. This often leads to indistinguishable and biased prompt-extracted features, hindering performance. To address this issue, we propose a plug-and-play Token Coordinated Prompt Attention (TCPA) module, which assigns specific coordinated prompts to different tokens for attention-based interactions. Firstly, recognizing the distinct functions of CLS and image tokens-global information aggregation and local feature extraction, we disentangle the prompts into CLS Prompts and Image Prompts, which interact exclusively with CLS tokens and image tokens through attention mechanisms. This enhances their respective discriminative abilities. Furthermore, as different image tokens correspond to distinct image patches and contain diverse information, we employ a matching function to automatically assign coordinated prompts to individual tokens. This enables more precise attention interactions, improving the diversity and representational capacity of the extracted features. Extensive experiments across various benchmarks demonstrate that TCPA significantly enhances the diversity and discriminative power of the extracted features.

paragraphs: Visual prompting adapts a pretrained Vision Transformer by learning a small set of prompts. This paper argues that sharing the same prompts across all tokens ignores their different roles and can yield features that are hard to distinguish or biased. Token Coordinated Prompt Attention addresses this by tailoring prompt interactions to the tokens they serve.

The module first separates prompts for the CLS token, which aggregates global information, from prompts for image tokens, which extract local features. Each group interacts exclusively with its corresponding token type. Because individual image tokens represent different patches, a matching function then assigns coordinated prompts to particular tokens. This adds specificity both between token roles and among local image regions.

Experiments across several benchmarks report substantial improvements in feature diversity and discriminative power. The findings support a more selective use of a small prompt set: adaptation depends on matching prompts to distinct informational roles. As a plug-and-play module, TCPA is intended to add that coordination to visual prompting rather than require an entirely new pretrained backbone.
summary.tldr: TCPA assigns prompts according to global and local token roles, improving the diversity and discriminative power of visual-prompting features.

title: Token Coordinated Prompt Attention is Needed for Visual Prompting

abstract: Achieving high-fidelity audio compression while preserving perceptual quality across diverse audio types remains a significant challenge in Neural Audio Coding (NAC). This paper introduces MUFFIN, a fully convolutional NAC framework that leverages psychoacoustically guided multi-band frequency reconstruction. Central to MUFFIN is the Multi-Band Spectral Residual Vector Quantization (MBS-RVQ) mechanism, which quantizes latent speech across different frequency bands. This approach optimizes bitrate allocation and enhances fidelity based on psychoacoustic studies, achieving efficient compression with unique perceptual features that separate content from speaker attributes through distinct codebooks. MUFFIN integrates a transformer-inspired convolutional architecture with proposed modified snake activation functions to capture fine frequency details with greater precision. Extensive evaluations on diverse datasets (LibriTTS, IEMOCAP, GTZAN, BBC) demonstrate MUFFIN’s ability to consistently surpass existing performance in audio reconstruction across various domains. Notably, a high-compression variant achieves an impressive SOTA 12.5 kHz rate while preserving reconstruction quality. Furthermore, MUFFIN excels in downstream generative tasks, demonstrating its potential as a robust token representation for integration with large language models. These results establish MUFFIN as a groundbreaking advancement in NAC and as the first neural psychoacoustic coding system. Speech demos and codes are available at https://demos46.github.io/muffin/ and https://github.com/dianwen-ng/MUFFIN.

paragraphs: MUFFIN is a neural audio-compression framework designed to preserve perceptual quality across different kinds of sound. Its approach uses psychoacoustic guidance to reconstruct multiple frequency bands, making the allocation of compressed information sensitive to how sound is perceived. The goal is efficient compression that retains the details important to listening quality.

The central mechanism quantizes latent speech representations across frequency bands using multi-band spectral residual vector quantization. Separate codebooks distinguish content from speaker attributes, while band-specific processing supports bitrate allocation. A fully convolutional architecture, inspired by transformers and equipped with modified snake activation functions, aims to capture fine frequency details more precisely.

Evaluations on LibriTTS, IEMOCAP, GTZAN, and BBC report consistently stronger reconstruction performance across the tested domains. The authors also report a high-compression variant that preserves reconstruction quality and strong results on downstream generative tasks. These findings suggest that MUFFIN’s compressed representations may be useful both for audio reconstruction and as tokens for integration with large language models.
summary.tldr: MUFFIN uses perceptually guided frequency-band compression to improve audio reconstruction and provide useful representations for generative tasks.

title: Multi-band Frequency Reconstruction for Neural Psychoacoustic Coding

abstract: We present SWE-Gym, the first environment for training real-world software engineering (SWE) agents. SWE-Gym contains 2,438 real-world Python task instances, each comprising a codebase with an executable runtime environment, unit tests, and a task specified in natural language. We use SWE-Gym to train language model based SWE agents, achieving up to 19% absolute gains in resolve rate on the popular SWE-Bench Verified and Lite test sets. We also experiment with inference-time scaling through verifiers trained on agent trajectories sampled from SWE-Gym. When combined with our fine-tuned SWE agents, we achieve 32.0% and 26.0% on SWE-Bench Verified and Lite, respectively, reflecting a new state-of-the-art for open-weight SWE agents. To facilitate further research, we publicly release SWE-Gym, models, and agent trajectories.
