They also report a favorable balance between accuracy and linear computational efficiency. The result supports explicitly representing light-field geometry inside an efficient backbone, so scalability does not depend solely on generic feature mixing.
summary.tldr: E²I-VRWKV adds explicit geometric guidance to an efficient light-field segmentation network, reaching 86.55% mIoU on UrbanLF-Real.

title: E$^2$I-VRWKV: Explicit EPI-Representation and Interaction-Aware Vision-RWKV for Light Field Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Existing embodied control research demonstrates remarkable performance improvements by scaling training data and model size. We instead explore inference-time strategy as an alternative axis. Non-deterministic generative models, such as diffusion and autoregressive models, have been widely adopted in the field of embodied control. However, the single-shot inference paradigm limits their performance. In this paper, we propose TapSampling, a plug-and-play framework for inference-time sampling. First, we introduce an Action-VAE that represents actions in a low-dimensional latent space by mapping policy-generated initial actions into a compressed posterior distribution, from which any number of latent samples can be drawn and decoded into candidate actions that approximate the true action distribution. Second, we formulate action verification as task-progress outcome prediction, using the intrinsic sequential structure of robotic datasets to train a semantically grounded verifier for interpretable action selection. Furthermore, TapSampling is a policy-agnostic framework. Extensive experiments in both simulated and real-world environments demonstrate that our method substantially improves multiple generalist policies without further policy finetuning. Code and models are available at the project page (https://aipixel.github.io/TapSampling/).

paragraphs: Generative robot policies can produce different plausible actions, but single-shot inference commits to just one output. TapSampling explores improving control by spending additional computation when selecting an action. Its plug-and-play framework generates multiple candidates and evaluates them according to predicted progress toward the task.

An Action-VAE maps policy-generated initial actions into a compressed posterior distribution in a low-dimensional latent space. Samples from that distribution are decoded into candidate actions that approximate the true action distribution. A separate verifier predicts task-progress outcomes, using the sequential structure of robotic datasets for training. This grounds action selection in an interpretable notion of progress.

The framework is policy-agnostic, and experiments in simulation and real-world environments show substantial improvements for multiple generalist policies without further policy fine-tuning. The finding demonstrates an additional route to better control beyond increasing policy size or training data. A policy's initial output becomes the basis for candidate exploration, while the verifier helps choose among the resulting possibilities.
summary.tldr: TapSampling improves robotic policies at inference time by sampling candidate actions and selecting them with a task-progress verifier.

abstract: Query by Committee is an effective approach to selective sampling in which disagreement amongst an ensemble of hypotheses is used to select data for labeling. Query by Bagging and Query by Boosting are two practical implementations of this approach that use Bagging and Boosting, respectively, to build the committees. For effective active learning, it is critical that the committee be made up of consistent hypotheses that are very different from each other. Decorate is a recently developed method that directly constructs such diverse committees using artificial training data. This paper introduces Active-Decorate, which uses Decorate committees to select good training examples. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that, in general, Active-Decorate outperforms both Query by Bagging and Query by Boosting.

Query by Bagging and Query by Boosting are two practical implementations of this approach that use Bagging and Boosting, respectively, to build the committees. For effective active learning, it is critical that the committee be made up of consistent hypotheses that are very different from each other. Decorate is a recently developed method that directly constructs such diverse committees using artificial training data. This paper introduces Active-Decorate, which uses Decorate committees to select good training examples. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that, in general, Active-Decorate outperforms both Query by Bagging and Query by Boosting.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which examples to send for labeling. In Query by Committee, several candidate models make predictions, and disagreement among them guides that choice. The paper emphasizes that useful committees need hypotheses that remain consistent with the training evidence while differing substantially from one another. Without meaningful differences, committee disagreement provides less guidance.

The proposed method, Active-Decorate, builds its committee using Decorate, a method that explicitly encourages diversity through artificial training data. Active-Decorate then uses that committee to select training examples. Its contribution connects a particular way of constructing diverse models to the selective sampling process, making committee construction central to which labels are requested.

The experiments compare this approach with Query by Bagging and Query by Boosting, which build committees using their respective ensemble methods. Extensive results show that Active-Decorate generally performs better than both. This is an empirical comparative finding, with the qualification that the advantage holds in general rather than universally. The results support deliberately promoting committee diversity for active learning.
summary.tldr: Active-Decorate uses deliberately diverse committees to choose examples for labeling and generally outperforms Query by Bagging and Query by Boosting.

title: Diverse ensembles for active learning

abstract: In dimensionality reduction approaches, the data are typically embedded in a Euclidean latent space. However for some data sets this is inappropriate. For example, in human motion data we expect latent spaces that are cylindrical or a toroidal, that are poorly captured with a Euclidean space. In this paper, we present a range of approaches for embedding data in a non-Euclidean latent space. Our focus is the Gaussian Process latent variable model. In the context of human motion modeling this allows us to (a) learn models with interpretable latent directions enabling, for example, style/content separation, and (b) generalize beyond the data set enabling us to learn transitions between motion styles even though such transitions are not present in the data.
originalAbstract: In dimensionality reduction approaches, the data are typically embedded in a Euclidean latent space. However for some data sets this is inappropriate. For example, in human motion data we expect latent spaces that are cylindrical or a toroidal, that are poorly captured with a Euclidean space. In this paper, we present a range of approaches for embedding data in a non-Euclidean latent space. Our focus is the Gaussian Process latent variable model. In the context of human motion modeling this allows us to (a) learn models with interpretable latent directions enabling, for example, style/content separation, and (b) generalize beyond the data set enabling us to learn transitions between motion styles even though such transitions are not present in the data.

paragraphs: Dimensionality reduction commonly places data in a Euclidean latent space. The paper argues that this geometry is inappropriate for some datasets. Human motion provides the motivating example: its latent structure may be better represented by a cylinder or torus, shapes that an ordinary Euclidean latent space captures poorly.

The authors present several approaches for embedding data into non-Euclidean latent spaces, focusing on the Gaussian Process latent variable model. The choice of latent-space structure is part of the model design. It determines the kind of representation available for organizing motion data and for interpreting directions of variation within that representation.

In human motion modeling, the resulting models have interpretable latent directions that can support separating style from content. They also generalize beyond the dataset by learning transitions between motion styles even when those transitions are absent from the data. The stated significance is both interpretability and this particular form of generalization, enabled by using latent spaces better suited to the motion structure.
summary.tldr: Non-Euclidean latent spaces support interpretable human-motion models and transitions between styles absent from the training data.

title: Topologically-constrained latent variable models

abstract: We introduce a new approach to non-linear regression called function factorization, that is suitable for problems where an output variable can reasonably be modeled by a number of multiplicative interaction terms between non-linear functions of the inputs. The idea is to approximate a complicated function on a high-dimensional space by the sum of products of simpler functions on lower-dimensional subspaces. Function factorization can be seen as a generalization of matrix and tensor factorization methods, in which the data are approximated by the sum of outer products of vectors. We present a non-parametric Bayesian approach to function factorization where the priors over the factorizing functions are warped Gaussian processes, and we do inference using Hamiltonian Markov chain Monte Carlo. We demonstrate the superior predictive performance of the method on a food science data set compared to Gaussian process regression and tensor factorization using PARAFAC and GEMANOVA models.
originalAbstract: We introduce a new approach to non-linear regression called function factorization, that is suitable for problems where an output variable can reasonably be modeled by a number of multiplicative interaction terms between non-linear functions of the inputs. The idea is to approximate a complicated function on a high-dimensional space by the sum of products of simpler functions on lower-dimensional subspaces. Function factorization can be seen as a generalization of matrix and tensor factorization methods, in which the data are approximated by the sum of outer products of vectors. We present a non-parametric Bayesian approach to function factorization where the priors over the factorizing functions are warped Gaussian processes, and we do inference using Hamiltonian Markov chain Monte Carlo. We demonstrate the superior predictive performance of the method on a food science data set compared to Gaussian process regression and tensor factorization using PARAFAC and GEMANOVA models.

paragraphs: Function factorization tackles nonlinear regression when an output can reasonably be described through multiplicative interactions between simpler functions of the inputs. It approximates a complicated function over many dimensions with a sum of products, where each factor operates on a lower-dimensional part of the input. The approach builds the overall prediction from simpler interacting components.

This construction extends the idea behind matrix and tensor factorization. Those methods approximate data using sums of outer products of vectors; here, the components are functions. The authors develop a nonparametric Bayesian formulation, placing warped Gaussian process priors over the factor functions and using Hamiltonian Markov chain Monte Carlo for inference.

On a food science dataset, the method predicts better than Gaussian process regression and the PARAFAC and GEMANOVA tensor factorization models. This provides empirical support for the approach in that application. Its motivation depends on the suitability of multiplicative interactions: the factorization is designed for problems where such a decomposition is a reasonable model of the output.
summary.tldr: Function factorization uses products of simpler Bayesian functions to model nonlinear interactions, improving predictions on a food science dataset.

title: Function factorization using warped Gaussian processes

abstract: We present a probabilistic model for clustering of objects represented via pair wise dissimilarities. We propose that even if an underlying vectorial representation exists, it is better to work directly with the dissimilarity matrix hence avoiding unnecessary bias and variance caused by embeddings.By using a Dirichlet process prior we are not obliged to fix the number of clusters in advance. Furthermore, our clustering model is permutation-, scale- and translation-invariant, and it is called the Translation-invariant Wishart Dirichlet(TIWD) process. A highly efficient MCMC sampling algorithm is presented. Experiments show that the TIWD process exhibits several advantages over competing approaches.

We propose that even if an underlying vectorial representation exists, it is better to work directly with the dissimilarity matrix hence avoiding unnecessary bias and variance caused by embeddings.By using a Dirichlet process prior we are not obliged to fix the number of clusters in advance. Furthermore, our clustering model is permutation-, scale- and translation-invariant, and it is called the Translation-invariant Wishart Dirichlet(TIWD) process. paragraphs: This paper develops a probabilistic clustering model for objects represented by pairwise dissimilarities. The authors advocate working directly with that matrix even when a vector representation exists. Their motivation is to avoid unnecessary bias and variance that can arise from first embedding the objects into another representation.

The proposed Translation-invariant Wishart-Dirichlet process uses a Dirichlet process prior, so the number of clusters does not have to be fixed in advance. The model is also invariant to permutation, scale, and translation. These properties define how its clustering formulation responds to changes in ordering and representation, making them part of the model's design rather than additional preprocessing choices.

The authors present an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling algorithm for inference. Experiments show several advantages over competing approaches, supporting the proposed combination of direct dissimilarity modeling and flexible cluster counts. The stated findings make a case for this probabilistic treatment of distance data; the preference for avoiding embeddings is presented as the authors' modeling argument.
summary.tldr: The TIWD process clusters dissimilarity data directly, with no fixed cluster count and permutation, scale, and translation invariance.

title: The Translation-invariant Wishart-Dirichlet Process for Clustering Distance Data

abstract: We introduce Probabilistic Matrix Addition (PMA) for modeling real-valued data matrices by simultaneously capturing covariance structure among rows and among columns. PMA additively combines two latent matrices drawn from two Gaussian Processes respectively over rows and columns. The resulting joint distribution over the observed matrix does not factorize over entries, rows, or columns, and can thus capture intricate dependencies in the matrix. Exact inference in PMA is possible, but involves inversion of large matrices, and can be computationally prohibitive. Efficient approximate inference is possible due to the sparse dependency structure among latent variables. We propose two families of approximate inference algorithms for PMA based on Gibbs sampling and MAP inference. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PMA for missing value prediction and multi-label classification problems.
originalAbstract: We introduce Probabilistic Matrix Addition (PMA) for modeling real-valued data matrices by simultaneously capturing covariance structure among rows and among columns. PMA additively combines two latent matrices drawn from two Gaussian Processes respectively over rows and columns. The resulting joint distribution over the observed matrix does not factorize over entries, rows, or columns, and can thus capture intricate dependencies in the matrix. Exact inference in PMA is possible, but involves inversion of large matrices, and can be computationally prohibitive. Efficient approximate inference is possible due to the sparse dependency structure among latent variables. We propose two families of approximate inference algorithms for PMA based on Gibbs sampling and MAP inference. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PMA for missing value prediction and multi-label classification problems.

paragraphs: Probabilistic Matrix Addition models real-valued matrices while capturing covariance among both rows and columns. It adds two latent matrices, one drawn from a Gaussian process over rows and the other from a Gaussian process over columns. This construction brings both types of relationships into the same probabilistic model.

The resulting distribution does not split into independent pieces at the entry, row, or column level, allowing it to express intricate matrix dependencies. Exact inference is possible, but it requires large matrix inversions that can make computation prohibitive. The paper therefore distinguishes the model’s representational capacity from the cost of directly performing inference.

To make inference more practical, the authors exploit sparse dependencies among the latent variables. They propose two families of approximate algorithms, based respectively on Gibbs sampling and maximum a posteriori inference. Applications to missing-value prediction and multi-label classification demonstrate effectiveness. The contribution combines a joint row-and-column dependency model with computational approaches designed to make that model usable.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic Matrix Addition combines row and column Gaussian-process structure, with approximate inference for prediction and classification tasks.

title: Probabilistic Matrix Addition

abstract: We present a novel probabilistic rating system for team competitions. Building upon TrueSkill(tm), we change the factor graph structure to cope with the problems of TrueSkill(tm), e.g., multiway ties and variable team size. We give detailed inference algorithms for the new structure. Experimental results show a significant improvement over TrueSkill(tm).
originalAbstract: We present a novel probabilistic rating system for team competitions. Building upon TrueSkill(tm), we change the factor graph structure to cope with the problems of TrueSkill(tm), e.g., multiway ties and variable team size. We give detailed inference algorithms for the new structure. Experimental results show a significant improvement over TrueSkill(tm).

paragraphs: Rating teams requires a model that can interpret competition outcomes when the participating groups have different sizes or several teams finish tied. This paper introduces a probabilistic rating system built on TrueSkill, targeting these situations as problems that the existing system needs to handle more effectively.

The central change is to the factor graph structure. A factor graph expresses how the quantities in a probabilistic model relate to one another, so changing its structure changes how competition results inform ratings. The authors also provide detailed inference algorithms for the revised structure, explaining how to carry out the calculations required by the new system.

The reported experiments show a significant improvement over TrueSkill. This supports the proposed combination of a revised model structure and corresponding inference procedures for team competitions. The contribution is therefore both a new way to organize the rating problem and algorithms for using that organization, with multiway ties and variable team sizes motivating the redesign.
summary.tldr: A revised TrueSkill-based probabilistic model improves team ratings while addressing multiway ties and variable team sizes.

title: A New Bayesian Rating System for Team Competitions
